Other Bath instruments include BASFI (functional index), BASMI (metrology index for mobility), and BASRI (radiographic index). DAS28 is used for RA, HAQ assesses functional disability in various conditions, and SLEDAI measures lupus activity.

D118.q: A 38-year-old woman with fibromyalgia also reports chronic fatigue, cognitive difficulties ('fibro fog'), and depression. These comorbid conditions are present in what percentage of fibromyalgia patients?
D118.rationale: 80-90% of fibromyalgia patients have significant comorbid conditions including chronic fatigue, cognitive dysfunction, depression, anxiety, irritable bowel syndrome, and sleep disorders (especially non-restorative sleep). This overlap suggests shared pathophysiology involving central sensitization and dysregulation of pain processing. 'Fibro fog' (cognitive dysfunction) includes problems with memory, attention, and processing speed. Depression and anxiety are particularly common (>50% prevalence) and should be actively screened for and treated as they worsen pain and functional outcomes. Comprehensive management must address these comorbidities through combination of pharmacotherapy (SNRIs, pregabalin), CBT, sleep hygiene, and graded exercise. Treating comorbid depression often improves pain symptoms.

D118.q: A 26-year-old woman presents with photosensitive rash, arthritis, and pleuritic chest pain. Labs show positive ANA 1:640 (speckled pattern). Which additional antibody is most specific for SLE diagnosis?
D118.rationale: Anti-dsDNA antibodies are highly specific (>95%) for SLE though only present in 50-70% of patients. High titers correlate with disease activity, especially lupus nephritis. According to 2019 EULAR/ACR classification criteria, anti-dsDNA and anti-Smith antibodies receive the highest weighting (6 points each) due to specificity. ANA is sensitive (>95%) but not specific (positive in 5-15% of healthy individuals and many other conditions). Anti-histone is associated with drug-induced lupus. Anti-Ro/SSA is present in 30-40% of SLE patients but also in Sjögren's and is associated with neonatal lupus/congenital heart block. Anti-centromere is specific for limited systemic sclerosis (CREST). Anti-Smith is specific but less sensitive than anti-dsDNA.

D118.q: A 55-year-old woman with Sjögren's syndrome complains of difficulty eating and multiple dental caries. Which complication of xerostomia (dry mouth) should you counsel her about?
a: Periodontal disease and dental caries are markedly increased
Oral complications are rare in Sjögren\'s
Candidiasis is the only significant oral complication
Tooth loss is uncommon if hygiene is maintained
D118.rationale: Xerostomia in Sjögren's leads to dramatically increased risk of dental caries (especially cervical caries), periodontal disease, oral candidiasis, and tooth loss due to loss of saliva's protective, antimicrobial, and buffering functions. Patients require aggressive preventive dental care including: fluoride supplements, frequent dental visits (every 3-4 months), excellent oral hygiene, sugar-free gum/candies to stimulate saliva, saliva substitutes, and consideration of pilocarpine (5 mg TID) or cevimeline to stimulate salivary flow. Untreated xerostomia can lead to severe dental destruction. Patients should avoid anticholinergic medications, tobacco, and alcohol which worsen dryness. Regular oral exams are essential as Sjögren's increases risk of oral lymphoma.

D118.q: A 45-year-old woman presents with skin thickening limited to fingers, face, and distal extremities (not extending proximal to elbows/knees), along with calcinosis, Raynaud's, esophageal dysmotility, and telangiectasias. What is the classification of her scleroderma?
D118.rationale: Limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis (lcSSc), previously called CREST syndrome (Calcinosis, Raynaud's, Esophageal dysmotility, Sclerodactyly, Telangiectasias), is characterized by skin thickening limited to distal extremities (below elbows/knees) and face. It has slower progression and better prognosis than diffuse disease but carries higher risk of pulmonary arterial hypertension and primary biliary cholangitis. Anti-centromere antibodies are present in 50-70%. Diffuse cutaneous SSc involves trunk and proximal extremities with rapid progression and risk of renal crisis and ILD. Localized scleroderma (morphea, linear) affects only skin without systemic involvement. Sine scleroderma has systemic features without skin thickening. Classification guides prognosis and screening protocols.

D118.q: A 78-year-old woman with suspected GCA has been on prednisone 60 mg for 5 days. Temporal artery biopsy is scheduled. How does corticosteroid therapy affect biopsy results?
a: Biopsy becomes negative after 24 hours of steroids
Histologic changes persist for 1-2 weeks despite steroids
Steroids must be stopped for 1 week before biopsy
Biopsy is not useful if steroids have been started
D118.rationale: Temporal artery biopsy can show diagnostic histologic changes (transmural inflammation, giant cells, intimal proliferation, fragmented internal elastic lamina) for up to 2 weeks after starting corticosteroids. Therefore, high-dose steroids should be started immediately when GCA is suspected (to prevent blindness), and biopsy can be performed within 1-2 weeks without significantly affecting diagnostic yield. Delaying steroids to obtain biopsy first risks irreversible vision loss. A negative biopsy doesn't exclude GCA due to 'skip lesions'; bilateral biopsies increase sensitivity. Alternative imaging (temporal artery ultrasound showing halo sign, or PET-CT/MRA showing vessel wall inflammation) may be used if biopsy is not feasible. Clinical diagnosis with elevated inflammatory markers may suffice in some cases.

D118.q: A 70-year-old man with PMR was started on prednisone 15 mg daily with excellent response. After 4 weeks, he is pain-free with normalized ESR. What is the appropriate next step in management?
a: Continue current dose for 6 months then stop
Begin slow taper (e.g., 2.5 mg every 2-4 weeks) over 12-18 months
D118.rationale: ACR/EULAR guidelines recommend gradual corticosteroid taper in PMR over 12-18 months (some patients require up to 2 years) to minimize relapse risk, which occurs in 50% of patients. A typical approach: continue initial dose (15-20 mg) until symptoms controlled (usually 4-8 weeks), then taper by 2.5 mg every 2-4 weeks down to 10 mg, then slower taper (1-2.5 mg every 4-8 weeks). Rapid taper or abrupt discontinuation leads to high relapse rates. If relapse occurs, increase to previous dose and restart taper more slowly. Some patients require low-dose steroids long-term. Methotrexate may be considered as steroid-sparing agent in refractory cases or those with steroid toxicity. Monitor for GCA symptoms throughout treatment.

D118.q: A 68-year-old man with Parkinson's disease on levodopa/carbidopa for 5 years reports that medication effectiveness wears off before next dose ('wearing-off phenomenon') and he experiences involuntary writhing movements ('dyskinesias') at peak dose. What is the most appropriate adjustment?
a: Decrease levodopa dose and add COMT inhibitor (entacapone)
D118.rationale: This patient has classic motor complications of chronic levodopa therapy: wearing-off (motor fluctuations) and peak-dose dyskinesias. Management strategies include: (1) Add COMT inhibitor (entacapone) to prolong levodopa effect and reduce fluctuations; (2) Add MAO-B inhibitor (rasagiline, selegiline); (3) Add dopamine agonist; (4) Give smaller, more frequent levodopa doses; (5) Consider long-acting levodopa formulations. For dyskinesias, REDUCE levodopa dose while extending coverage with adjunctive agents or add amantadine (anti-dyskinesia effect). Simply increasing levodopa worsens dyskinesias. Advanced therapies for motor complications include deep brain stimulation, levodopa-carbidopa intestinal gel, or apomorphine infusion. Anticholinergics are generally avoided in elderly due to cognitive side effects.

D118.q: A 35-year-old woman with RRMS presents with acute onset of right leg weakness and numbness over 2 days. MRI shows new T2 hyperintense lesion in left centrum semiovale with gadolinium enhancement. What is the appropriate treatment for this acute relapse?
a: Oral prednisone 60 mg daily for 7 days
IV methylprednisolone 1000 mg daily for 3-5 days
Supportive care only as most relapses resolve spontaneously
D118.rationale: Acute MS relapses causing functional impairment are treated with high-dose IV corticosteroids (methylprednisolone 1000 mg daily for 3-5 days) to hasten recovery. This shortens relapse duration but doesn't affect long-term disability. Oral high-dose prednisone may be equivalent but IV is preferred for severe relapses. If incomplete recovery, a second course or plasma exchange (5-7 exchanges) may be considered. Mild relapses without functional impairment may be observed. Corticosteroids treat the acute inflammation but don't prevent future relapses—that's the role of DMTs. Starting or escalating DMT is appropriate if relapses are frequent or severe, but doesn't treat the current attack. IV steroids are typically followed by oral prednisone taper in some protocols.

D118.q: A 38-year-old woman with migraine takes sumatriptan 14 days per month and ibuprofen 18 days per month. She now has headaches 20 days per month. What is the most likely cause of her chronic headaches?
D118.rationale: Medication overuse headache (MOH, formerly 'rebound headache') is defined by the International Headache Society as headache ≥15 days/month in a patient with pre-existing headache disorder who overuses acute headache medication for >3 months. Overuse is defined as: triptans, ergots, opioids, or combination analgesics ≥10 days/month; or simple analgesics (NSAIDs, acetaminophen) ≥15 days/month. Treatment involves: (1) Education about MOH; (2) Initiation of preventive medication; (3) Withdrawal of overused medication (may cause temporary worsening for 2-10 days); (4) Bridge therapy with steroids or other agents. MOH resolves in 50-70% within 2 months of withdrawal. Prevention is key—counsel all migraine patients to limit acute medication use.
D118.video_source: Dr. Luis E Zayas, MD PT

D118.q: A 52-year-old man presents with diplopia, ataxia, and areflexia following a gastrointestinal illness. He has no limb weakness. This presentation is most consistent with which GBS variant?
D118.rationale: Miller Fisher syndrome (MFS) is a GBS variant characterized by the classic triad: ophthalmoplegia (cranial nerve palsies causing diplopia), ataxia, and areflexia. Unlike classic GBS (AIDP), limb weakness is minimal or absent. MFS is associated with anti-GQ1b antibodies in >90% of cases and often follows Campylobacter jejuni infection. Treatment is supportive as most patients recover spontaneously within weeks to months; severe cases may receive IVIG. AIDP is the most common GBS form (85-90% in Western countries) with ascending paralysis and demyelination. AMAN is an axonal variant common in Asia. CIDP is chronic (>8 weeks) demyelinating neuropathy, not an acute GBS variant. Recognizing MFS prevents unnecessary testing for other causes of ataxia and ophthalmoplegia.

D118.q: A 45-year-old woman with MG presents with severe generalized weakness, difficulty swallowing, and shortness of breath. FVC is 18 mL/kg (normal >60). What is the most appropriate immediate management?
a: Intubation and mechanical ventilation, plus IVIG or plasmapheresis
D118.rationale: This patient is in myasthenic crisis, defined as weakness requiring intubation/ventilatory support. It occurs in 15-20% of MG patients and is a medical emergency. Management includes: (1) Airway protection and mechanical ventilation (intubate if FVC <20 mL/kg, NIF <-30, or clinical signs of respiratory failure); (2) ICU monitoring; (3) Emergent immunotherapy with IVIG (0.4 g/kg/day × 5 days) or plasmapheresis (both equally effective); (4) Identify and treat triggers (infection, medication changes, surgery). STOP or reduce anticholinesterase (pyridostigmine) as it may increase secretions. Corticosteroids should be held initially as they can transiently worsen weakness. Mortality is 4-8% with prompt treatment. Recovery typically takes 2-4 weeks.

D118.q: A 28-year-old woman with epilepsy controlled on valproic acid is planning pregnancy. What counseling should you provide regarding antiepileptic drugs (AEDs) and pregnancy?
a: Continue valproic acid as seizure control is most important
Stop all AEDs during pregnancy to avoid teratogenicity
Switch to lamotrigine or levetiracetam and add high-dose folic acid
AEDs have no effect on pregnancy outcomes
D118.rationale: AAN/AES guidelines strongly recommend AVOIDING valproate in women of childbearing potential due to high risk of major congenital malformations (10-20%, especially neural tube defects) and cognitive/developmental impairment in children. Safer alternatives include lamotrigine and levetiracetam (both have lower teratogenicity risk 2-3%). Women should take high-dose folic acid (4-5 mg daily) before conception and throughout pregnancy to reduce neural tube defect risk. Stopping AEDs completely is dangerous as seizures during pregnancy (especially generalized tonic-clonic) pose risks to mother and fetus (trauma, hypoxia, miscarriage). The goal is optimal seizure control with the lowest effective dose of the safest AED. Pregnancy should be planned, and AED adjustments made before conception when possible.

D118.topic: Transient Ischemic Attack - Dual Antiplatelet Therapy
D118.q: A 65-year-old man presents within 12 hours of a minor ischemic stroke (NIHSS 2). MRI confirms small acute infarct. He has no indication for anticoagulation. According to recent guidelines, what is the optimal antiplatelet regimen?
a: Aspirin 81 mg + clopidogrel 75 mg daily for 21 days, then single antiplatelet
D118.rationale: Based on the CHANCE and POINT trials, AHA/ASA guidelines recommend dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT) with aspirin 50-325 mg + clopidogrel 75 mg (loading dose 300-600 mg) for 21 days after minor ischemic stroke (NIHSS ≤3) or high-risk TIA (ABCD2 ≥4) presenting within 24 hours, followed by single antiplatelet (typically clopidogrel) thereafter. DAPT reduces early recurrent stroke risk by ~25% compared to aspirin alone but increases bleeding risk if continued beyond 21-90 days. This applies only to non-cardioembolic stroke; patients with atrial fibrillation require anticoagulation. The benefit is greatest when started within 24 hours and in the first 7-21 days when stroke recurrence risk is highest.

D118.q: A 48-year-old woman presents with numbness and tingling in the thumb, index, middle, and radial half of ring finger, worse at night. Phalen's test is positive at 45 seconds. What is the most sensitive and specific diagnostic test?
D118.rationale: Nerve conduction studies (NCS) and electromyography (EMG) are the gold standard for confirming carpal tunnel syndrome, with sensitivity 85-90% and specificity >95%. NCS shows prolonged median nerve distal motor and sensory latencies across the wrist. While clinical diagnosis is often accurate, NCS/EMG is recommended before surgery to confirm diagnosis, assess severity, and exclude other conditions (cervical radiculopathy, polyneuropathy). Phalen's test (wrist flexion reproducing symptoms) has sensitivity 68% and specificity 73%. Tinel's sign (tapping over median nerve) is less sensitive/specific. MRI can show median nerve swelling but is not routinely needed. Initial treatment for mild-moderate CTS includes wrist splinting (especially at night), activity modification, and NSAIDs. Severe or refractory cases require surgical release.

D118.q: A 42-year-old office worker presents with lateral elbow pain for 6 weeks, worse with gripping and lifting objects. Examination reveals tenderness over lateral epicondyle and pain with resisted wrist extension. What is the most appropriate initial management?
a: Rest, ice, NSAIDs, and physical therapy with eccentric exercises
D118.rationale: Lateral epicondylitis is a tendinopathy (not inflammation) of the common extensor tendon origin, particularly extensor carpi radialis brevis. First-line treatment is conservative: relative rest (avoid aggravating activities), ice, NSAIDs, counterforce bracing, and physical therapy emphasizing eccentric strengthening and stretching. 80-95% of cases resolve within 1 year with conservative care. Corticosteroid injections provide short-term relief (4-6 weeks) but show no long-term benefit and may increase recurrence risk; reserve for refractory cases. Platelet-rich plasma (PRP) has emerging evidence but is not first-line. Surgery (tendon debridement/release) is considered only after 6-12 months of failed conservative therapy. MRI is rarely needed unless diagnosis is uncertain or other pathology suspected.

D118.q: A 52-year-old Hispanic male presents for routine physical. He is asymptomatic. BMI is 32 kg/m². Random glucose today is 186 mg/dL. Per ADA guidelines, what is the MOST appropriate next step?
a: Diagnose T2DM and initiate metformin immediately
Order fasting plasma glucose or HbA1c to confirm diagnosis
Reassure patient and recheck in 6 months
Order oral glucose tolerance test only
D118.rationale: ADA 2024 guidelines require confirmation with repeat testing (FPG ≥126 mg/dL, HbA1c ≥6.5%, or repeat random glucose ≥200 mg/dL with symptoms) unless patient has clear hyperglycemic crisis. A single random glucose of 186 mg/dL without symptoms is insufficient for diagnosis. Confirmation prevents overdiagnosis and ensures accuracy.

D118.q: A 48-year-old woman is newly diagnosed with T2DM (HbA1c 7.8%, eGFR 92 mL/min). She has no contraindications to metformin. What is the BEST initial dosing strategy to minimize GI side effects?
a: Start metformin 500 mg once daily with largest meal, titrate every 1-2 weeks
Start metformin 1000 mg twice daily immediately for rapid control
Start metformin ER 2000 mg at bedtime
Start metformin 850 mg three times daily with meals
D118.rationale: ADA recommends starting metformin at low dose (500 mg once or twice daily with meals) and gradually titrating every 1-2 weeks to minimize GI side effects (nausea, diarrhea) which are dose-related and cause-related discontinuation in 5-10% of patients. Extended-release formulations can also reduce GI effects but starting with standard low dose is most effective.

D118.q: A 61-year-old male with T2DM (HbA1c 8.2% on metformin 2000 mg daily) has history of MI 2 years ago and current EF 40%. Which medication class provides the GREATEST cardiovascular benefit per ADA guidelines?
D118.rationale: ADA 2024 strongly recommends SGLT2 inhibitors (empagliflozin, canagliflozin, dapagliflozin) for patients with T2DM and established ASCVD or heart failure due to proven cardiovascular outcomes benefits including reduced CV mortality, MI, and heart failure hospitalizations in landmark trials (EMPA-REG, CANVAS, DECLARE). This is independent of HbA1c-lowering effect.

D118.q: A 55-year-old obese woman (BMI 38) with T2DM (HbA1c 9.1%) has no history of CVD. She desires weight loss. After metformin optimization, which GLP-1 receptor agonist provides the GREATEST weight reduction based on clinical trials?
D118.rationale: Semaglutide 1 mg weekly demonstrates superior weight loss (mean 4.5-6.5 kg) compared to other GLP-1 RAs in head-to-head trials (SUSTAIN trials). Higher dose semaglutide 2.4 mg (Wegovy) shows even greater weight loss (12-15% body weight). GLP-1 RAs also reduce HbA1c, CV events, and have low hypoglycemia risk. Liraglutide shows ~3-4 kg loss, dulaglutide ~2-3 kg.

D118.q: A 78-year-old man with T2DM has multiple comorbidities (CHF, CKD stage 4, prior stroke), limited life expectancy, and history of severe hypoglycemia. What is the MOST appropriate HbA1c target per ADA guidelines?
D118.rationale: ADA recommends individualized HbA1c targets. For older adults with multiple comorbidities, limited life expectancy, or high hypoglycemia risk, a less stringent target of <8.0% is appropriate to avoid treatment-related harms. Overly aggressive targets in this population increase hypoglycemia risk without meaningful microvascular benefit. Healthy older adults may target <7.0-7.5%.

D118.q: A 44-year-old woman with T2DM on empagliflozin (SGLT2i) and metformin presents with nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain for 2 days. Glucose is 178 mg/dL. You suspect euglycemic DKA. Which lab finding would CONFIRM this diagnosis?
a: Serum bicarbonate <18 mEq/L with anion gap >12 and ketonemia
D118.rationale: Euglycemic DKA (euDKA) is a serious complication of SGLT2 inhibitors characterized by metabolic acidosis (bicarb <18, pH <7.3), elevated anion gap (>12), and ketonemia/ketonuria despite relatively normal glucose (<250 mg/dL). Risk factors include reduced caloric intake, illness, surgery, or alcohol use. SGLT2i should be held during illness and acute medical events to prevent euDKA.

D118.q: A 42-year-old man is newly diagnosed with T2DM. He has no visual symptoms. Per ADA guidelines, when should initial dilated retinal examination be performed?
D118.rationale: ADA recommends initial dilated comprehensive eye examination at the time of T2DM diagnosis because duration of hyperglycemia before diagnosis is unknown and retinopathy may already be present in 20-30% at diagnosis. If no retinopathy, repeat every 1-2 years. Type 1 DM screening begins 5 years after diagnosis. Early detection allows timely intervention to prevent vision loss.

D118.q: A 58-year-old woman with T2DM for 8 years presents for annual exam. Urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio (UACR) is 42 mg/g (repeated test confirms 38 mg/g). eGFR is 68 mL/min. What stage of diabetic kidney disease is this?
D118.rationale: KDIGO classification: UACR 30-300 mg/g = moderately increased albuminuria (A2, formerly 'microalbuminuria'). UACR >300 mg/g = severely increased (A3, formerly 'macroalbuminuria'). This patient has stage G2A2 CKD (eGFR 60-89 + UACR 30-300). Recommend ACEi/ARB, SGLT2i (if eGFR allows), optimize BP <130/80, and monitor annually per ADA/KDIGO guidelines.

D118.q: A 35-year-old woman presents with fatigue, weight gain of 15 lbs, cold intolerance, and constipation for 3 months. TSH is 12.8 mIU/L (normal 0.4-4.0), Free T4 is 0.6 ng/dL (normal 0.8-1.8). What is the diagnosis?
D118.rationale: Primary (overt) hypothyroidism is defined by elevated TSH (>4-5 mIU/L) AND low free T4. Subclinical hypothyroidism has elevated TSH with NORMAL free T4. Secondary (central) hypothyroidism shows LOW or inappropriately normal TSH with low T4. Most common cause is Hashimoto's thyroiditis. This patient requires levothyroxine replacement therapy.

D118.q: A 45-year-old woman (weight 70 kg) is newly diagnosed with primary hypothyroidism (TSH 18 mIU/L). She has no cardiac disease. What is the MOST appropriate initial levothyroxine dose per ATA guidelines?
D118.rationale: ATA guidelines recommend initial levothyroxine dosing of 1.6 mcg/kg/day (rounded to nearest 12.5-25 mcg increment) for healthy adults without cardiac disease. For 70 kg patient: 1.6 × 70 = 112 mcg daily. Lower starting doses (25-50 mcg) are reserved for elderly patients, those with cardiac disease, or severe long-standing hypothyroidism to avoid precipitating angina or arrhythmias.

D118.q: A 52-year-old woman taking levothyroxine 125 mcg daily has TSH 8.2 mIU/L despite good compliance. She recently started taking calcium carbonate 1000 mg twice daily for osteopenia. What is the BEST recommendation?
a: Separate levothyroxine and calcium by at least 4 hours
D118.rationale: Calcium carbonate, iron, PPIs, aluminum hydroxide, soy, and bile acid sequestrants can impair levothyroxine absorption. ATA recommends taking levothyroxine on empty stomach, 60 minutes before breakfast, and separating from interfering medications by at least 4 hours. After correcting timing, recheck TSH in 6-8 weeks before dose adjustment. Coffee may also reduce absorption.

D118.q: A 38-year-old woman trying to conceive has fatigue and TSH 6.8 mIU/L (normal 0.4-4.0), free T4 1.2 ng/dL (normal). TPO antibodies are positive. What is the MOST appropriate management per ATA guidelines?
a: No treatment, monitor TSH every 6-12 months
Order thyroid ultrasound before treatment decision
D118.rationale: ATA recommends treating subclinical hypothyroidism (TSH 4-10 mIU/L with normal T4) when: 1) TSH >10, 2) positive TPO antibodies, 3) symptoms, 4) pregnancy/planning pregnancy, or 5) goiter. This patient meets THREE criteria (positive TPO, symptoms, planning pregnancy). Pregnancy requires TSH <2.5 mIU/L in first trimester. Start low-dose levothyroxine (25-50 mcg) and titrate to TSH <2.5.

D118.q: A 32-year-old woman presents with palpitations, 12-lb weight loss, heat intolerance, and tremor. TSH <0.01 mIU/L, free T4 3.2 ng/dL (elevated). Diffuse goiter and exophthalmos noted. What is the MOST likely diagnosis?
D118.rationale: Graves' disease is the most common cause of hyperthyroidism (60-80% of cases), especially in younger women. Classic presentation: suppressed TSH, elevated free T4/T3, diffuse goiter, and specific findings of exophthalmos (Graves' ophthalmopathy) and pretibial myxedema. TSI (thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulin) antibodies confirm diagnosis. Toxic adenoma lacks ophthalmopathy and shows focal uptake on scan.

D118.q: A 45-year-old man is diagnosed with Graves' disease (TSH <0.01, free T4 elevated, positive TSI). He has resting HR 108 bpm and fine tremor. What medication should be initiated FIRST for symptomatic relief while awaiting endocrine referral?
D118.rationale: Beta-blockers (propranolol 20-40 mg TID or metoprolol) provide rapid symptomatic relief of adrenergic symptoms (palpitations, tremor, anxiety, tachycardia) within hours while awaiting definitive therapy. Non-selective beta-blockers like propranolol also decrease peripheral T4 to T3 conversion. Antithyroid drugs (methimazole preferred over PTU except in pregnancy first trimester) require weeks for effect and should be initiated by endocrinology.

D118.q: A 50-year-old woman has a 1.8 cm thyroid nodule discovered on carotid ultrasound. She is asymptomatic with normal TSH. Per ATA guidelines, what is the NEXT best step?
D118.rationale: ATA recommends thyroid ultrasound for all palpable nodules or those >1 cm incidentally found to assess size, characteristics, and risk stratification using validated systems (ATA, ACR TI-RADS). High-risk features include microcalcifications, irregular margins, taller-than-wide shape, hypoechogenicity. FNA is indicated for nodules >1 cm with suspicious features or >1.5-2 cm regardless of features. TSH guides further testing.

D118.q: A 42-year-old woman status-post total thyroidectomy for papillary thyroid cancer (low-risk, stage I) is on levothyroxine. What is the appropriate TSH target per ATA guidelines?
D118.rationale: ATA recommends risk-stratified TSH targets post-thyroidectomy for differentiated thyroid cancer: High-risk = TSH <0.1 (suppressed); Intermediate-risk = TSH 0.1-0.5; Low-risk = TSH 0.5-2.0 (low-normal range). Low-risk patients don't benefit from aggressive suppression and avoiding it reduces adverse effects (atrial fibrillation, bone loss). Patients with persistent disease may need more aggressive suppression.

D118.q: A 38-year-old woman presents with 6 months of progressive fatigue, 15-lb weight loss, dizziness upon standing, and hyperpigmentation of palmar creases. BP 88/54 mmHg. Labs: Na 128 mEq/L, K 5.8 mEq/L. What is the MOST likely diagnosis?
D118.rationale: Primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison disease) presents with mineralocorticoid deficiency (hypotension, hyponatremia, hyperkalemia) AND glucocorticoid deficiency (fatigue, weight loss). Hyperpigmentation occurs from elevated ACTH (compensatory response) stimulating melanocytes. Secondary AI (pituitary/hypothalamic) lacks hyperpigmentation and hyperkalemia (aldosterone intact). Diagnosis: 8 AM cortisol <3 mcg/dL or failed ACTH stimulation test. Most common cause: autoimmune.

D118.q: A 45-year-old man with known Addison disease presents to ED with severe vomiting, confusion, and hypotension (BP 78/42). He missed his hydrocortisone doses for 3 days due to illness. What is the MOST appropriate immediate treatment?
a: IV hydrocortisone 100 mg bolus plus IV normal saline
D118.rationale: Adrenal crisis is life-threatening requiring immediate treatment: 1) IV hydrocortisone 100 mg bolus followed by 50-100 mg IV/IM every 6-8 hours (or continuous infusion 200-300 mg/24h), 2) Aggressive IV normal saline resuscitation (1-2L rapidly), 3) Treat precipitant (infection, etc). Do NOT delay for confirmatory testing. Mineralocorticoid replacement (fludrocortisone) unnecessary initially as high-dose hydrocortisone has sufficient mineralocorticoid activity. Dexamethasone 4 mg is alternative if confirmatory testing needed.

D118.q: A 48-year-old woman presents with progressive weight gain (central obesity), facial rounding, easy bruising, proximal muscle weakness, and new hypertension. Which test is BEST for initial screening for Cushing syndrome?
D118.rationale: Endocrine Society recommends 24-hour urine free cortisol (UFC) as one of three first-line screening tests for Cushing syndrome (along with late-night salivary cortisol and 1-mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test). UFC >3-4× upper limit of normal strongly suggests Cushing's. At least TWO abnormal screening tests recommended before pursuing further workup (ACTH, imaging). Random cortisol unhelpful due to pulsatile secretion.

D118.q: A patient with suspected Cushing syndrome takes dexamethasone 1 mg at 11 PM. The 8 AM cortisol is 18 mcg/dL (normal suppression: <1.8 mcg/dL). What does this result indicate?
D118.rationale: Normal overnight 1-mg dexamethasone suppression test shows 8 AM cortisol <1.8 mcg/dL (some use <5 mcg/dL cutoff). Failure to suppress indicates autonomous cortisol production consistent with Cushing syndrome. This test has ~95% sensitivity but lower specificity (false positives with obesity, depression, medications). Next steps: confirm with additional screening tests, then measure ACTH to differentiate ACTH-dependent (pituitary/ectopic) from ACTH-independent (adrenal) causes.

D118.q: A 42-year-old woman presents with episodic severe headaches, palpitations, diaphoresis, and hypertension (BP during episode 210/118). Episodes last 15-30 minutes and occur 2-3 times weekly. Between episodes, BP is 138/86. What is the MOST likely diagnosis?
D118.rationale: Classic triad of pheochromocytoma: episodic headaches, palpitations, and diaphoresis with paroxysmal hypertension. 'Rule of 10s': 10% bilateral, 10% extra-adrenal, 10% malignant, 10% familial. Can mimic panic attacks but distinction is severe hypertension during episodes. Diagnosis: 24-hour urine or plasma fractionated metanephrines (preferred screening). CT/MRI adrenal once biochemically confirmed. Life-threatening if unrecognized before surgery/pregnancy.

D118.q: A 50-year-old man with treatment-resistant hypertension (on 3 medications) has persistent hypokalemia (K 3.1 mEq/L) without diuretic use. You suspect primary hyperaldosteronism. What is the BEST initial screening test?
a: Plasma aldosterone concentration (PAC) to plasma renin activity (PRA) ratio
D118.rationale: Aldosterone-to-renin ratio (ARR) is the preferred screening test for primary hyperaldosteronism (Conn syndrome). PAC elevated (>15 ng/dL) with suppressed PRA (<1 ng/mL/hr) yields ARR >20-30, suggesting autonomous aldosterone production. Confirmatory testing (saline suppression, captopril challenge) follows positive screen. Then adrenal CT to differentiate adenoma (unilateral) from bilateral hyperplasia. Most common cause of secondary HTN (5-10% of hypertensive patients). Often presents with resistant HTN and/or hypokalemia.

D118.q: A 28-year-old woman presents with irregular menses (4-5 cycles/year), hirsutism, acne, and obesity (BMI 34). Labs show elevated total testosterone and LH:FSH ratio 3:1. Pelvic ultrasound shows bilateral enlarged ovaries with multiple small follicles. What comorbidity screening is MOST important?
D118.rationale: PCOS patients have 50-70% prevalence of insulin resistance and increased risk of T2DM (4-fold higher), metabolic syndrome, and CVD. ADA and Endocrine Society recommend screening ALL PCOS patients for T2DM with 2-hour OGTT (more sensitive than FPG) or HbA1c at diagnosis and every 3 years, or more frequently if obese or other risk factors. First-line treatment: lifestyle modification and metformin (improves insulin resistance, may restore ovulation).

D118.q: A 35-year-old woman presents with 6 weeks of depressed mood, anhedonia, insomnia, poor concentration, fatigue, feelings of worthlessness, and 10-lb weight loss. She denies suicidal ideation. No manic/hypomanic episodes. How many DSM-5 criteria does she meet for Major Depressive Episode?
D118.rationale: DSM-5 Major Depressive Episode requires ≥5 of 9 symptoms during 2-week period with at least ONE being depressed mood OR anhedonia. SIG E CAPS mnemonic: Sleep disturbance, Interest/anhedonia, Guilt/worthlessness, Energy loss, Concentration problems, Appetite/weight changes, Psychomotor changes, Suicidal ideation. This patient has 7: depressed mood, anhedonia, insomnia, poor concentration, fatigue, worthlessness, weight loss. Diagnosis: Major Depressive Disorder (MDD), single episode, moderate severity.

D118.q: A 42-year-old man is diagnosed with moderate MDD without psychotic features. He has no comorbid conditions. Which medication class is considered FIRST-LINE treatment with best tolerability profile?
D118.rationale: SSRIs (sertraline, escitalopram, fluoxetine, citalopram, paroxetine) are first-line for MDD due to efficacy, safety, and tolerability. Side effects: GI upset, sexual dysfunction, initial anxiety. SNRIs (venlafaxine, duloxetine) are also first-line. TCAs and MAOIs are effective but relegated to later-line due to side effects and safety concerns (TCA overdose lethality, MAOI dietary restrictions). Benzodiazepines not indicated for MDD. Therapeutic response takes 4-6 weeks; adequate trial is 8-12 weeks at therapeutic dose.

D118.q: A 38-year-old woman with first episode of MDD achieved full remission on sertraline 100 mg daily after 3 months. She asks about stopping medication now that she feels better. What is the MINIMUM recommended continuation treatment duration per APA guidelines?
D118.rationale: APA practice guidelines recommend continuing antidepressant therapy for at least 4-6 months after achieving full remission (continuation phase) to prevent relapse. First episode with full recovery: treat 6-12 months total then consider tapering. Recurrent episodes (≥2-3): consider longer maintenance (years to indefinite) as recurrence risk is 50-85%. Never abruptly discontinue SSRIs due to discontinuation syndrome; taper over 2-4 weeks minimum.

D118.topic: Major Depressive Disorder - Suicide Risk Assessment
D118.q: A 55-year-old man with MDD states 'I'd be better off dead' during visit. Which question is MOST important to assess imminent suicide risk?
a: Have you felt depressed most of the time?
Do you have a specific plan for how you would kill yourself?
Do you feel guilty about things?
D118.rationale: Suicide risk assessment evaluates: ideation, plan, means, intent, prior attempts. Specific plan with access to lethal means and intent indicates HIGH imminent risk requiring immediate intervention (emergency department, psychiatric hospitalization). Additional risk factors: male, older age, living alone, alcohol use, hopelessness, recent loss. Directly asking about suicide does NOT increase risk. Screen with PHQ-9 item 9 or Columbia Suicide Severity Rating Scale (C-SSRS). Document thoroughly and safety plan.

D118.q: A 32-year-old woman with MDD reports hypersomnia (12 hours/day), increased appetite with 15-lb weight gain, leaden paralysis, and extreme sensitivity to interpersonal rejection. This presentation suggests which MDD specifier?
D118.rationale: DSM-5 'atypical features' specifier includes: mood reactivity PLUS ≥2 of: hypersomnia, hyperphagia/weight gain, leaden paralysis (heavy limbs), rejection sensitivity. More common in females and associated with earlier onset, longer episodes, greater comorbidity. May preferentially respond to MAOIs or bupropion. Melancholic features include anhedonia, early morning awakening, weight LOSS, excessive guilt. Accurate specifier identification guides treatment selection.

D118.topic: Bipolar I Disorder - Manic Episode Criteria
D118.q: A 28-year-old man presents after 1 week of decreased need for sleep (3 hours/night), pressured speech, grandiose delusions (believes he's a famous musician), impulsive spending ($15,000 on equipment), and distractibility. No substance use. Per DSM-5, what is the diagnosis?
a: Bipolar I Disorder, current manic episode
D118.rationale: DSM-5 Manic Episode: ≥1 week (or any duration if hospitalized) of abnormally elevated/expansive/irritable mood AND increased goal-directed activity, PLUS ≥3 of DIG FAST: Distractibility, Impulsivity/Indiscretion, Grandiosity, Flight of ideas, Activity increase, Sleep deficit, Talkative/pressured speech. Must cause marked impairment or require hospitalization. ONE manic episode = Bipolar I diagnosis (prior/future depressions not required). Bipolar II requires hypomanic + depressive episodes, never full mania.

D118.q: A 32-year-old woman is newly diagnosed with Bipolar I Disorder after manic episode. She is currently euthymic. Which medication is considered FIRST-LINE for long-term mood stabilization and mania prevention?
D118.rationale: Lithium remains gold-standard first-line mood stabilizer for Bipolar I with strongest evidence for mania prevention, depression prevention, and suicide reduction. Alternatives: valproate, lamotrigine (better for bipolar depression), atypical antipsychotics (quetiapine, aripiprazole). Lithium requires monitoring: levels (0.6-1.2 mEq/L), renal function, thyroid, ECG (>50 yo). Narrow therapeutic window; toxicity >1.5. Contraindicated in pregnancy (Ebstein anomaly). SSRIs can precipitate mania; avoid monotherapy.

D118.q: A 45-year-old man on lithium 900 mg daily for Bipolar I presents with coarse tremor, confusion, ataxia, and diarrhea. Lithium level is 2.1 mEq/L (therapeutic 0.6-1.2). What is the MOST appropriate immediate action?
a: Reduce lithium dose to 600 mg daily and recheck level in 1 week
Hold lithium and refer to emergency department immediately
Continue current dose and add benztropine
D118.rationale: Lithium toxicity (>1.5 mEq/L) is medical emergency requiring immediate hospitalization. Mild (1.5-2.0): nausea, tremor, polyuria. Moderate (2.0-2.5): confusion, ataxia, dysarthria. Severe (>2.5): seizures, arrhythmias, renal failure, coma. Treatment: IV hydration, sodium repletion, hemodialysis if severe. Risk factors: dehydration, NSAIDs, ACEi, thiazides, renal impairment. Patient education critical: maintain hydration, avoid NSAIDs, report symptoms early. Monitor lithium level 5 days after dose change, then every 3-6 months.

D118.topic: Bipolar II Disorder - Hypomania vs Mania
D118.q: A 35-year-old woman describes a 5-day period last month of elevated mood, decreased sleep (4 hours/night feeling rested), increased productivity, talkativeness, and starting multiple projects. She went to work daily and friends noticed she seemed 'different but not concerning.' She has history of recurrent major depressive episodes. What is the MOST likely diagnosis?
D118.rationale: Bipolar II: ≥1 hypomanic episode AND ≥1 major depressive episode, never full mania. Hypomania: ≥4 consecutive days of elevated mood + ≥3 DIG FAST symptoms, noticeable change from baseline BUT not severe enough to cause marked impairment or require hospitalization (key distinction from mania). Still functional but observable by others. This patient meets hypomanic criteria (5 days, multiple symptoms, observable) plus depression history. Treatment: mood stabilizers (lamotrigine preferred for bipolar depression), avoid antidepressant monotherapy.

D118.q: A 42-year-old woman reports 8 months of persistent, excessive worry about multiple issues (finances, health, family) that she cannot control. She has restlessness, muscle tension, poor concentration, and insomnia. The worry causes significant work impairment. How many DSM-5 criteria does she meet for GAD?
D118.rationale: DSM-5 GAD criteria: ≥6 months excessive anxiety/worry about multiple events, difficult to control, causing significant distress/impairment, PLUS ≥3 of 6 symptoms (only 1 required in children): Restlessness, Easy fatigability, Concentration difficulty, Irritability, Muscle tension, Sleep disturbance. This patient has 4: restlessness, muscle tension, poor concentration, insomnia. First-line treatment: SSRIs/SNRIs (escitalopram, sertraline, duloxetine, venlafaxine) and/or CBT. Benzodiazepines for short-term only due to dependence risk.

D118.q: A 38-year-old man is diagnosed with GAD. He prefers medication to therapy. He has no depression. Which medication is BEST first-line choice with lowest abuse potential?
D118.rationale: SSRIs (escitalopram, sertraline, paroxetine) and SNRIs (venlafaxine, duloxetine) are first-line pharmacotherapy for GAD with no abuse potential. Onset 2-4 weeks. Benzodiazepines work rapidly but reserved for short-term use (<2-4 weeks) during SSRI titration due to dependence, tolerance, cognitive effects. Buspirone (5-HT1A partial agonist) is effective but slower onset (2-4 weeks). CBT is evidence-based and preferred; combination therapy most effective.

D118.q: A 30-year-old woman describes recurrent unexpected episodes of intense fear peaking within minutes, with palpitations, chest pain, dyspnea, dizziness, derealization, and fear of dying. She has had 4 episodes in past month and now fears having another attack. Medical workup negative. What is the diagnosis?
D118.rationale: DSM-5 Panic Disorder: Recurrent unexpected panic attacks PLUS ≥1 month of worry about additional attacks or maladaptive behavior change (avoidance). Panic attack = abrupt surge of fear with ≥4 of 13 symptoms: palpitations, sweating, trembling, dyspnea, choking, chest pain, nausea, dizziness, chills/heat, paresthesias, derealization/depersonalization, fear of losing control, fear of dying. Must rule out medical causes (cardiac, thyroid, pheochromocytoma). Treatment: SSRIs/SNRIs + CBT; benzodiazepines PRN short-term.

D118.q: A 35-year-old woman with newly diagnosed Panic Disorder has 2-3 panic attacks weekly. She wants medication for long-term management. Which medication provides both acute relief and long-term prevention?
a: Sertraline daily plus alprazolam as needed during titration
D118.rationale: Optimal panic disorder treatment combines daily SSRI/SNRI (sertraline, paroxetine, venlafaxine) for long-term prevention PLUS short-term benzodiazepine (alprazolam, clonazepam) as needed for breakthrough attacks during SSRI titration (first 4-6 weeks). SSRIs reduce attack frequency/severity but take weeks to work. Taper benzos once SSRI effective. Monotherapy with PRN benzos doesn't prevent attacks and risks dependence. CBT with exposure therapy highly effective; recommend combination approach.

D118.q: A 40-year-old man with panic disorder now avoids grocery stores, driving on highways, and crowded places due to fear of having a panic attack where escape would be difficult. This describes which additional diagnosis?
D118.rationale: Agoraphobia: anxiety about ≥2 of 5 situations (public transportation, open spaces, enclosed spaces, crowds, outside home alone) due to fear of panic-like symptoms where escape difficult or help unavailable. Often co-occurs with panic disorder (50-60%) but can exist independently. Leads to avoidance and significant life restriction. DSM-5 codes separately from panic disorder. Treatment: CBT with gradual exposure therapy is most effective; SSRIs also helpful. Avoidance perpetuates anxiety; exposure breaks cycle.

D118.q: A 35-year-old veteran was in combat 18 months ago. He has recurrent nightmares, flashbacks, hypervigilance, avoids military-related content, feels detached from family, and has angry outbursts. Symptoms last 8 months. How long must symptoms persist for PTSD diagnosis per DSM-5?
D118.rationale: DSM-5 PTSD requires: 1) Trauma exposure, 2) Symptoms from FOUR clusters for >1 month: Intrusions (flashbacks, nightmares), Avoidance (trauma reminders), Negative cognitions/mood (detachment, negative beliefs), Arousal/reactivity changes (hypervigilance, irritability, reckless behavior), 3) Significant distress/impairment. <1 month = Acute Stress Disorder. This veteran meets criteria. First-line treatment: trauma-focused CBT (prolonged exposure, CPT) and/or SSRIs/SNRIs (sertraline, paroxetine). Prazosin for nightmares.

D118.q: A 42-year-old woman is diagnosed with PTSD after sexual assault 1 year ago. She has severe avoidance and intrusive symptoms. What is the MOST evidence-based first-line treatment per VA/DoD guidelines?
D118.rationale: Trauma-focused psychotherapy is first-line for PTSD per VA/DoD and APA guidelines. Two strongest evidence-based therapies: 1) Prolonged Exposure (PE): gradual, repeated exposure to trauma memories and avoided situations, 2) Cognitive Processing Therapy (CPT): addressing maladaptive beliefs about trauma. SSRIs (sertraline, paroxetine) are first-line pharmacotherapy if therapy unavailable/refused or severe symptoms. Benzodiazepines NOT recommended (may worsen PTSD, no evidence). EMDR (Eye Movement Desensitization and Reprocessing) also evidence-based.

D118.q: A 50-year-old veteran with PTSD on sertraline has persistent trauma-related nightmares disrupting sleep despite SSRI optimization. Which medication has specific evidence for reducing PTSD nightmares?
D118.rationale: Prazosin, an alpha-1 adrenergic antagonist, has evidence for reducing trauma-related nightmares and improving sleep in PTSD (though recent large VA trial showed mixed results). Dose: start 1-2 mg qhs, titrate to 2-15 mg based on response. Monitor orthostatic hypotension. Not first-line for overall PTSD but useful adjunct for nightmare-predominant symptoms. Trazodone helps sleep but lacks nightmare-specific evidence. SSRIs address core PTSD symptoms but nightmares often persist. Benzodiazepines not recommended.

D118.q: A 24-year-old man presents with 4 months of auditory hallucinations (voices commenting on his actions), bizarre delusions (believes FBI is monitoring him via implants), disorganized speech, and marked social withdrawal. Functioning declined significantly. No substance use. What is the MINIMUM duration for schizophrenia diagnosis?
D118.rationale: DSM-5 Schizophrenia requires: ≥2 of 5 symptoms (delusions, hallucinations, disorganized speech, grossly disorganized/catatonic behavior, negative symptoms) for ≥1 month (Criterion A), with continuous signs of disturbance for ≥6 months (may include prodromal/residual periods). At least ONE symptom must be delusions, hallucinations, or disorganized speech. Significant functional decline required. <6 months = Schizophreniform Disorder. First episode psychosis requires urgent psychiatric referral and initiation of antipsychotic (second-generation preferred).

D118.q: A 28-year-old man is diagnosed with first-episode schizophrenia with prominent hallucinations and delusions. No prior antipsychotic exposure. Which antipsychotic class is preferred FIRST-LINE due to better tolerability?
D118.rationale: Second-generation (atypical) antipsychotics are preferred first-line for schizophrenia due to lower extrapyramidal symptoms (EPS) risk compared to first-generation (typical) agents. Options: risperidone, olanzapine, quetiapine, aripiprazole, lurasidone. All similarly effective for positive symptoms; differ in side effect profiles. Olanzapine/clozapine: highest metabolic risk. Risperidone/paliperidone: higher prolactin elevation. Aripiprazole: lower metabolic/prolactin effects. Monitor: weight, glucose, lipids, prolactin. Clozapine reserved for treatment-resistant schizophrenia (failed ≥2 antipsychotics) due to agranulocytosis risk requiring ANC monitoring.

D118.q: A 45-year-old man drinks 8-10 beers daily. He has tried to cut down unsuccessfully multiple times, spends much time drinking/recovering, has tolerance, experiences withdrawal tremors without alcohol, continues despite recurrent arguments with wife, and has missed work repeatedly. How many DSM-5 criteria for Alcohol Use Disorder does he meet?
D118.rationale: DSM-5 Alcohol Use Disorder: ≥2 of 11 criteria in 12 months. Severity: 2-3 = mild, 4-5 = moderate, 6+ = severe. This patient meets 7: tolerance, withdrawal, larger amounts/longer than intended, unsuccessful efforts to cut down, time spent on alcohol, important activities given up, continued use despite problems. Criteria include impaired control (4), social impairment (3), risky use (2), pharmacologic (tolerance/withdrawal). Treatment: psychosocial interventions, naltrexone/acamprosate for cravings, benzodiazepines for withdrawal.

D118.q: A 52-year-old man with severe Alcohol Use Disorder achieves abstinence after detox. He desires medication to help maintain sobriety by reducing cravings. Which medication is FDA-approved and evidence-based for this indication?
D118.rationale: Three FDA-approved medications for AUD: 1) Naltrexone (oral/injectable): opioid antagonist reduces cravings and rewarding effects of alcohol, 2) Acamprosate: modulates glutamate, reduces cravings/protracted withdrawal, 3) Disulfiram: aversion therapy (acetaldehyde accumulation causes unpleasant reaction). Naltrexone and acamprosate have strongest evidence for maintaining abstinence. Naltrexone contraindicated with opioid use. Combine with psychosocial treatment (AA, CBT, motivational enhancement). Benzodiazepines for acute withdrawal only, not maintenance. Thiamine prevents Wernicke's but doesn't reduce cravings.

D118.q: A 62-year-old woman with T2DM (HbA1c 10.2%) on metformin 2000 mg and glipizide 10 mg BID has persistent hyperglycemia. You decide to initiate basal insulin. What is the recommended starting dose of insulin glargine per ADA?
D118.rationale: ADA recommends starting basal insulin at 0.1-0.2 units/kg/day (typically 10 units once daily) in T2DM to minimize hypoglycemia risk. Titrate by 2-4 units every 3-7 days based on fasting glucose to target <130 mg/dL. Continue metformin (reduces insulin requirements and weight gain). Consider discontinuing sulfonylurea if hypoglycemia occurs. Insulin glargine (U-100, U-300), detemir, or degludec are long-acting basal options. Patient education on injection technique, storage, and hypoglycemia recognition is critical.

D118.q: A 58-year-old man with T2DM on insulin glargine and metformin presents with tremor, diaphoresis, confusion. Fingerstick glucose is 48 mg/dL. He is conscious and able to swallow. What is the MOST appropriate immediate treatment?
a: 15-20 grams fast-acting carbohydrate (4 oz juice or glucose tablets)
D118.rationale: Rule of 15: For conscious patient able to swallow with glucose <70 mg/dL, give 15-20g fast-acting carbohydrate (4 oz juice, 3-4 glucose tablets, 1 tablespoon honey), recheck in 15 minutes, repeat if needed, then eat meal/snack. Glucagon 1 mg IM/SC reserved for unconscious/unable to swallow or IV D50 in hospital setting. After treatment, investigate cause (missed meal, excess insulin, exercise, new medication) and adjust regimen. Document hypoglycemia awareness status; impaired awareness requires less stringent targets.

D118.q: A 68-year-old woman has routine labs showing TSH 0.2 mIU/L (low, normal 0.4-4.0), free T4 1.3 ng/dL (normal 0.8-1.8). She is asymptomatic. What is this condition and its primary risk?
a: Overt hyperthyroidism; risk of thyroid storm
Subclinical hyperthyroidism; risk of atrial fibrillation and osteoporosis
Euthyroid sick syndrome; no treatment needed
Primary hypothyroidism; risk of myxedema coma
D118.rationale: Subclinical hyperthyroidism: suppressed TSH (<0.4 mIU/L) with NORMAL free T4/T3. Prevalence increases with age. Risks in older adults: atrial fibrillation (HR 1.4-3.1), reduced bone mineral density/fractures, possible cardiovascular events. ATA recommends: 1) Repeat in 2-3 months to confirm, 2) Measure free T3 (may be elevated), 3) Consider treatment if TSH <0.1, age >65, cardiac disease, or osteoporosis risk factors. Treatment: antithyroid drugs, RAI, or surgery depending on etiology (toxic nodule, Graves').

D118.q: A patient with T2DM on metformin and SGLT2 inhibitor (empagliflozin) develops acute gastroenteritis with vomiting. Which medication adjustment is MOST important to prevent serious complication?
a: Double the metformin dose to prevent hyperglycemia
Temporarily discontinue SGLT2 inhibitor until illness resolves
D118.rationale: SGLT2 inhibitors should be held during acute illness, surgery, reduced caloric intake, or dehydration due to euglycemic DKA risk. Also hold metformin if risk of dehydration/renal impairment (lactic acidosis risk). Sick day rules: 1) Never stop insulin (may need increase), 2) Monitor glucose frequently, 3) Stay hydrated, 4) Test ketones if glucose >250, 5) Hold metformin/SGLT2i, 6) Continue basal insulin but adjust prandial based on intake. Contact provider if persistent vomiting, ketones, or glucose >250.

D118.q: A 55-year-old man with T2DM for 10 years reports numbness and tingling in both feet. On exam, he has decreased sensation to 10-g monofilament. What is the MOST important preventive counseling?
a: Foot care education including daily inspection and proper footwear
Discontinue metformin to prevent B12 deficiency
Start opioid analgesics for pain control
D118.rationale: Diabetic peripheral neuropathy (DPN) affects 50% of diabetics and increases foot ulcer/amputation risk. ADA recommends annual foot exam with 10-g monofilament, visual inspection, pulses. Loss of protective sensation requires intensive prevention: daily foot inspection (patient/family), proper footwear, professional foot care, prompt treatment of minor injuries, podiatry referral. For neuropathic pain: gabapentin, pregabalin, duloxetine, or tricyclics (NOT opioids first-line). Optimize glycemic control to slow progression.

D118.q: A 45-year-old woman on fluoxetine 60 mg daily is started on tramadol for back pain by orthopedics. Two days later, she presents with agitation, diaphoresis, tremor, hyperreflexia, clonus, and fever (101.2°F). What is the MOST likely diagnosis?
D118.rationale: Serotonin syndrome results from excess serotonergic activity, often from drug combinations (SSRI + tramadol, SSRI + triptans, SSRI + linezolid, SSRI + MAOI). Hunter Criteria: exposure + spontaneous clonus OR inducible clonus + agitation/diaphoresis OR ocular clonus + agitation/diaphoresis OR tremor + hyperreflexia OR hypertonia + temperature >38°C + ocular/inducible clonus. Triad: neuromuscular (clonus, hyperreflexia), autonomic (diaphoresis, fever, tachycardia), mental status (agitation). Treatment: stop offending agents, supportive care, cyproheptadine if severe. Can be fatal if untreated.

D118.q: A 32-year-old man started sertraline for GAD 2 weeks ago. He reports new onset sexual dysfunction (delayed ejaculation). What is the BEST initial management strategy?
a: Continue current dose; side effect often improves with time
D118.rationale: Sexual dysfunction (decreased libido, delayed orgasm/ejaculation, anorgasmia) occurs in 25-70% on SSRIs via serotonin 5-HT2 effects. Management strategies: 1) Wait 4-6 weeks; may improve spontaneously, 2) Reduce dose if possible, 3) Switch to lower-risk antidepressant (bupropion, mirtazapine), 4) Add bupropion or sildenafil, 5) Drug holidays (not recommended with short half-life SSRIs). Don't abruptly discontinue effective medication for tolerable side effect without discussing options. Bupropion has lowest sexual dysfunction risk among antidepressants.

D118.q: A 38-year-old woman with Bipolar II is started on lamotrigine for mood stabilization. What serious adverse effect requires SLOW titration and immediate discontinuation if rash develops?
D118.rationale: Lamotrigine carries risk of serious rashes including Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS) and toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN), especially with rapid titration or concomitant valproate (which doubles lamotrigine levels). Required slow titration: weeks 1-2: 25 mg daily, weeks 3-4: 50 mg daily, week 5: 100 mg daily, target 200 mg daily (adjust if on valproate or enzyme inducers). Discontinue immediately if ANY rash develops. SJS risk ~0.1% in adults, higher in children. Patient education critical: report any rash, fever, lymphadenopathy immediately.

D118.q: A 30-year-old man started on olanzapine for schizophrenia 3 months ago. He has gained 25 lbs. Labs show fasting glucose 118 mg/dL, triglycerides 245 mg/dL. Per APA guidelines, what is the appropriate monitoring frequency for metabolic parameters?
a: Baseline, monthly × 3 months, quarterly, then annually
D118.rationale: APA/ADA consensus guidelines for antipsychotic metabolic monitoring: Baseline: weight/BMI, waist circumference, BP, fasting glucose, lipids. Then: weight at each visit initially; BMI/waist at 4, 8, 12 weeks then quarterly; BP, glucose, lipids at 12 weeks then annually (more frequently if abnormal). Olanzapine and clozapine highest metabolic risk (weight gain, T2DM, dyslipidemia). Consider switching to lower-risk agent (aripiprazole, lurasidone, ziprasidone) if significant weight gain or metabolic abnormalities develop.

D118.q: A 68-year-old man with T2DM for 15 years, history of MI, HbA1c 8.8% asks about aggressive glucose lowering to prevent complications. Based on ACCORD trial findings, what is the appropriate counseling?
a: Target HbA1c <6% to maximally reduce CV events
Intensive glucose lowering (HbA1c <6%) in high-risk patients increases mortality without CV benefit
Aggressive lowering always beneficial regardless of age or comorbidities
HbA1c target doesn\'t matter in established CVD
D118.rationale: ACCORD trial (2008) demonstrated that intensive glucose lowering (target HbA1c <6%) in high-risk T2DM patients (long duration, CVD, multiple risk factors) INCREASED all-cause mortality compared to standard therapy (target 7.0-7.9%) without reducing major CV events. Likely due to increased severe hypoglycemia and weight gain. Changed practice: individualize targets, less stringent for older adults with established CVD, limited life expectancy. ADVANCE and VADT trials also showed limited macrovascular benefit with intensive control. Microvascular benefits still exist.

D118.q: A 32-year-old woman on levothyroxine 100 mcg for hypothyroidism just discovered she's pregnant (6 weeks). TSH was 2.1 mIU/L pre-pregnancy. What is the MOST appropriate management per ATA guidelines?
a: Continue same dose, no changes needed
D118.rationale: Thyroid hormone requirements increase 30-50% during pregnancy due to increased TBG, placental metabolism, and fetal needs. ATA recommends: 1) Increase levothyroxine by 25-30% (or take 2 extra doses weekly) as soon as pregnancy confirmed, 2) Check TSH every 4 weeks in first half, every 6 weeks in second half, 3) Target trimester-specific TSH goals (<2.5 mIU/L first trimester). Untreated hypothyroidism risks miscarriage, preterm birth, impaired fetal neurodevelopment. Return to pre-pregnancy dose postpartum; recheck TSH 6 weeks after delivery.

D118.q: A 50-year-old woman with MDD has failed adequate trials (8-12 weeks at therapeutic doses) of sertraline and venlafaxine with minimal response. What defines treatment-resistant depression (TRD)?
a: Failure of 2+ adequate antidepressant trials from different classes
D118.rationale: Treatment-resistant depression (TRD): failure to respond to ≥2 adequate trials of antidepressants from different classes (adequate = therapeutic dose for 6-8 weeks minimum, ideally 8-12 weeks). This patient meets criteria. Next steps: 1) Confirm diagnosis and medication adherence, 2) Assess comorbidities (bipolar, anxiety, substance use, medical conditions), 3) Optimize current medication, 4) Consider augmentation (lithium, T3, atypical antipsychotic), switching to MAOI, or 5) Non-pharmacologic interventions (ECT, TMS, esketamine, psychotherapy). ECT most effective treatment for severe TRD.

D118.q: A 55-year-old man has taken alprazolam 2 mg TID for 5 years for GAD. He wants to discontinue it. What is the MOST appropriate tapering strategy to avoid withdrawal seizures?
a: Gradual taper reducing by 10-25% every 1-2 weeks, possible switch to long-acting benzodiazepine
Switch to alcohol for withdrawal symptoms
D118.rationale: Benzodiazepine withdrawal can be life-threatening (seizures, delirium). Safe taper: 1) Reduce by 10-25% every 1-2 weeks (slower if symptoms), 2) Consider switching to long-acting equivalent (clonazepam, diazepam) before taper, 3) Slower taper in final weeks (may take 6-12 months total), 4) Supportive care and CBT. Withdrawal symptoms: anxiety, insomnia, tremor, perceptual disturbances, seizures (rare but serious). Never abruptly discontinue long-term benzodiazepines. Address underlying anxiety disorder with SSRI/CBT before/during taper.

D118.q: A 58-year-old woman with T2DM on metformin 2000 mg daily for 8 years presents with paresthesias in feet, pale conjunctiva. CBC shows MCV 108 fL (macrocytic). What vitamin deficiency is associated with long-term metformin use?
D118.rationale: Metformin reduces vitamin B12 absorption in 10-30% of long-term users, especially at doses >2000 mg/day or duration >4 years. Mechanism: impaired calcium-dependent B12-IF complex absorption in terminal ileum. Manifestations: macrocytic anemia, peripheral neuropathy (may be confused with diabetic neuropathy), glossitis. ADA recommends periodic B12 screening in metformin users, especially with peripheral neuropathy or anemia. Treatment: oral B12 1000 mcg daily or IM B12 if severe. Continue metformin with supplementation; benefits outweigh risks.

D118.q: A 40-year-old woman is started on valproate for Bipolar I disorder. What laboratory monitoring is MOST critical due to potentially fatal adverse effect?
a: CBC with platelets and liver function tests
D118.rationale: Valproate requires monitoring for: 1) Hepatotoxicity (potentially fatal, especially first 6 months; check baseline and periodic LFTs), 2) Thrombocytopenia/platelet dysfunction (check baseline CBC, platelets), 3) Pancreatitis (rare but serious). Also: therapeutic level 50-125 mcg/mL, teratogenicity (neural tube defects - contraindicated in pregnancy/childbearing potential unless no alternatives), PCOS, weight gain. Baseline labs: LFTs, CBC, platelets; repeat LFTs at 2, 4, 8, 12 weeks then periodically. Educate about signs of hepatotoxicity (nausea, vomiting, jaundice, abdominal pain) and bleeding.

D118.q: A 50-year-old male veteran presents for annual physical. He has insomnia and irritability. What is the BEST validated brief screening tool for PTSD in primary care?
D118.rationale: PC-PTSD-5 is a validated 5-item yes/no screening tool for PTSD in primary care. Asks about: 1) Disturbing memories/thoughts, 2) Nightmares, 3) Avoidance, 4) Hypervigilance, 5) Feeling numb/detached. Score ≥3 positive screen, warrants full PTSD assessment. Takes <1 minute. VA recommends annual PTSD screening in all veterans. Other tools: PTSD Checklist (PCL-5) for diagnosis/severity monitoring (20 items). PHQ-9 screens depression, GAD-7 screens anxiety. Early identification improves outcomes; many with PTSD present with somatic complaints.

D118.q: A 25-year-old woman describes intense fear of social situations where she might be scrutinized (eating in public, public speaking, conversations). She fears embarrassment and avoids these situations, causing significant work impairment. Symptoms present for 14 months. What is the diagnosis?
D118.rationale: DSM-5 Social Anxiety Disorder: marked fear/anxiety about ≥1 social situations where scrutinized by others (social interactions, being observed, performing), fears negative evaluation, situations avoided or endured with intense anxiety, ≥6 months duration, significant distress/impairment. Most common anxiety disorder (lifetime prevalence ~12%). Specify: performance only (public speaking/performing) or generalized. Treatment: CBT with exposure therapy (most effective), SSRIs/SNRIs (paroxetine, sertraline, venlafaxine), beta-blockers for performance anxiety PRN (propranolol 10-40 mg 1 hour before event).

D118.q: A 32-year-old man describes intrusive thoughts about contamination (obsessions) that cause significant anxiety. He washes hands 40-50 times daily, taking 3-4 hours (compulsions) to reduce anxiety. This causes severe distress and job problems. What is the diagnosis?
D118.rationale: DSM-5 Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder: Obsessions (recurrent intrusive thoughts causing anxiety) and/or Compulsions (repetitive behaviors/mental acts to reduce anxiety), time-consuming (>1 hour/day) or cause significant distress/impairment. Common themes: contamination/cleaning, symmetry/ordering, forbidden thoughts, harm. Treatment: CBT with exposure and response prevention (ERP) - most effective, SSRIs at HIGH doses (higher than depression doses; e.g., fluoxetine 60-80 mg, sertraline 200 mg), or combination. Treatment-resistant: augment with atypical antipsychotic.

D118.q: A 22-year-old woman with anorexia nervosa (BMI 15.5) presents for follow-up. Which cardiac finding is MOST commonly associated with severe anorexia?
D118.rationale: Anorexia nervosa causes significant cardiac complications: sinus bradycardia (HR <50), hypotension, prolonged QTc (risk sudden death), mitral valve prolapse, pericardial effusion, decreased LV mass. Electrolyte abnormalities (hypokalemia, hypophosphatemia especially during refeeding) further increase arrhythmia risk. Medical instability criteria requiring hospitalization: HR <40, BP <90/60, QTc >450 msec, severe electrolyte abnormalities. Monitor: ECG, electrolytes, phosphorus, glucose. Refeeding syndrome risk during nutritional rehabilitation. Mortality rate 5-10%, highest of any psychiatric disorder (mostly cardiac/suicide).

D118.q: A 3-year-old child presents with fever of 102.5°F for 2 days, tugging at the right ear, and irritability. Otoscopic exam reveals a bulging, erythematous tympanic membrane with limited mobility on pneumatic otoscopy. The child has no known drug allergies. Per AAP guidelines, what is the most appropriate initial treatment?
a: Amoxicillin 80-90 mg/kg/day divided twice daily for 10 days
Azithromycin 10 mg/kg on day 1, then 5 mg/kg for 4 days
D118.rationale: Per AAP 2013 guidelines, high-dose amoxicillin (80-90 mg/kg/day) is first-line for uncomplicated AOM in children with no recent antibiotic exposure. The child is <2 years equivalent (severe symptoms warrant treatment), has bilateral/severe symptoms, and treatment duration is 10 days for children <2 years or those with severe symptoms. Azithromycin is not first-line due to increasing resistance. Watchful waiting is only appropriate for children >6 months with non-severe unilateral AOM.

D118.q: A 5-year-old with penicillin allergy (urticarial rash) was diagnosed with AOM 48 hours ago. She has persistent fever of 103°F and worsening ear pain despite acetaminophen. What is the next best step in management?
a: Continue current management and reassess in 24 hours
Switch to azithromycin 10 mg/kg daily for 5 days
Prescribe cefdinir 14 mg/kg/day divided twice daily
D118.rationale: Treatment failure is defined as lack of improvement within 48-72 hours. For penicillin allergy without anaphylaxis, third-generation cephalosporins like cefdinir or cefpodoxime are appropriate per AAP guidelines. Azithromycin has high resistance rates for S. pneumoniae and H. influenzae. Tympanocentesis is reserved for severe cases unresponsive to multiple antibiotics or immunocompromised patients. The non-severe penicillin allergy allows use of cephalosporins.

D118.q: A 32-year-old presents with 12 days of purulent nasal discharge, facial pressure, and maxillary tooth pain. Symptoms initially improved on day 5 but worsened again on day 9. Temperature is 99.1°F. What diagnosis and management is most appropriate per IDSA guidelines?
a: Viral rhinosinusitis; supportive care with saline irrigation
Acute bacterial sinusitis; amoxicillin-clavulanate 875/125 mg BID for 5-7 days
Chronic sinusitis; referral to ENT for possible surgery
Acute bacterial sinusitis; amoxicillin 500 mg TID for 5-7 days
D118.rationale: This represents 'double worsening' (initial improvement followed by worsening), one of three criteria for acute bacterial rhinosinusitis per IDSA guidelines. The others are: symptoms >10 days without improvement, or severe symptoms (fever ≥39°C plus purulent discharge) for ≥3 consecutive days. Amoxicillin-clavulanate is preferred over amoxicillin due to increasing beta-lactamase producing organisms. Duration is 5-7 days in adults (vs 10-14 days previously).

D118.q: A 28-year-old with penicillin anaphylaxis history presents with acute bacterial sinusitis confirmed by symptoms >10 days. Which antibiotic is most appropriate?
a: Doxycycline 100 mg BID or levofloxacin 500 mg daily
Azithromycin 500 mg day 1, then 250 mg daily for 4 days
D118.rationale: For true penicillin allergy (anaphylaxis), doxycycline or respiratory fluoroquinolones (levofloxacin, moxifloxacin) are recommended per IDSA guidelines. Cephalosporins carry 1-10% cross-reactivity risk with anaphylactic penicillin allergy. Azithromycin has high resistance rates (>30% for S. pneumoniae). Clindamycin has poor coverage for H. influenzae, a common pathogen in acute bacterial rhinosinusitis.

D118.q: A 45-year-old presents with 8 days of rhinorrhea, facial pressure, and cough. No fever, and symptoms have been stable without worsening. What is the most appropriate management?
a: Supportive care with intranasal corticosteroids and saline irrigation
D118.rationale: This patient does not meet IDSA criteria for acute bacterial rhinosinusitis: symptoms <10 days without severe features or double worsening pattern. Most rhinosinusitis is viral and self-limited. Supportive care includes intranasal corticosteroids (reduce inflammation), saline irrigation, analgesics, and decongestants. Antibiotics are not indicated and contribute to resistance. Only 0.5-2% of viral rhinosinusitis develops bacterial superinfection.

D118.q: A 28-year-old otherwise healthy patient presents with 5 days of productive cough, rhinorrhea, and sore throat. No fever, vital signs normal, lung exam reveals scattered rhonchi that clear with cough. What is the most appropriate management?
a: Azithromycin 500 mg day 1, then 250 mg daily for 4 days
Supportive care with antitussives and reassurance
Albuterol inhaler and prednisone 40 mg for 5 days
D118.rationale: Acute bronchitis is typically viral (90-95%) and does not require antibiotics in otherwise healthy patients. ACCP and CDC guidelines recommend against routine antibiotic use. Supportive care includes antitussives (dextromethorphan), NSAIDs, and hydration. Cough typically lasts 2-3 weeks. Antibiotics are indicated only with suspected pertussis (cough >2-3 weeks, paroxysmal) or in patients with COPD with increased dyspnea and purulent sputum. Steroids and bronchodilators have limited benefit in non-asthmatic acute bronchitis.

D118.q: A 62-year-old with moderate COPD (on maintenance tiotropium) presents with 3 days of increased dyspnea, increased sputum volume that has turned green, and increased cough. Vital signs: Temp 99.8°F, RR 24, SpO2 91% on room air (baseline 94%). What is the most appropriate treatment?
a: Continue current COPD medications only, no antibiotics needed
Azithromycin 500 mg daily for 5 days plus prednisone 40 mg for 5 days
Amoxicillin-clavulanate 875/125 mg BID for 5 days plus prednisone 40 mg for 5 days
Levofloxacin 750 mg daily for 7 days plus albuterol nebulizer
D118.rationale: This is acute exacerbation of COPD (AECOPD) meeting Anthonisen criteria with all three cardinal symptoms: increased dyspnea, increased sputum volume, and increased sputum purulence. Per GOLD guidelines, antibiotics PLUS systemic corticosteroids are indicated. First-line antibiotics: amoxicillin-clavulanate, doxycycline, or macrolide. Amoxicillin-clavulanate is preferred with moderate-severe COPD for coverage of H. influenzae and beta-lactamase producers. Prednisone 40 mg for 5 days improves recovery and reduces treatment failure.

D118.q: A 45-year-old with asthma presents with 10 days of paroxysmal cough, especially at night, with post-tussive emesis. Inspiratory whoop noted. No fever. Which test and treatment are indicated?
a: Chest X-ray; azithromycin 500 mg daily for 5 days
PCR or culture for Bordetella pertussis; azithromycin 500 mg daily for 5 days
No testing needed; supportive care only as this is likely viral
D118.rationale: Clinical presentation suggests pertussis (whooping cough): prolonged cough >7-10 days, paroxysmal nature, post-tussive emesis, and inspiratory whoop. PCR is most sensitive diagnostic test (culture is specific but less sensitive). Treatment with macrolide (azithromycin 500 mg x5 days or 1g single dose) is recommended if within 3 weeks of cough onset to reduce transmission and shorten symptoms. After 3 weeks, antibiotics don't significantly alter clinical course but may still be given to limit spread.

D118.q: A 35-year-old presents with 4 days of cough and clear sputum. Temp 99.1°F, lungs clear. Patient demands antibiotics stating 'I always get bronchitis and need antibiotics.' What is the best approach?
a: Prescribe azithromycin to maintain patient satisfaction
Prescribe delayed antibiotic prescription to use if not better in 7 days
Explain viral etiology, provide supportive care education, and offer follow-up
Order chest X-ray to rule out pneumonia before deciding
D118.rationale: Antibiotic stewardship is critical. Per CDC and ACCP guidelines, acute bronchitis in healthy adults does not warrant antibiotics. Best practice involves: educating patient on viral etiology (90-95%), expected duration (2-3 weeks for cough), symptomatic treatment options, and when to return (fever, dyspnea, duration >3 weeks). Studies show patient education and shared decision-making improve satisfaction without antibiotics. Delayed prescriptions may be considered but still promote inappropriate use. Chest X-ray is not indicated without fever, tachypnea, or abnormal lung exam.

D118.q: A 24-year-old presents with clear rhinorrhea, sneezing, nasal congestion, and itchy eyes occurring every spring for the past 5 years. What is the most effective first-line pharmacologic treatment?
a: Intranasal corticosteroid (fluticasone 2 sprays each nostril daily)
D118.rationale: Intranasal corticosteroids are the most effective single-agent therapy for allergic rhinitis per AAO-HNSF and AAAAI guidelines, superior to oral antihistamines for nasal congestion, rhinorrhea, and sneezing. They treat both early and late-phase allergic responses. Onset is 12-24 hours with maximum benefit in 1-2 weeks. Oral antihistamines are less effective for congestion but can be added for ocular symptoms. Decongestants don't address underlying inflammation. Intranasal decongestants risk rhinitis medicamentosa if used >3 days.

D118.q: A 6-year-old with moderate-severe allergic rhinitis has inadequate symptom control on intranasal fluticasone alone. What is the most appropriate next step?
a: Increase intranasal steroid to three times daily
Add oral antihistamine (cetirizine) to intranasal steroid
Switch to oral leukotriene receptor antagonist (montelukast)
Refer for allergy testing and immunotherapy
D118.rationale: Per AAO-HNSF guidelines, combination therapy with intranasal corticosteroid PLUS oral antihistamine is superior to either agent alone for moderate-severe allergic rhinitis. This combination addresses both nasal and ocular symptoms with complementary mechanisms. Intranasal steroids should not be increased beyond recommended dosing. Montelukast is less effective than intranasal steroids. Immunotherapy is reserved for patients failing pharmacotherapy or those desiring disease modification.

D118.q: A 42-year-old has been using oxymetazoline nasal spray for 3 weeks for nasal congestion. Now reports worsening congestion requiring more frequent dosing. Nasal mucosa appears erythematous and edematous. What is the diagnosis and treatment?
a: Rhinitis medicamentosa; discontinue oxymetazoline and start intranasal corticosteroid
D118.rationale: Rhinitis medicamentosa (rebound congestion) results from prolonged use (>3-5 days) of intranasal decongestants like oxymetazoline. Treatment involves immediate discontinuation of the offending agent and initiation of intranasal corticosteroid to manage withdrawal congestion. May require 1-2 weeks for improvement. Some practitioners use short course oral steroids or gradual weaning (discontinue one nostril first). Patient education is critical: topical decongestants should never be used >3 consecutive days.

D118.q: A 5-year-old presents with 2 days of purulent yellow discharge from both eyes, matting of eyelashes in the morning, and conjunctival injection. No fever, vision intact, pupils reactive. What is the most appropriate treatment?
a: Topical erythromycin 0.5% ointment QID for 5-7 days
Supportive care with warm compresses only
D118.rationale: Bacterial conjunctivitis presents with purulent discharge, morning matting, and injection without vision changes. Most cases in children are self-limited, but topical antibiotics shorten duration and reduce transmission. Erythromycin ointment or polymyxin B-trimethoprim drops are first-line per AAO guidelines. Fluoroquinolone drops are reserved for contact lens wearers or treatment failures. Oral antibiotics are not indicated for uncomplicated conjunctivitis. Topical steroids are contraindicated without ophthalmology consultation (risk of HSV, fungal, or bacterial worsening).

D118.q: A 28-year-old presents with 3 days of red, watery eyes with clear discharge, photophobia, and palpable preauricular lymph node. Reports recent upper respiratory infection. What is the most likely diagnosis and management?
a: Allergic conjunctivitis; topical antihistamine/mast cell stabilizer
Viral conjunctivitis; supportive care and transmission precautions
Acute angle-closure glaucoma; emergent ophthalmology referral
D118.rationale: Viral conjunctivitis (often adenoviral) presents with watery discharge, photophobia, preauricular lymphadenopathy, and often follows URI. It is highly contagious and self-limited (7-14 days). Management is supportive: cool compresses, artificial tears, and strict hand hygiene. Transmission precautions include avoiding shared towels and staying home from work/school while symptomatic. Topical antibiotics do not alter course and may cause sensitization. Refer if vision changes, severe pain, or no improvement in 2 weeks.

D118.q: A 19-year-old with known seasonal allergies presents with bilateral itchy, red eyes with watery discharge and eyelid edema. Denies pain or vision changes. What is first-line treatment?
a: Artificial tears and cool compresses only
D118.rationale: Allergic conjunctivitis presents with bilateral itching (hallmark symptom), watery discharge, and chemosis. Topical antihistamine/mast cell stabilizers (olopatadine, ketotifen) are first-line per AAO guidelines, providing rapid relief and prevention. Combination antibiotic-steroids are inappropriate without bacterial infection and steroid risks. Oral antihistamines help but are less effective than topical therapy. Artificial tears provide adjunctive relief. Triggers include pollen, pet dander, and dust mites.
