What is the most likely diagnosis and your legal obligation?
a: Abusive head trauma (shaken baby syndrome); mandatory report to child protective services is legally required
Accidental head trauma from a short fall; document carefully and discharge
Glutaric aciduria type 1; obtain urine organic acids before reporting
Osteogenesis imperfecta; obtain genetic testing before reporting
D119.rationale: Abusive head trauma (AHT), formerly called shaken baby syndrome, is the leading cause of fatal head injury in infants. The classic triad is bilateral subdural hematomas, retinal hemorrhages, and encephalopathy — this combination in a non-ambulatory infant is highly specific for AHT and inconsistent with a short fall. All U.S. states mandate that licensed healthcare providers report suspected child abuse to CPS; failure to report is a criminal offense. Metabolic conditions (glutaric aciduria type 1) and OI should be considered in the differential, but neither causes retinal hemorrhages, and workup for these does NOT delay mandatory reporting when abuse is suspected. **Board tip:** Mandatory reporter obligations: suspicion alone (not certainty) triggers the legal duty to report. You do not need to prove abuse — 'reasonable suspicion' is the standard. CPS, not the provider, investigates.

D119.q: A 2-year-old is brought in for a well-child visit. During the exam, you note multiple bruises in various stages of healing — some on the back, buttocks, and ears. The mother says he 'falls a lot.' You also note a loop-shaped mark on the lower back. Which features are most concerning for physical abuse rather than accidental injury?
a: Bruises on the back, buttocks, ears, and loop-shaped patterned marks — these are unusual locations and patterns inconsistent with accidental injury
Bruises on the shins and forehead — common in toddlers who fall
A single bruise on the knee after a reported fall
Frenulum tear in a 10-year-old who fell off a bicycle
D119.rationale: The mnemonic 'TEN-4 FACES' (bruises on Torso, Ears, Neck in a child <4 years, or Frenulum, Any bruising on child <4 months [any bruise], Cheeks, Eyes, Subconjunctival hemorrhage) identifies bruising patterns with high specificity for physical abuse. Loop-shaped, cord-shaped, or belt-buckle-shaped patterned bruises suggest inflicted injury with an object. In contrast, shins, knees, and forehead are typical sites for accidental bruising in ambulatory children. Frenulum tears in non-mobile infants are highly suspicious for forced feeding or blow to the mouth. **Board tip:** Remember: 'Those who don't cruise rarely bruise.' Any bruising in a pre-ambulatory infant (<6–9 months) should be considered abuse until proven otherwise.

D119.q: A 4-year-old girl is brought in by her foster mother with a scald burn on the buttocks and perineum. The burn has a clear waterline (sharp, uniform margins), affecting the buttocks symmetrically while sparing the flexural creases. The foster mother reports the child was 'put in hot water as punishment.' What type of burn pattern confirms inflicted injury, and what is the next step?
a: Forced immersion scald burn (sharply demarcated stocking/glove or donut distribution); report to CPS and obtain burn surgery consultation
Accidental splash scald burn; wound care and follow up in 1 week
Contact burn from a stovetop; apply silver sulfadiazine and refer to dermatology
Chemical burn from cleaning product; document history and discharge with teaching
D119.rationale: Forced immersion scalds are pathognomonic for child abuse. Features indicating inflicted immersion: sharply demarcated margins ('waterline'), symmetric distribution on the buttocks/perineum/extremities (unlike splash burns which are irregular and asymmetric), sparing of flexural creases (child braced against container), and bilateral 'stocking/glove' pattern on extremities. The 'donut sign' — sparing of the central buttocks (pressed against the cooler tub floor) with burned perimeter — is classic. Accidental scalds create irregular splash patterns. CPS report is mandatory. **Board tip:** Burn patterns in child abuse: forced immersion = sharp waterline, symmetric; cigarette burns = circular, punched-out lesions typically on hands/feet/genitalia; contact burns = object-shaped (iron, radiator).

D119.q: A 6-year-old girl is brought in by her mother because of vaginal discharge and what the mother describes as 'behavioral changes' — the child has been sexualized in play with dolls and uses explicit sexual language inappropriate for her age. The hymen appears normal on exam. What is the appropriate evaluation and next step?
a: Obtain NAAT testing for gonorrhea and chlamydia, consult child advocacy center/SANE team, and report to CPS regardless of physical exam findings
Reassure mother that normal hymen examination rules out sexual abuse
Prescribe metronidazole for bacterial vaginosis and follow up in 2 weeks
Refer to gynecology for colposcopy before CPS report
D119.rationale: The behavioral indicators described (sexualized play, explicit sexual language beyond developmental norms) are strong markers of sexual abuse. Critically, a normal or nonspecific hymenal examination does NOT rule out sexual abuse — most sexually abused children have a normal genital exam because many forms of abuse leave no physical findings, and genital tissue heals rapidly. NAAT STI testing is indicated, as gonorrhea or chlamydia in a prepubertal child is a marker of sexual abuse. Child Advocacy Centers (CACs) provide multidisciplinary forensic evaluation. CPS report is legally required. **Board tip:** Normal genital exam ≠ no sexual abuse. Suspicious behavioral indicators (age-inappropriate sexual knowledge, sexualized play) trigger mandatory reporting without requiring physical evidence.

D119.q: A 3-year-old boy is consistently brought to your clinic underweight (below 3rd percentile), always appearing hungry and wearing clothing inappropriate for the season. You notice he eats ravenously when offered crackers in the exam room. His labs show anemia and low albumin. His mother rarely maintains eye contact and often cannot recall basic developmental history. His growth chart shows a consistent downward crossing of growth percentiles. What type of maltreatment is most likely occurring and what is your next step?
a: Medical neglect and physical neglect with failure to thrive; file a CPS report and arrange for inpatient hospitalization for nutritional rehabilitation and safety evaluation
Organic failure to thrive from an undiagnosed GI disorder; order extensive GI workup before CPS involvement
Poverty-related malnutrition; refer to WIC and social services only
Constitutional growth delay; reassure and recheck in 6 months
D119.rationale: Non-organic (neglect-related) failure to thrive is characterized by progressive malnutrition, absent organic cause, inappropriate dress or hygiene, and ravenous eating behavior when food is available (indicating chronic food insecurity). Low albumin confirms nutritional deprivation. Constitutional growth delay has otherwise normal nutrition, development, and care. Poverty-related malnutrition may overlap with neglect, but the convergence of hunger signs, anemia, hypoalbuminemia, and parental disengagement indicates neglect requiring CPS report — not social services referral alone. Inpatient hospitalization serves dual purposes: nutritional rehab AND safe environment for multidisciplinary team assessment. **Board tip:** Neglect is the most common form of child maltreatment and the most common cause of non-organic failure to thrive. When in doubt, report — CPS determines intent; clinicians determine suspicion.

D119.q: An 18-month-old with a history of eczema presents 15 minutes after eating peanut butter for the first time with hives, facial swelling, vomiting, and audible wheezing. His oxygen saturation is 93%. What is the first-line treatment?
a: Intramuscular epinephrine (0.01 mg/kg, 1:1000 concentration) in the anterolateral thigh
D119.rationale: This is anaphylaxis — a severe, potentially fatal systemic allergic reaction. Epinephrine IM (anterolateral thigh) is the ONLY first-line treatment for anaphylaxis; it reverses bronchospasm, vasodilation, and angioedema. Epinephrine must be given immediately — delay increases mortality. Antihistamines (diphenhydramine, cetirizine) do not treat airway edema, hypotension, or bronchospasm and should never be used as monotherapy or first-line for anaphylaxis. Albuterol may be added as adjunct for bronchospasm but does not treat systemic anaphylaxis. After epinephrine, give IV fluids, oxygen, and observe for biphasic reaction (4–12 hours). **Board tip:** Anaphylaxis = epinephrine FIRST — not antihistamines, not steroids. Epinephrine saves lives. Prescribe an epinephrine auto-injector (EpiPen) for home use at discharge and refer to allergology.

D119.q: A 3-year-old girl has had chronic dry, itchy skin since infancy, worse in the winter and in elbow/knee creases. She has a strong family history of asthma and allergic rhinitis. Exam shows lichenified, excoriated patches in the antecubital and popliteal fossae and behind the ears. Her IgE is elevated. What is the first-line treatment and the most important maintenance principle?
a: Fragrance-free moisturizer applied liberally multiple times daily (skin barrier repair) as first-line; low-potency topical corticosteroid for flares
Oral diphenhydramine daily for itch control
Topical calcineurin inhibitors (tacrolimus) as first-line for all ages
Eliminate all dietary proteins including milk, egg, and wheat
D119.rationale: Atopic dermatitis (AD) management follows a step-up approach. The cornerstone is aggressive skin barrier repair with liberal, frequent application of thick emollients (creams/ointments — not lotions). Mild-moderate flares are treated with low-to-mid-potency topical corticosteroids. Oral antihistamines have limited evidence for itch control and cause sedation without addressing inflammation. Tacrolimus (a topical calcineurin inhibitor) is effective but carries an FDA black-box warning for use in children <2 years and is second-line, not first-line. Dietary elimination without confirmed food allergy is not indicated and may cause nutritional deficiencies. **Board tip:** AD treatment hierarchy: emollients (always) → topical steroids (flares) → TCI (tacrolimus/pimecrolimus, maintenance on sensitive areas) → dupilumab (severe/refractory). Wet wrap therapy for severe flares is highly effective in children.

D119.q: A 7-year-old boy with moderate persistent asthma also has chronic nasal congestion, sneezing, and itchy eyes that worsen in spring. His asthma control is poor despite appropriate inhaler use. Skin prick testing confirms sensitivity to tree pollen and dust mites. What is the benefit of treating his allergic rhinitis aggressively in the context of asthma?
a: Treating allergic rhinitis with intranasal corticosteroids improves asthma control — upper and lower airway inflammation are linked ('united airway' concept)
Allergic rhinitis and asthma are independent — nasal treatment will not affect asthma control
Oral antihistamines are preferred over intranasal steroids in asthmatic children
Allergen immunotherapy is contraindicated in children under 12
D119.rationale: The 'united airway' or 'one airway, one disease' concept recognizes that allergic rhinitis and asthma share pathophysiology and commonly co-occur (up to 80% of asthmatic patients have rhinitis). Effective treatment of upper airway inflammation with intranasal corticosteroids (INCs — first-line for allergic rhinitis) reduces nasal discharge draining into lower airways, decreases systemic inflammation, and improves asthma outcomes. Oral antihistamines treat nasal symptoms but do not reduce inflammation as effectively as INCs and may cause sedation. Allergen immunotherapy (subcutaneous or sublingual) is appropriate for children ≥5 years with confirmed allergy and moderate-severe symptoms. **Board tip:** When pediatric asthma is poorly controlled, always evaluate for and treat comorbid allergic rhinitis — it is one of the most common asthma triggers and management gap.

D119.q: A 12-month-old with moderate atopic dermatitis had a positive skin prick test to egg. His parents ask when and how they should introduce egg into his diet. What does current AAP/LEAP trial evidence recommend?
a: Early introduction of allergenic foods (including egg and peanut) in high-risk infants is recommended at 4–6 months to REDUCE food allergy risk, not delay it
Delay all egg introduction until 24 months in children with eczema
Avoid egg entirely until formal allergy testing at 3 years of age
Introduce egg only in an allergist's office due to the eczema history
D119.rationale: The landmark LEAP (Learning Early About Peanut Allergy) trial and subsequent guidelines from the AAP and NIAID reversed previous avoidance recommendations. Early introduction of allergenic foods (peanut, egg) at 4–6 months of age in high-risk infants (severe eczema or egg allergy) significantly reduces the risk of developing food allergy. For infants with mild-moderate eczema, early introduction at home is recommended. For infants with severe eczema or existing egg allergy, allergy evaluation before peanut introduction is recommended (but not indefinite avoidance). Delaying allergenic food introduction increases allergy risk. **Board tip:** LEAP trial showed ~80% reduction in peanut allergy with early introduction in high-risk infants. AAP now supports introduction of allergenic foods at ~4–6 months — this is a major guideline change from prior 'avoidance' recommendations.

D119.q: A 9-year-old boy has a history of seasonal allergic rhinitis controlled with intranasal fluticasone. He now presents with worsening symptoms year-round and newly developed mild persistent asthma. His parents ask about allergen immunotherapy (AIT). What is the appropriate counseling?
a: AIT (allergy shots or sublingual drops) is appropriate for children with confirmed allergen sensitivity, poorly controlled symptoms on medications, and concurrent asthma — it can modify the disease and reduce asthma progression
AIT is contraindicated in children with asthma
AIT is only available for children ≥18 years
AIT provides only temporary symptom relief and does not modify the disease course
D119.rationale: Allergen immunotherapy (subcutaneous injections or sublingual immunotherapy) is indicated for children with moderate-severe allergic rhinitis not adequately controlled with pharmacotherapy, confirmed allergen sensitization, and/or allergic asthma. AIT is the only disease-modifying treatment for IgE-mediated allergic disease — it reduces symptom severity, medication requirements, and the risk of developing new sensitivities. AIT has been shown to reduce the progression from allergic rhinitis to asthma and prevent new allergen sensitization. Asthma is not a contraindication but must be well-controlled before starting (FEV1 >70%). **Clinical pearl:** SLIT (sublingual immunotherapy) is increasingly used in children as an alternative to shots; it is FDA-approved for dust mites and certain pollens and can be administered at home.

D119.q: A 16-year-old sexually active female presents for a well-teen visit. She does not want her parents to know she is sexually active. Which of the following describes the appropriate approach to confidentiality and STI screening in adolescents?
a: Provide confidential STI screening (NAAT for chlamydia/gonorrhea, HIV, syphilis per CDC) and contraception counseling without parental consent — minor consent laws protect STI care in all 50 states
Refuse to provide STI screening without parental consent
Notify parents because the patient is under 18 and cannot consent to STI testing
Provide STI testing only if the minor is emancipated
D119.rationale: All 50 U.S. states have minor consent laws that allow adolescents to consent to STI diagnosis and treatment without parental consent or notification. The AAP, ACOG, and USPSTF all recommend confidential sexual health services for adolescents to reduce barriers to care. The GAPS (Guidelines for Adolescent Preventive Services) and CDC recommend annual chlamydia/gonorrhea screening for all sexually active females ≤25 years, HIV screening starting at age 13–64, and syphilis screening based on risk. Confidentiality should be maintained except for mandatory reporting (abuse, imminent harm to self/others). **Board tip:** Areas where minors can consent without parental permission vary by state but consistently include: STI testing/treatment, contraception, substance abuse treatment, and mental health crisis care (in most states). KNOW this for the boards.

D119.q: A 15-year-old female athlete presents for her sports physical. Her mother mentions she restricts her eating, exercises excessively, and has missed her last 4 menstrual periods. Her BMI is 17.2 kg/m². She denies binge-purge behaviors. Vital signs show bradycardia (HR 46 bpm) and orthostatic hypotension. What is the most appropriate next step?
a: Restrict athletic participation, evaluate for anorexia nervosa, check ECG, metabolic panel, CBC, and refer to multidisciplinary eating disorder team
Reassure — amenorrhea is common in female athletes and no intervention is needed
Prescribe combined oral contraceptives to restore menses
Recommend increased caloric intake and recheck in 3 months
D119.rationale: This presentation is consistent with anorexia nervosa and the Female Athlete Triad (energy deficiency, amenorrhea, low bone density). Bradycardia and orthostatic hypotension indicate cardiovascular compromise requiring immediate clearance from sports — athletes with resting HR <50 bpm, orthostatic changes, or electrolyte abnormalities should not participate. ECG is needed to assess QT prolongation (risk of arrhythmia in malnutrition). Multidisciplinary care (physician, dietitian, psychologist) is essential. OCPs do not restore natural menstrual function or protect bone density without nutritional rehabilitation. Reassurance without intervention is dangerous. **Board tip:** The Female Athlete Triad = low energy availability + functional hypothalamic amenorrhea + low bone mineral density. Medical clearance criteria for return-to-sport include BMI ≥18.5, HR >50, normal electrolytes, and weight restoration progress.

D119.q: A 17-year-old male presents with his parents, who are concerned about his marijuana use. He uses marijuana daily, has declining grades, dropped out of sports, and states 'I don't really care about much anymore.' He denies depression. The CRAFFT screening tool score is 4. What is the appropriate response?
a: Brief motivational intervention in the office, provide referral for substance use counseling, and schedule close follow-up — CRAFFT ≥2 indicates significant risk
Inform parents of all details of the visit regardless of patient consent
Prescribe bupropion for suspected depression-related cannabis use
Perform a urine drug screen without telling the patient and share results with parents
D119.rationale: The CRAFFT screening tool (Car, Relax, Alone, Forget, Friends, Trouble) is validated for adolescent substance use screening; a score ≥2 indicates significant risk and warrants brief intervention and referral to treatment (SBIRT model — Screening, Brief Intervention, Referral to Treatment). Daily cannabis use in adolescents is associated with impaired neurodevelopment, amotivational syndrome, and academic failure. Confidentiality is maintained for substance use (except imminent danger), though parents may be involved with patient consent. Performing covert drug testing violates patient trust and undermines the therapeutic relationship. Bupropion is not indicated without a formal depression diagnosis. **Clinical pearl:** Adolescent cannabis use is associated with a 4–7× increased risk of psychosis, particularly in those with family history of schizophrenia. Early intervention before addiction develops is key.

D119.q: During a well-teen visit for a 14-year-old girl, you administer the PHQ-A (Patient Health Questionnaire for Adolescents). She scores 18/27, reports persistent sadness for 3 weeks, loss of interest in activities, insomnia, and states 'sometimes I wish I wasn't here.' She denies a specific plan. What is the most appropriate immediate action?
a: Conduct a full suicide risk assessment (Columbia Protocol/C-SSRS), involve parents with patient's knowledge, arrange same-day mental health referral or emergency evaluation if risk is high
Prescribe fluoxetine and schedule a 4-week follow-up
Reassure the patient that these feelings are normal for teenagers and recheck PHQ-A in 1 month
Provide a mental health referral and discharge without further assessment
D119.rationale: A PHQ-A score ≥15 indicates severe depression, and any passive suicidal ideation (even without a plan) requires immediate structured suicide risk assessment using a validated tool (C-SSRS — Columbia Suicide Severity Rating Scale). The statement 'I wish I wasn't here' is passive suicidal ideation and must not be minimized. Based on risk level, the patient may need same-day psychiatric evaluation or ED referral. Parents should be informed (with the patient present) when there is safety risk — this supersedes confidentiality. Fluoxetine (SSRI) is first-line for adolescent depression but cannot be started without safety assessment and is not an acute safety measure. **Board tip:** Fluoxetine is the only FDA-approved antidepressant for depression in children ≥8 years. All antidepressants carry an FDA black-box warning for increased suicidal ideation in children and adolescents — close monitoring in the first weeks is mandatory.

D119.q: A 17-year-old male presents for a well-teen visit. He is in 11th grade, plays sports, and has no past medical history. Per GAPS (Guidelines for Adolescent Preventive Services) and AAP Bright Futures recommendations, which of the following screening and vaccination elements is appropriate at this visit?
a: Depression screening (PHQ-A), lipid screening if risk factors present, Tdap booster if not received since age 11, annual meningococcal conjugate vaccine (MenACWY) booster if first dose was at age 11–12, HPV series if not complete, and confidential substance use and sexual health screening
Full CBC and comprehensive metabolic panel as routine screening labs
HIV screening only if the patient discloses sexual activity
Cholesterol screening only after age 20 in males
D119.rationale: AAP Bright Futures and GAPS recommend the following for all adolescent well visits: universal depression screening (PHQ-A), confidential HEADSSS psychosocial interview (Home, Education, Activities, Drugs, Sex, Suicide/Safety), and adolescent-specific immunizations. At age 16–17, MenACWY booster is recommended if the first dose was given at 11–12 (2-dose series at 11–12 then 16). Tdap is given at 11–12 (one dose lifetime). HPV vaccine series (2 doses if started ≤14; 3 doses if started ≥15) should be completed. Lipid screening: universal non-fasting lipid panel at 9–11 and 17–21, or earlier with risk factors. HIV screening: universal opt-out screening is recommended for all patients 13–64 regardless of disclosure. **Board tip:** HEADSSS psychosocial screen is THE tool for comprehensive adolescent well visit assessment. Always conduct the interview alone (without parents) to allow confidential disclosure.

D119.q: A 7-year-old is evaluated for possible ADHD. His mother says he is hyperactive at home but his teacher reports no concerns at school. He performs well academically. Which statement best applies to this presentation per DSM-5?
a: He meets DSM-5 criteria because symptoms are present at home
He does not meet DSM-5 criteria because symptoms must occur in two or more settings
He should be started on methylphenidate and reassessed in 4 weeks
The school report is less reliable than the parent report for DSM-5 diagnosis
D119.rationale: DSM-5 requires ADHD symptoms to be present in two or more settings (e.g., home, school, work). Symptoms present only at home without school confirmation do not meet diagnostic criteria and may suggest situational or family-related factors. **Board tip:** Always verify symptoms across settings — if only one setting reports concerns, ADHD is not diagnosable per DSM-5.

D119.q: Per DSM-5, what is the minimum number of inattentive or hyperactive-impulsive symptoms required to diagnose ADHD in a child aged 6 years?
D119.rationale: DSM-5 requires at least 6 symptoms of inattention or 6 symptoms of hyperactivity-impulsivity (or both) in children up to age 16. For adolescents 17 and older and adults, the threshold drops to 5 symptoms. Symptoms must persist for at least 6 months and be inconsistent with developmental level. **Board tip:** The threshold is 6 for children, 5 for adults — a commonly tested distinction.

D119.q: A mother asks about medication options for her 5-year-old son recently diagnosed with ADHD. He attends a structured preschool program. What should be the first-line management per AAP guidelines?
a: Start methylphenidate at the lowest available dose
Start amphetamine salts given superior efficacy in preschoolers
Refer for behavior therapy before initiating any medication
Start atomoxetine as it is safer in young children
D119.rationale: AAP guidelines recommend behavior therapy as the first-line treatment for preschool-aged children (4–5 years) with ADHD. Parent training in behavior management and teacher-based interventions should be exhausted before considering medication. If behavior therapy is insufficient, methylphenidate (not amphetamines) may be considered in preschoolers. **Board tip:** Behavior therapy FIRST for preschoolers — medication is a second step in this age group.

D119.q: A 10-year-old with ADHD is started on methylphenidate. Which monitoring parameter must be assessed at every follow-up visit?
a: Blood pressure, heart rate, height, and weight
D119.rationale: Stimulant medications (methylphenidate and amphetamines) can elevate blood pressure and heart rate. They also suppress appetite, leading to weight loss and potential growth delay. At every visit, providers should measure BP, HR, height, weight, and assess appetite and sleep. **Board tip:** Growth and cardiovascular monitoring are mandatory at every stimulant follow-up — especially height/weight plotted on a growth chart.

D119.q: A 9-year-old girl on methylphenidate for ADHD has been doing well academically. However, her parents report she becomes very irritable, tearful, and 'bounces off the walls' in the late afternoon after school. What is this phenomenon called?
D119.rationale: The rebound effect occurs as short-acting methylphenidate wears off in the late afternoon, causing a temporary worsening of ADHD symptoms plus irritability. This is the rebound (or 'crash') phenomenon. Management options include switching to a long-acting formulation, adding a small afternoon dose, or transitioning to non-stimulant therapy. **Board tip:** Late-afternoon irritability after stimulants = rebound effect — a classic board scenario.

D119.q: A 12-year-old boy has ADHD and a comorbid tic disorder. His tics have worsened since starting amphetamine salts. Which medication would be MOST appropriate as an alternative that also addresses both ADHD and tics?
a: Switch to methylphenidate at a higher dose
Discontinue all ADHD medications and monitor
Start bupropion as a dual-purpose agent
D119.rationale: Guanfacine (alpha-2A adrenergic agonist) is an FDA-approved non-stimulant for ADHD that also reduces tic severity. It is particularly useful when stimulants exacerbate tics. Clonidine is another alpha-2 agonist option. Stimulants (both amphetamines and methylphenidate) can worsen tics. **Board tip:** ADHD + tics → guanfacine or clonidine (non-stimulant alpha-2 agonists that treat both conditions).

D119.q: An 8-year-old boy with ADHD is started on atomoxetine. His mother asks how this medication works differently from stimulants. What is the most accurate explanation?
a: It increases dopamine release in the prefrontal cortex via amphetamine-like mechanism
It is a selective norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor that works over several weeks
It directly stimulates alpha-1 receptors in the brainstem
It acts within 30 minutes and can be given as needed
D119.rationale: Atomoxetine is a selective norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor (SNRI-like mechanism) — NOT a stimulant and not a controlled substance. It takes 4–6 weeks to reach full therapeutic effect and must be given daily. Unlike stimulants, it does not have abuse potential. **Board tip:** Atomoxetine = non-stimulant, non-controlled, takes weeks to work, good for patients with substance abuse history or those who cannot tolerate stimulants.

D119.q: A 14-year-old with ADHD is being evaluated for stimulant therapy. He has a history of marijuana use on weekends. Which consideration is MOST important regarding stimulant prescribing in this patient?
a: Stimulants are contraindicated in any patient with substance use history
Untreated ADHD itself increases risk for substance abuse; treated ADHD may reduce this risk
Atomoxetine is preferred because it has no abuse potential and eliminates substance use risk
Amphetamines should be chosen over methylphenidate as they are less prone to diversion
D119.rationale: Research shows untreated ADHD is an independent risk factor for substance use disorders (SUD). Appropriate treatment of ADHD with stimulants may actually reduce the risk of SUD long-term. However, stimulants should be prescribed cautiously with close monitoring, preferring long-acting formulations (harder to abuse/divert) and considering non-stimulants if diversion risk is high. **Board tip:** ADHD itself increases SUD risk — treating ADHD reduces SUD risk, but use long-acting formulations to minimize diversion.

D119.q: A 10-year-old boy is started on methylphenidate 5 mg twice daily. After 4 weeks his mother reports minimal improvement in focus. His BP and HR are within normal limits. What is the appropriate next step?
a: Increase the methylphenidate dose and reassess in 4 weeks
Add a SSRI for comorbid anxiety before adjusting stimulant dose
D119.rationale: When initial stimulant dosing is insufficient, the appropriate approach is to titrate upward. Methylphenidate is typically increased every 1–4 weeks based on response and tolerability, up to the maximum dose. If an adequate trial at maximum dose fails, then switching to the other stimulant class (amphetamines) or a non-stimulant is appropriate. **Board tip:** Titrate dose before switching class — incomplete response to low-dose stimulant warrants dose increase, not class change.

D119.q: Which ADHD presentation is characterized primarily by difficulties sustaining attention, losing items, being easily distracted, and forgetting daily activities WITHOUT significant hyperactivity?
D119.rationale: DSM-5 specifies three presentations: (1) Combined (both inattentive and hyperactive-impulsive criteria met), (2) Predominantly Inattentive (≥6 inattentive symptoms, <6 hyperactive-impulsive), and (3) Predominantly Hyperactive-Impulsive (≥6 hyperactive-impulsive, <6 inattentive). Girls are more commonly diagnosed with the inattentive presentation and may be underdiagnosed. **Board tip:** Inattentive ADHD ('daydreamer') — commonly missed in girls; no hyperactivity required.

D119.q: A 9-year-old with ADHD is trialed on methylphenidate without response after dose optimization. Which stimulant class should be tried next?
a: Start a combination of methylphenidate plus guanfacine immediately
Proceed directly to atomoxetine without trying another stimulant
D119.rationale: Methylphenidate and amphetamines are the two main stimulant classes for ADHD. If one class fails after adequate trial and dose optimization, switching to the other class is appropriate before moving to non-stimulants. Approximately 30–40% of patients who do not respond to one stimulant class will respond to the other. **Board tip:** Two stimulant classes = methylphenidate and amphetamines; try both before going to non-stimulants.

D119.q: A parent asks whether their child with ADHD will need to take stimulant medication on weekends and holidays. What is the most accurate guidance?
a: Stimulants must be taken 7 days a week to maintain therapeutic blood levels
Stimulant holidays can be taken on weekends/summers but must be individualized based on functional needs
Stopping stimulants on weekends causes withdrawal and worsens ADHD
Weekend drug holidays are never recommended due to rebound hyperactivity
D119.rationale: Drug holidays (weekends, summers) are sometimes recommended to allow for growth rebound and assess current symptom severity without medication. The decision is individualized based on whether the child needs medication for non-academic activities, social functioning, and growth concerns. Stimulants do not cause physiological dependence in therapeutic doses. **Board tip:** Drug holidays are permissible and sometimes recommended — individualize based on the child's needs and growth monitoring.

D119.q: A 10-year-old with ADHD has been on long-acting amphetamine for 6 months. His parents report he has dropped from the 45th to the 20th percentile for height. What is the best management step?
a: Discontinue amphetamines permanently and start atomoxetine
Consider planned medication holidays and reassess growth trajectory
Switch to methylphenidate as it has no effect on growth
Add growth hormone therapy to compensate
D119.rationale: Stimulants can suppress appetite and slow growth velocity, a well-documented side effect. Management includes monitoring growth at each visit, considering drug holidays during summers to allow catch-up growth, optimizing meal timing around medication, and evaluating whether the growth effect justifies continued treatment. Growth typically normalizes over time. **Board tip:** Growth suppression with stimulants → consider drug holidays + monitor — not immediate discontinuation as first step.

D119.q: A parent of a 6-year-old recently diagnosed with ADHD insists on behavioral therapy but wants to know what specific techniques teachers should use. Which school-based intervention is most evidence-based for ADHD?
a: Sensory integration therapy in a quiet room
Daily report cards with contingency management and classroom accommodations
Elimination diet with food dye restriction
D119.rationale: Evidence-based school interventions for ADHD include: daily report cards (target behaviors rated daily, linked to home rewards), classroom accommodations (preferential seating, extended time, reduced assignments), contingency management (immediate reinforcement for on-task behavior), and organizational skill training. Sensory or psychoanalytic therapies lack strong evidence. **Board tip:** Daily report cards + classroom accommodations = gold-standard school-based ADHD interventions.

D119.q: A 13-year-old boy with ADHD and well-controlled symptoms on long-acting methylphenidate presents for a routine visit. His resting BP is 130/82 mmHg (95th+ percentile for age). He has no cardiac history. What is the most appropriate next step?
a: Immediately discontinue methylphenidate and switch to atomoxetine
Obtain an EKG and refer to cardiology before any medication change
Recheck blood pressure after 30 minutes of rest; if still elevated, reduce or hold stimulant dose
Continue current dose as mild BP elevation is expected with stimulants
D119.rationale: Stimulants can raise blood pressure. An elevated reading should first be confirmed by rechecking after rest. If consistently elevated at or above the 95th percentile, dose reduction or switching to a non-stimulant (like atomoxetine or guanfacine) is appropriate. Guanfacine has the benefit of treating ADHD while also lowering BP. An EKG is indicated if structural cardiac disease is suspected but not routinely for hypertension alone. **Board tip:** Persistent BP elevation on stimulants → reduce dose or switch to guanfacine (which lowers BP and treats ADHD).

D119.q: A 6-year-old with intermittent asthma (symptoms ≤2 days/week, no nighttime symptoms, no interference with activity, FEV1 ≥80%) requires a prescription. What is the appropriate NAEPP Step 1 treatment?
a: Short-acting beta-2 agonist (SABA) as needed only
Daily ICS plus long-acting beta-2 agonist (LABA)
D119.rationale: NAEPP Step 1 (intermittent asthma) requires only a short-acting beta-2 agonist (SABA, e.g., albuterol) used as needed. No daily controller medication is required at Step 1. Stepping up to Step 2 (adding low-dose ICS) is appropriate when symptoms occur more than 2 days per week or the patient has ≥2 exacerbations per year requiring systemic steroids. **Board tip:** Step 1 = SABA PRN only; Step 2 = add low-dose ICS as the first controller medication.

D119.q: A 9-year-old with persistent asthma is on Step 2 therapy (low-dose ICS) but continues to have symptoms 4 days per week with one nighttime awakening per week. What is the best Step-Up approach per NAEPP guidelines?
a: Add an oral leukotriene receptor antagonist as the only change
Step up to medium-dose ICS or add LABA to low-dose ICS (Step 3)
Initiate oral prednisone daily as maintenance therapy
D119.rationale: NAEPP Step 3 options for children 5–11 years include: medium-dose ICS, OR low-dose ICS plus LABA, OR low-dose ICS plus leukotriene receptor antagonist. Stepping from Step 2 to Step 3 is appropriate when symptoms are not controlled on low-dose ICS alone. Note: LABA monotherapy without ICS is contraindicated in asthma. **Board tip:** Step 3 for children = medium-dose ICS OR low-dose ICS + LABA — key step-up from Step 2.

D119.q: A mother of an 8-year-old with asthma reports her child is using the albuterol metered-dose inhaler without a spacer. Why should a spacer be recommended?
a: Spacers allow higher doses to be administered safely
Spacers increase drug deposition in the lungs and reduce oropharyngeal deposition
Spacers convert the MDI to a dry powder inhaler
Spacers are only required for inhaled corticosteroids, not SABAs
D119.rationale: Spacers (valved holding chambers) significantly improve drug delivery to the lower airways and reduce oropharyngeal deposition, which decreases local side effects (e.g., oral candidiasis with ICS) and improves efficacy. They are recommended for all children using metered-dose inhalers (MDIs), especially for ICS. Children under 5–6 years old require a spacer with a mask. **Board tip:** Spacer = better lung delivery + fewer oral side effects — recommend for ALL children using MDIs, especially ICS.

D119.q: A 10-year-old boy with asthma develops wheezing and dyspnea specifically when playing soccer but is otherwise asymptomatic. Spirometry is normal at rest. What is the most likely diagnosis and initial management?
a: Vocal cord dysfunction; refer to speech therapy
Exercise-induced bronchoconstriction; prescribe SABA 15 minutes before exercise
Step 2 persistent asthma; start daily low-dose ICS
Cardiac arrhythmia; obtain EKG and Holter monitor
D119.rationale: Exercise-induced bronchoconstriction (EIB) presents as wheezing, coughing, or dyspnea triggered by exercise, typically starting 5–10 minutes into exercise and peaking after cessation. Spirometry is normal at rest. First-line management is a SABA (albuterol) inhaled 15–30 minutes before exercise. If inadequately controlled, daily ICS or LTRA can be added. **Board tip:** EIB = pre-exercise SABA 15 min before activity — classic board management.

D119.q: Which of the following is the most common trigger for asthma exacerbations in school-age children?
D119.rationale: Viral upper respiratory infections (especially rhinovirus) are the most common trigger for asthma exacerbations in children, responsible for approximately 80% of exacerbations in school-age children. Other important triggers include allergens (dust mites, pet dander, cockroaches, mold), tobacco smoke, exercise, cold air, and air pollutants. **Board tip:** Viral URIs = #1 asthma trigger in children — exacerbations spike in September ('September epidemic') when school resumes.

D119.q: A parent asks what color zone on the asthma action plan indicates the child is doing well and no intervention is needed. Which answer is correct?
a: Yellow zone — caution, add rescue medications
Green zone — doing well, continue controller medications only
Blue zone — emergency department visit required
D119.rationale: Asthma action plans use a traffic light system: Green zone = doing well (peak flow ≥80% personal best, no symptoms) — continue controller medications. Yellow zone = caution (peak flow 50–79%, mild symptoms) — add rescue SABA. Red zone = danger (peak flow <50%, severe symptoms) — immediate SABA and seek emergency care. **Board tip:** Green = continue controllers; Yellow = add SABA rescue; Red = emergency care — know all three zones.

D119.q: A 7-year-old with Step 4 asthma (high-dose ICS plus LABA) continues to have frequent exacerbations. He has elevated blood eosinophils. Which biologic medication targeting the IL-5 pathway would be appropriate to consider?
D119.rationale: Mepolizumab is an anti-IL-5 monoclonal antibody approved for severe eosinophilic asthma in patients ≥6 years. It reduces eosinophils and decreases exacerbation frequency. Omalizumab targets IgE (for allergic asthma), dupilumab targets IL-4/IL-13 receptor, and benralizumab targets the IL-5 receptor alpha. For elevated eosinophils, anti-IL-5 biologics (mepolizumab, benralizumab) are most appropriate. **Board tip:** Eosinophilic asthma + biologic → anti-IL-5 agents; allergic asthma (high IgE) → omalizumab.

D119.q: A mother of a 5-year-old with persistent asthma asks about the difference between a 'controller' and a 'rescue' inhaler. What is the most accurate explanation?
a: Controller inhalers are used only during attacks; rescue inhalers prevent future attacks
Controller inhalers are taken daily to prevent symptoms; rescue inhalers provide quick relief during acute symptoms
Both inhalers work the same way but differ in cost
Rescue inhalers are inhaled corticosteroids taken twice daily
D119.rationale: Controller medications (e.g., inhaled corticosteroids, LABAs, LTRAs) are taken daily to reduce airway inflammation and prevent symptoms — they do not provide immediate relief. Rescue medications (e.g., short-acting beta-2 agonists like albuterol) provide rapid bronchodilation for acute symptoms but do not treat underlying inflammation. **Board tip:** Controller = daily prevention; Rescue = PRN quick relief — ICS is controller, albuterol is rescue.

D119.q: A 12-year-old with allergic asthma has a serum total IgE of 650 IU/mL and positive skin testing to dust mites. Despite high-dose ICS plus LABA, he has 3 exacerbations per year. Which add-on therapy is most appropriate?
D119.rationale: Omalizumab (anti-IgE) is approved for moderate-to-severe persistent allergic asthma in patients ≥6 years with elevated IgE and positive skin testing. It reduces exacerbation frequency and allows ICS dose reduction. It is given subcutaneously every 2–4 weeks. Oral corticosteroids are Step 6 (last resort due to side effects). **Board tip:** Omalizumab = elevated IgE + allergic asthma + Step 5–6 uncontrolled = right answer on boards.

D119.q: A 3-year-old with recurrent wheezing responds well to albuterol during episodes but has no symptoms between episodes and normal growth. She has no eczema or family history of asthma. What is the most appropriate management?
a: Start daily low-dose ICS as early persistent asthma
Prescribe SABA for episodic use only and reassess — may be transient early childhood wheezing
Initiate a LABA for prevention of future episodes
Refer immediately for pulmonary function testing
D119.rationale: Not all wheezing in young children represents asthma. Transient early childhood wheezing (often viral-induced) is common in infants and toddlers and frequently resolves by age 3–5. In children without atopic features (no eczema, no allergic rhinitis, no family history), episodic wheezing with normal intervals suggests transient wheezing. SABA PRN for episodes is appropriate; daily ICS is not yet indicated. **Board tip:** Episodic viral wheezing in toddlers without atopy = likely transient wheezing, not asthma — SABA PRN, not daily ICS.

D119.q: Which inhaled corticosteroid side effect is most important to counsel parents about when starting a 6-year-old on daily ICS therapy?
a: Permanent growth stunting requiring GH replacement
Oral candidiasis (thrush) if inhaler technique is improper without spacer/rinsing
Adrenal suppression requiring stress dosing for all fevers
D119.rationale: Oral candidiasis (thrush) is a local side effect of ICS caused by oropharyngeal deposition of steroid. It is prevented by using a spacer and rinsing the mouth with water after each use. Low-dose ICS use has a minimal effect on growth (approximately 1 cm/year in first year, not progressive). Adrenal suppression is a concern only with very high doses. **Board tip:** ICS local side effect = oral candidiasis → prevent with spacer + mouth rinse.

D119.q: A 10-year-old with asthma presents with acute wheezing, HR 118, RR 28, oxygen saturation 93% on room air, and moderate retractions. He is given albuterol x3 back-to-back with minimal improvement. What is the next most appropriate intervention?
a: Discharge with increased albuterol frequency at home
Administer systemic corticosteroids (oral prednisolone or IV methylprednisolone)
Initiate inhaled ipratropium as sole treatment
D119.rationale: In moderate-to-severe asthma exacerbations not responding to initial SABA, systemic corticosteroids (oral prednisolone or IV methylprednisolone) are indicated to reduce airway inflammation. Ipratropium (SAMA) can be added to albuterol in severe exacerbations for additional bronchodilation. Intubation is a last resort for impending respiratory failure. **Board tip:** SABA-unresponsive exacerbation → add systemic corticosteroids; severe exacerbation → combine SABA + ipratropium + steroids.

D119.q: At what well-child visits does the AAP recommend universal ASD screening using the M-CHAT (Modified Checklist for Autism in Toddlers)?
D119.rationale: The AAP recommends universal ASD screening with the M-CHAT at the 18-month and 24-month well-child visits. These visits coincide with the developmental window when ASD features become apparent. A positive screen should prompt further developmental evaluation and referral, not just watchful waiting. **Board tip:** M-CHAT at 18 months AND 24 months — two specific ages, both required for universal screening.

D119.q: Per DSM-5, autism spectrum disorder is defined by deficits in which two core domains?
a: Social communication/interaction AND restricted/repetitive behaviors or interests
Executive function AND sensory processing abnormalities
D119.rationale: DSM-5 reorganized ASD into two core domains: (1) Persistent deficits in social communication and social interaction (across multiple contexts), and (2) Restricted, repetitive patterns of behavior, interests, or activities. Sensory abnormalities were added as a component of domain 2. Language disorder is no longer a separate criterion but may be specified. **Board tip:** ASD = 2 DSM-5 domains: social communication deficits + restricted/repetitive behaviors — both required.

D119.q: A 2-year-old boy was developing normally with first words by 12 months and 2-word phrases by 18 months. At 22 months, his parents report he has lost all language and social skills, stopped making eye contact, and now lines up toys repetitively. What is the most important immediate action?
a: Reassure parents this is normal toddler regression
Initiate urgent developmental evaluation and ASD assessment — regression is a red flag
Obtain MRI brain to rule out neurological tumor
D119.rationale: Developmental regression — loss of previously acquired skills — is a red flag that warrants immediate evaluation. This is most commonly associated with autism spectrum disorder (in approximately 20–30% of ASD cases) but must also prompt workup for Landau-Kleffner syndrome, Rett syndrome, and metabolic/neurological causes. Loss of language + social skills after normal development is a classic ASD presentation with regression. **Board tip:** Developmental regression = urgent ASD evaluation — NEVER reassure as normal.

D119.q: A 3-year-old girl is diagnosed with autism spectrum disorder. Her parents ask what the most evidence-based therapy is to improve her communication and adaptive behaviors. What should be recommended?
a: Sensory integration therapy as primary treatment
Play therapy without structured behavioral interventions
D119.rationale: Applied Behavior Analysis (ABA) is the most evidence-based behavioral intervention for ASD. It uses principles of behavioral reinforcement to improve communication, social skills, adaptive behaviors, and reduce problem behaviors. Early intensive ABA (25–40 hours/week) started before age 5 produces the best outcomes. Dietary interventions (gluten-free/casein-free) lack strong evidence. **Board tip:** ABA = gold standard behavioral therapy for ASD; early and intensive is key.

D119.q: A 4-year-old with ASD has frequent seizures beginning at age 3. His parents ask if this is related to his autism. What is the most accurate response?
a: Seizure disorders are unrelated to ASD and indicate a separate neurological diagnosis
Epilepsy occurs in approximately 20-30% of individuals with ASD and is a known comorbidity
Seizures in ASD are caused by ABA therapy and should prompt treatment cessation
Epilepsy occurs only in ASD associated with intellectual disability
D119.rationale: Epilepsy is the most common neurological comorbidity of ASD, occurring in approximately 20–30% of individuals. The risk is higher in those with intellectual disability and/or genetic syndromes. Other common ASD comorbidities include gastrointestinal problems (constipation, GERD), sleep disturbances (insomnia), ADHD, and anxiety. **Board tip:** ASD comorbidities: epilepsy (20-30%), GI problems, sleep disorders, ADHD, anxiety — epilepsy is the most common neurological comorbidity.

D119.q: A 3-year-old boy is newly diagnosed with ASD. He is an only child with no family history of developmental disorders. His pediatrician recommends genetic testing. Which genetic test should be ordered first?
a: Fragile X DNA testing as the only needed test
Whole exome sequencing as initial test
D119.rationale: Chromosomal microarray (CMA) is the recommended first-line genetic test in ASD, detecting copy number variants (CNVs) not visible on standard karyotype. Fragile X DNA testing (FMR1 gene) should also be routinely ordered, especially in boys, as Fragile X is the most common single-gene cause of ASD and intellectual disability. Whole exome sequencing is considered if CMA and Fragile X are negative. **Board tip:** ASD genetic workup = CMA first (detects CNVs) + Fragile X testing; Fragile X = most common single-gene cause.

D119.q: A 30-month-old is referred for ASD evaluation after a positive M-CHAT screen. Which finding on further evaluation would MOST support an ASD diagnosis?
a: Delayed speech (only 10 words) with normal social interaction and pointing
Lack of pointing, no response to name, absence of social smile, and repetitive hand flapping
Oppositional behavior with tantrums but appropriate eye contact and social reciprocity
Global developmental delay in motor and cognitive domains only
D119.rationale: Core ASD features include: lack of pointing (joint attention deficit), not responding to name, absent or reduced social smile, reduced eye contact, and restricted/repetitive behaviors (e.g., hand flapping, lining objects). These jointly reflect deficits in both DSM-5 ASD domains. Isolated speech delay with intact social skills is more consistent with a language disorder than ASD. **Board tip:** ASD red flags: no pointing, no response to name, no social smile, repetitive behaviors — social communication deficits are core.

D119.q: Parents of a child with ASD ask about the importance of early intervention. What is the most accurate statement regarding early intervention in ASD?
a: Early intervention before age 5 improves outcomes but results plateau after 6 months of therapy
Intensive early intervention (starting before age 3) produces the greatest gains in language, cognition, and adaptive behavior
Early intervention is only beneficial for children with mild ASD
Speech therapy alone is as effective as multi-disciplinary early intervention
D119.rationale: Early, intensive, multi-disciplinary intervention before age 3–5 produces the most significant and lasting gains in language development, cognitive abilities, social skills, and adaptive functioning. This is due to neuroplasticity — the brain is most malleable in early childhood. ABA is the cornerstone, often combined with speech therapy, occupational therapy, and developmental intervention. **Board tip:** Early + intensive intervention = best ASD outcomes; the earlier the better due to neuroplasticity.

D119.q: A child with ASD has significant sleep difficulty — taking 2+ hours to fall asleep and waking multiple times nightly. His parents are exhausted. Which pharmacologic intervention has the best evidence for sleep onset difficulty in ASD?
D119.rationale: Melatonin has the strongest evidence for sleep onset delay in ASD. Studies show it reduces sleep onset latency and improves total sleep time with a favorable safety profile. It is typically given 30–60 minutes before desired sleep time. Behavioral sleep interventions (consistent bedtime routine, sleep hygiene) should be first-line, with melatonin added if behavioral strategies are insufficient. **Board tip:** ASD sleep problems → melatonin (strong evidence, safe, good first pharmacologic step).

D119.q: A 5-year-old girl is referred for ASD evaluation. She speaks in long sentences but repetitively quoting from TV shows. She has difficulty with peer interactions and insists on rigid routines. Intelligence testing shows above-average IQ. Per DSM-5, what would her diagnosis be?
a: PDD-NOS (pervasive developmental disorder not otherwise specified)
Autism spectrum disorder, without intellectual or language impairment
D119.rationale: DSM-5 eliminated separate diagnoses of Asperger syndrome, PDD-NOS, and childhood disintegrative disorder — all are now classified as 'Autism Spectrum Disorder' with specifiers. Specifiers include: with/without intellectual impairment, with/without language impairment, severity level (1–3). This girl has ASD without intellectual impairment and without language impairment (she has language but uses it atypically). **Board tip:** DSM-5 eliminated Asperger's — it is now ASD Level 1 without intellectual/language impairment.

D119.q: A term newborn's heel-stick newborn metabolic screen is drawn at 24 hours of life. The nursery calls with an abnormal result for phenylketonuria (PKU). The infant is feeding well. What is the most appropriate next step?
a: Immediately start a phenylalanine-restricted diet without confirmatory testing
Repeat the screen and obtain confirmatory plasma amino acid analysis; do not delay treatment if confirmed
Reassure parents this is a common false positive and retest at 2 weeks
Obtain an MRI brain to assess for neurological damage before confirming diagnosis
D119.rationale: A positive newborn metabolic screen requires confirmatory testing before diagnosis, but action should not be delayed. For PKU, confirmatory plasma phenylalanine levels should be obtained urgently, and if confirmed, a phenylalanine-restricted diet must begin immediately to prevent intellectual disability. Early treatment (within first weeks of life) is essential for normal neurodevelopmental outcomes. **Board tip:** Abnormal newborn screen → confirm quickly + treat immediately if confirmed — do not simply reassure.

D119.q: Which of the following represents a critical congenital heart disease (CCHD) screening method recommended for all newborns before hospital discharge per AAP guidelines?
a: Routine chest X-ray in all newborns
Pulse oximetry screening of the right hand and one foot
Echocardiogram in all newborns before discharge
D119.rationale: CCHD screening using pulse oximetry of the pre-ductal (right hand) and post-ductal (foot) measurements is mandated in all states for newborns before discharge. A difference >3% between sites or SpO2 <95% triggers further evaluation. CCHD screening detects lesions like hypoplastic left heart, total anomalous pulmonary venous return, and transposition of the great arteries. **Board tip:** CCHD screen = pulse oximetry (right hand + foot) before discharge — mandatory, cost-effective, detects ductal-dependent lesions.

D119.q: A 3-day-old male appears jaundiced to the nipple line. His total serum bilirubin is 9 mg/dL. He is breastfed and feeding every 2 hours with 6–8 wet diapers/day. What is the most appropriate management?
a: Admit for phototherapy immediately given visible jaundice
Plot bilirubin on hour-specific nomogram; if below threshold for age, encourage continued breastfeeding and recheck as needed
Switch to formula to clear bilirubin faster
Order direct Coombs test and blood type before any management
D119.rationale: Neonatal jaundice management is guided by the hour-specific Bhutani nomogram, which determines phototherapy thresholds based on total serum bilirubin and postnatal age in hours and risk factors. A bilirubin of 9 mg/dL at 72 hours (3 days) in a low-risk term infant is typically below phototherapy threshold. Continued breastfeeding (adequate hydration) and close follow-up are appropriate. **Board tip:** Neonatal jaundice → use the Bhutani nomogram with postnatal age in hours, not just bilirubin level alone.

D119.q: Which vaccines are given at the 2-month well-child visit per the ACIP schedule?
a: DTaP, IPV, Hib, PCV15, HepB, Rotavirus
D119.rationale: At the 2-month visit, ACIP recommends: DTaP (diphtheria-tetanus-acellular pertussis), IPV (inactivated polio), Hib (Haemophilus influenzae type b), PCV15 (15-valent pneumococcal conjugate), HepB (hepatitis B — 2nd dose), and RV (rotavirus — oral). This is a high-yield vaccine schedule question. The same combination is repeated at 4 and 6 months. **Board tip:** 2-4-6 month vaccines: DTaP, IPV, Hib, PCV, HepB, RV — memorize this 6-vaccine set.

D119.q: A mother brings her 9-month-old for a well-child visit. Which developmental milestone should a typical 9-month-old demonstrate?
a: Object permanence, stranger anxiety, and pincer grasp beginning
Stacking 2 blocks and using a cup independently
D119.rationale: At 9 months, expected milestones include: gross motor (sits unsupported, pulls to stand), fine motor (raking grasp advancing to early pincer grasp), language (babbling, mama/dada non-specific), social (stranger anxiety, object permanence — searches for hidden objects). Two-word phrases emerge at ~18–24 months; walking at 12 months; block stacking at 15 months. **Board tip:** 9-month milestones: object permanence + stranger anxiety + early pincer grasp — key social and cognitive markers.

D119.q: An exclusively breastfed 4-month-old presents for a well-child visit. Her mother asks when to start solid foods and whether any supplements are needed. What is the most appropriate guidance?
a: Start pureed vegetables at 4 months; no supplements needed for breastfed infants
Continue exclusive breastfeeding until 6 months; supplement with vitamin D 400 IU/day and iron 1 mg/kg/day starting at 4 months
Start rice cereal at 4 months to improve sleep; iron supplementation only if formula-fed
Continue breastfeeding until 12 months; no vitamin D or iron needed if mother is healthy
D119.rationale: AAP recommends exclusive breastfeeding for the first 6 months. Breastfed infants require: (1) Vitamin D 400 IU/day starting in the first few days of life (breast milk is deficient in vitamin D), and (2) Iron 1 mg/kg/day starting at 4 months (breast milk iron is insufficient after depletion of fetal stores). Solid foods should be introduced around 6 months when developmental readiness is present. **Board tip:** Breastfed infants need: Vitamin D from birth, iron at 4 months — two key supplements for exclusively breastfed babies.

D119.q: At the 12-month well-child visit, which vaccines are administered for the first time (initial dose)?
a: MMR and Varicella (first doses), HepA (first dose)
Rotavirus booster and Hib booster only
D119.rationale: At the 12-month visit, the following vaccines are given for the first time: MMR (measles-mumps-rubella, 1st dose), Varicella (1st dose), and HepA (hepatitis A, 1st dose — 2nd dose 6 months later). PCV booster and Hib booster are also given at 12–15 months. MMR and Varicella are live attenuated vaccines that should not be given to immunocompromised patients. **Board tip:** 12-month new vaccines: MMR + Varicella + HepA — first doses of live vaccines (MMR, Varicella) given at 12 months.

D119.q: Parents ask when their newborn can safely ride in a rear-facing car seat in the back seat. What is the current AAP guidance on car seat safety?
a: Rear-facing until 1 year old, then forward-facing
Rear-facing in the back seat until age 2 OR until the child reaches the maximum height/weight limit for the seat
Forward-facing with 5-point harness from birth until age 4
Booster seat from birth until 65 lbs
D119.rationale: Current AAP guidance (updated 2018): keep children in rear-facing car seats in the back seat as long as possible — until they reach the maximum height or weight limit of their rear-facing seat (often age 2 or beyond). Rear-facing is safer in frontal crashes (most common) because it distributes crash forces over the entire back. After rear-facing limit, use a forward-facing 5-point harness, then a belt-positioning booster. **Board tip:** Rear-facing as long as possible (until height/weight limit), always in the back seat — updated guidance from age 1 to 'as long as possible.'

D119.q: A newborn hearing screen using otoacoustic emissions (OAE) fails in the left ear. The parents are concerned. What is the most appropriate next step?
a: Refer for cochlear implant evaluation immediately
Rescreen in the newborn nursery; if fails again, refer for auditory brainstem response (ABR) by 1 month
Reassure parents — most failed OAE screens are false positives and resolve spontaneously
Schedule a behavioral audiogram at 6 months of age
D119.rationale: The EHDI (Early Hearing Detection and Intervention) program follows the 1-3-6 rule: screen by 1 month, confirm diagnosis by 3 months, enroll in intervention by 6 months. A failed OAE screen should be rescreened; if fails again, refer for diagnostic ABR by 1 month of age. Early intervention for hearing loss (by 6 months) is critical for language development. **Board tip:** Failed newborn hearing screen → 1-3-6 rule: diagnose by 3 months, intervene by 6 months.

D119.q: A 6-month-old presents for a well-child visit. The parents ask when to introduce solid foods. The infant can sit with support, shows interest in food, and has lost the tongue-thrust reflex. What guidance should be given?
a: Wait until 9 months for all solid foods regardless of developmental readiness
This infant shows developmental readiness; introduce single-ingredient pureed foods and common allergens can be introduced early
Introduce only rice cereal first and delay all other foods until 9 months
Solid foods should never be introduced before 12 months per AAP guidelines
D119.rationale: Signs of readiness for solid foods (typically ~6 months): sitting with support, head control, interest in food, loss of tongue-thrust reflex, and ability to move food to the back of the mouth. Single-ingredient pureed foods can be started. Updated AAP guidelines (2023) recommend introducing common allergens (peanut products, egg, etc.) early (around 6 months) to prevent food allergy development. **Board tip:** Solid food readiness at 6 months: sitting + head control + no tongue-thrust; introduce allergens early to prevent sensitization.

D119.q: During a 2-week newborn visit, a mother reports her infant is breastfeeding 10-12 times per day, has 4-5 yellow seedy stools, and the birth weight was 3.5 kg. Today the infant weighs 3.4 kg. What is the most appropriate response?
a: Immediately start supplemental formula — infant has not regained birth weight by 2 weeks
Reassure — 10% weight loss is acceptable in the first week; return to birth weight is expected by 2 weeks. At 3.4 kg (3% below), this may require close monitoring
Admit for failure to thrive evaluation
Advise stopping breastfeeding and switching to formula
D119.rationale: Newborns typically lose up to 7–10% of birth weight in the first few days, then regain to birth weight by 10–14 days. At 2 weeks, this infant is 3% below birth weight (3.4/3.5 = 97%), which warrants close monitoring with a weight check in a few days and assessment of feeding technique. If feeding 10–12x/day with adequate stool output, breastfeeding may be adequate. Supplemental formula may be needed if weight gain doesn't occur. **Board tip:** Newborn weight: up to 10% loss acceptable in first week; birth weight regained by 2 weeks — reassess with monitoring if borderline.

D119.q: A 4-month-old is brought in for a well-child visit. His mother asks about safe sleep practices. Which recommendation is MOST important to prevent SIDS?
a: Place infant prone to strengthen neck muscles
Place infant supine (on back) on a firm, flat, non-inclined sleep surface in their own space free of loose bedding
Co-sleeping with parents in adult bed reduces SIDS risk through parental monitoring
Wedge positioners can be used to keep infants on their side safely
D119.rationale: AAP safe sleep guidelines (2022): Always place infants on their BACK (supine) on a firm, flat, non-inclined surface. Use a safety-approved crib or bassinet. Keep soft objects, loose bedding, positioners, and bumper pads out of the sleep space. Room-sharing (but NOT bed-sharing) is recommended. Prone sleeping increases SIDS risk significantly. **Board tip:** Safe sleep = Back to sleep, firm flat surface, no loose bedding, room-share not bed-share — all 4 elements are testable.

D119.q: A 9-month-old comes for a well-child visit. Her parents report they have been giving her cow's milk in a bottle since 8 months to save money. What guidance should be provided?
a: Cow's milk is fine after 6 months as a formula substitute
Cow's milk should not replace breast milk or formula until 12 months due to low iron, high renal solute load, and risk of GI blood loss
Whole milk is acceptable but skim milk is not until age 2
Cow's milk can be introduced at 9 months if the infant is eating solid foods
D119.rationale: Cow's milk is not recommended as the primary drink before 12 months because: (1) it is low in iron, increasing iron deficiency anemia risk; (2) it has a high renal solute load that immature kidneys cannot handle; and (3) it can cause occult GI blood loss in infants. After 12 months, whole milk (not skim/low-fat) is appropriate until age 2. Small amounts of cow's milk in cooking/with solids is acceptable before 12 months. **Board tip:** Cow's milk as primary drink = wait until 12 months; whole milk until age 2; no skim milk before 2 years.

D119.q: At the 6-month well-child visit, which of the following vaccines is given for the THIRD dose in the primary series?
a: DTaP, IPV, Hib, PCV, HepB, and Rotavirus
D119.rationale: The 6-month visit completes the primary series for DTaP (3rd dose), IPV (3rd dose), Hib (3rd dose), PCV (3rd dose), HepB (3rd/final dose), and Rotavirus (3rd dose for Rotateq; Rotarix requires only 2 doses). Annual influenza vaccine also starts at 6 months. This is the same vaccine cluster as 2 and 4 months, completing the primary immunization series. **Board tip:** 2-4-6 months = DTaP, IPV, Hib, PCV, HepB, RV (primary series); flu vaccine starts at 6 months.

D119.q: A first-time mother asks about anticipatory guidance for her 2-month-old. Which guidance is MOST appropriate for this age?
a: Introduce solid foods as the infant's appetite is increasing
Discuss safe sleep, tummy time when awake and supervised, when to seek care for fever, and normal developmental expectations
Encourage use of infant walkers to promote early walking
Start fluoride supplementation if water is not fluoridated
D119.rationale: At the 2-month visit, anticipatory guidance includes: (1) Safe sleep (back to sleep, firm surface), (2) Supervised tummy time when awake to prevent positional plagiocephaly and strengthen neck/trunk, (3) Fever management (rectal temp ≥100.4°F in infants <2 months = emergency), (4) Normal development expectations (social smile emerging, cooing), and (5) Shaken baby syndrome prevention. Fluoride starts at 6 months; solid foods at 6 months. **Board tip:** 2-month anticipatory guidance: safe sleep + tummy time + fever education (temp ≥100.4°F → ER in young infants).

D119.q: A 2.5-year-old presents with 2 days of ear pain, fever of 38.9°C, and irritability. Otoscopy reveals a bulging, erythematous tympanic membrane with decreased mobility. He has no drug allergies. What is the most appropriate management?
a: Watchful waiting for 48–72 hours with close follow-up
Amoxicillin 90 mg/kg/day in 2 divided doses for 10 days
D119.rationale: For children 2 years and older with mild-to-moderate AOM, watchful waiting (48–72 hours) is an option if symptoms are non-severe (fever <39°C, mild ear pain). However, this child has fever ≥38.9°C and appears ill — this is a more severe presentation. When treating AOM, high-dose amoxicillin (90 mg/kg/day in 2 divided doses) is first-line per AAP guidelines due to increasing penicillin-resistant S. pneumoniae. The higher dose overcomes intermediate resistance. **Board tip:** AOM treatment = amoxicillin 90 mg/kg/day (HIGH dose) — the high dose is key; low-dose is insufficient.

D119.q: A 2-year-old with AOM has a history of recurrent hives and lip swelling with amoxicillin. What is the most appropriate antibiotic choice?
D119.rationale: Hives and angioedema to amoxicillin suggest a possible IgE-mediated penicillin allergy. A 2nd or 3rd generation cephalosporin (e.g., cefdinir, cefuroxime) is appropriate when the penicillin allergy is non-severe (not anaphylaxis) — cross-reactivity between penicillins and cephalosporins is low (~1–2%). If the reaction was anaphylaxis, use azithromycin or clindamycin instead. **Board tip:** Penicillin allergy + AOM → cephalosporin (if non-anaphylactic); azithromycin (if true anaphylaxis) — know the hierarchy.

D119.q: A 6-year-old presents with 5 days of left ear pain. On exam, the tympanic membrane is perforated with purulent discharge in the ear canal. What is the management of AOM with tympanic membrane perforation?
a: Watchful waiting is appropriate since the ear is draining and pressure is released
Immediate antibiotic treatment — TM perforation is an indication for antibiotics regardless of age or severity
Urgent ENT referral for surgical repair before antibiotics
Topical antibiotic ear drops only; oral antibiotics are not needed
D119.rationale: Tympanic membrane perforation due to AOM is an absolute indication for antibiotic treatment — watchful waiting is NOT appropriate with perforation. High-dose amoxicillin is first-line. Perforation generally heals spontaneously within weeks. The drainage relieves pain, so the child may appear better despite needing treatment. Topical antibiotics (e.g., ofloxacin drops) may be added. **Board tip:** TM perforation = immediate antibiotics, no watchful waiting — this is a key exception to the observation option.

D119.q: A 3-year-old is diagnosed with otitis media with effusion (OME) — fluid behind the tympanic membrane without signs of acute infection. The tympanic membrane is not bulging and the child has no fever or ear pain. What is the initial management?
a: Watchful waiting for 3 months; refer to ENT if persistent beyond 3 months with hearing loss
D119.rationale: Otitis media with effusion (OME, 'glue ear') is fluid in the middle ear without acute infection signs. Most cases resolve spontaneously within 3 months. AAP guidelines recommend watchful waiting for 3 months. Antibiotics are NOT indicated for OME. Decongestants and antihistamines are ineffective. If OME persists beyond 3 months with associated hearing loss or developmental concerns, ENT referral for possible tympanostomy tube placement is appropriate. **Board tip:** OME = watchful waiting 3 months; no antibiotics; tubes only for persistent OME with hearing loss.

D119.q: A 7-year-old presents with 3 days of sore throat, fever of 39.1°C, anterior cervical lymphadenopathy, and tonsillar exudates. He has no cough. A rapid antigen detection test (RADT) is positive for group A Streptococcus. What is the treatment?
a: Amoxicillin for 10 days as first-line therapy for GAS pharyngitis
Penicillin V for 5 days (shorter course sufficient)
No antibiotic needed; supportive care only for sore throat
D119.rationale: Amoxicillin for 10 days is first-line treatment for group A Streptococcal (GAS) pharyngitis in children. Amoxicillin is preferred over penicillin V due to better palatability and equivalent efficacy. Penicillin V for 10 days is an acceptable alternative. Azithromycin is reserved for penicillin-allergic patients. Treatment prevents rheumatic fever, reduces symptom duration, and prevents spread. A 10-day course is required (shorter courses have higher failure rates). **Board tip:** GAS pharyngitis → amoxicillin 10 days first-line; penicillin allergy → azithromycin; always 10 days.

D119.q: A 10-year-old presents with sore throat and 3 of 4 Centor criteria. A rapid strep test is negative. What is the most appropriate next step?
a: Treat empirically with antibiotics regardless of negative RADT
Obtain a throat culture — negative RADT alone is insufficient to exclude GAS in children
Discharge with supportive care only — negative RADT confirms no strep
D119.rationale: In children and adolescents, a negative RADT should be backed up with a throat culture because RADT sensitivity is 70–90% — false negatives occur. A throat culture (gold standard, sensitivity 90–95%) should be sent when the RADT is negative but clinical suspicion remains. In adults, a negative RADT is sufficient to exclude GAS (lower pretest probability). **Board tip:** RADT negative in a CHILD → send throat culture; in adults → RADT negative is sufficient to exclude GAS.

D119.q: A 5-year-old presents with sore throat, diffuse sandpaper-like rash starting on the trunk spreading to extremities, strawberry tongue, and flushed face with circumoral pallor. A rapid strep test is positive. What is the diagnosis and treatment?
a: Toxic shock syndrome; IV clindamycin and IVIG
D119.rationale: Scarlet fever is caused by Group A Streptococcus (GAS) producing pyrogenic exotoxins. Classic features: (1) sandpaper rash (fine erythematous papules on erythematous base, sparing palms/soles initially), (2) strawberry tongue (red with prominent papillae), (3) circumoral pallor, (4) flushed cheeks, and (5) Pastia's lines (rash concentration in skin folds). Treatment: amoxicillin 10 days (same as GAS pharyngitis). **Board tip:** Scarlet fever = GAS + sandpaper rash + strawberry tongue + circumoral pallor → amoxicillin 10 days.

D119.q: A 15-month-old presents with AOM. Per AAP guidelines, what is the minimum age at which watchful waiting is an acceptable option for a child with NON-severe unilateral AOM?
D119.rationale: Per AAP 2013 AOM guidelines: children <6 months = always treat. Children 6–23 months = always treat bilateral AOM; treat unilateral severe AOM; can observe unilateral non-severe AOM if reliable follow-up is ensured. Children ≥24 months = watchful waiting is acceptable for non-severe unilateral or bilateral AOM if reliable follow-up is ensured. At 15 months, this child is in the 6–23 month category — watchful waiting may apply ONLY for unilateral non-severe AOM with close follow-up. **Board tip:** AOM watchful waiting by age: <2yo = treat bilateral; 2yo+ = can observe non-severe; <6mo = always treat.

D119.q: A 4-year-old has had bilateral ear effusions and documented hearing loss (35 dB) for 6 months. He has mild speech delay. His pediatrician has been observing with watchful waiting. What is the next most appropriate step?
a: Continue watchful waiting for another 3 months
Prescribe a 10-day course of amoxicillin for OME
Refer to ENT for consideration of tympanostomy tube placement
Order CT temporal bones to evaluate for cholesteatoma
D119.rationale: Tympanostomy tube (PE tube) insertion is indicated for OME that: (1) persists ≥3 months with bilateral hearing loss ≥25 dB, (2) is associated with developmental delay, speech delay, or learning difficulties, or (3) is bilateral and persistent ≥3 months. This child has 6 months of OME, significant hearing loss (35 dB), and speech delay — he clearly meets criteria for ENT referral and likely tympanostomy tubes. **Board tip:** OME + persistent hearing loss + speech delay = ENT for tympanostomy tubes — don't wait further.

D119.q: A 6-year-old penicillin-allergic child (anaphylaxis history) has GAS pharyngitis confirmed by positive throat culture. What is the most appropriate antibiotic alternative?
D119.rationale: For true penicillin allergy (anaphylaxis = IgE-mediated), cephalosporins should be avoided due to cross-reactivity risk (~1–2% but still a concern in anaphylaxis history). Azithromycin (5-day course) or clarithromycin (10-day course) are appropriate macrolide alternatives. Clindamycin is also an option. TMP-SMX is NOT effective against GAS pharyngitis. **Board tip:** GAS + penicillin anaphylaxis → azithromycin or clindamycin; avoid cephalosporins in true anaphylaxis; TMP-SMX does NOT cover GAS.

D119.q: A 9-year-old presents with sore throat for 2 days. He has no fever, no exudates, no lymphadenopathy, but has rhinorrhea, hoarseness, and a mild cough. A Centor score is calculated. What is the most appropriate management?
a: Perform RADT and treat if positive
No testing needed — viral pharyngitis is likely; supportive care only
Empiric antibiotics for 5 days given age and severity
Throat culture to definitively exclude GAS
D119.rationale: The modified Centor/McIsaac criteria for GAS: fever, tonsillar exudates, anterior cervical LAD, absence of cough (each +1 point); age 3–14 (+1), age >45 (-1). This child has 0 criteria (has cough, no fever/exudate/LAD) → low risk for GAS. Viral symptoms (rhinorrhea, hoarseness, cough) strongly suggest viral pharyngitis. No testing or antibiotics are needed; supportive care is appropriate. **Board tip:** Viral pharyngitis signs = cough + rhinorrhea + hoarseness — these AGAINST GAS; Centor 0-1 = no test/treat.

D119.q: An 8-year-old is diagnosed with scarlet fever and treated with amoxicillin. Three days later, he is afebrile and his rash is resolving. The skin on his fingertips and toes begins peeling. His mother is alarmed. What should you tell her?
a: This is a sign of treatment failure; change antibiotics immediately
Desquamation (skin peeling) following scarlet fever rash is a normal expected finding that occurs 1–2 weeks after the rash appears
This indicates toxic epidermal necrolysis — admit to burn unit
Peeling indicates spreading GAS infection; add clindamycin
D119.rationale: Desquamation (skin peeling) is a classic, expected finding in scarlet fever that occurs 1–2 weeks after the initial rash, typically starting on the fingertips, toes, and groin. It does not indicate treatment failure or a new problem. It is caused by the same pyrogenic exotoxins that cause the rash.
