If persists at 32 weeks → plan C-section delivery at 36-37 weeks. **Board tip:** Distinguish: Placenta previa = painless bleeding. Placenta abruption = painful bleeding + uterine rigidity. Vasa previa = rupture of fetal vessels over os = fetal blood loss (fetal emergency).

D120.q: A 24-year-old at 36 weeks has BP 158/105, proteinuria 2+, and headache. No prior hypertension. What is the diagnosis and management?
a: Preeclampsia with severe features — requires hospitalization, IV labetalol or hydralazine for acute BP control, IV magnesium sulfate for seizure prophylaxis, and delivery planning (≥37 weeks = deliver)
D120.rationale: Preeclampsia with severe features (BP ≥160/110 on two occasions, severe-range symptoms: headache, visual changes, RUQ pain, pulmonary edema, platelets <100K, creatinine doubled): hospitalize, IV magnesium sulfate (eclampsia seizure prevention), IV antihypertensive for BP ≥160/110. Delivery at ≥37 weeks or earlier if severe/unstable. **Board tip:** Preeclampsia definition: new-onset hypertension (≥140/90) + proteinuria OR severe end-organ damage after 20 weeks. MgSO4 is the drug of choice for eclampsia prevention AND treatment. Give calcium gluconate as MgSO4 antidote if toxicity occurs (respiratory depression, loss of DTRs).

D120.q: Which vaccine is recommended at every pregnancy, regardless of prior immunization history, at 27-36 weeks gestation?
a: Tdap — provides passive immunity (anti-pertussis antibodies) to newborn through the placenta before birth, protecting the infant before their own vaccination at 2 months
D120.rationale: Tdap is recommended at 27-36 weeks in EVERY pregnancy (not just first pregnancy) because placental antibody transfer peaks in third trimester — maternal vaccination protects the newborn in the first weeks of life before they can receive their own pertussis vaccination at 2 months. **Board tip:** Ideal timing: 27-32 weeks for maximum placental antibody transfer. Also recommended: influenza vaccine (any trimester), COVID-19 vaccine (updated formulation). Vaccines contraindicated in pregnancy: live vaccines (MMR, varicella, live-attenuated flu nasal spray). ONLY give inactivated influenza.

D120.q: Group B Streptococcus (GBS) screening is performed at which gestational age?
a: 35-37 weeks — vaginal/rectal culture; if positive, intrapartum IV penicillin during labor prevents neonatal GBS sepsis
D120.rationale: GBS screening: vaginal-rectal culture at 35-37 weeks. GBS-positive mothers receive IV penicillin (or ampicillin) during active labor (intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis — IAP). GBS is a leading cause of neonatal early-onset sepsis. IAP reduces GBS neonatal infection by >80%. **Board tip:** IAP indications even without culture result: unknown GBS status + labor <37 weeks, ROM ≥18 hours, or intrapartum fever ≥100.4°F. Penicillin allergy: clindamycin (if susceptible) or cefazolin (if low anaphylaxis risk). Vancomycin if high-risk penicillin allergy.

D120.q: A 32-year-old at 30 weeks presents with right upper quadrant pain, nausea, vomiting, and elevated liver enzymes (AST 280, ALT 310), low platelets (88K), and hemolysis. BP is 150/95. What is the diagnosis?
a: HELLP Syndrome (Hemolysis, Elevated Liver enzymes, Low Platelets) — a severe variant of preeclampsia requiring expedient delivery, IV MgSO4, and possibly steroids for fetal lung maturity if <34 weeks
Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy — ursodiol only
D120.rationale: HELLP Syndrome: Hemolysis (fragmented RBCs on smear, elevated LDH/bilirubin) + Elevated Liver enzymes + Low Platelets. A severe form of preeclampsia. Management: stabilize mother, IV MgSO4, antihypertensives, consider antenatal corticosteroids if <34 weeks, and expedite delivery. DIC can develop. **Board tip:** Mississippi Classification: Class 1 = platelets <50K (most severe), Class 2 = 50-100K, Class 3 = 100-150K. Tennessee Classification: complete vs. partial HELLP. Delivery is the only definitive treatment. Rarely recurs in subsequent pregnancies (<5%).

D120.q: A patient at 34 weeks gestation develops pruritus (severe itching without rash), particularly on the palms and soles at night. Liver function tests show elevated bile acids. What is the diagnosis and immediate concern?
a: PUPP (Pruritic urticarial papules and plaques of pregnancy) — topical steroids

Intrahepatic Cholestasis of Pregnancy (ICP) — elevated bile acids (>10 μmol/L, severe >40) associated with increased risk of sudden fetal demise; treat with ursodiol, increase fetal monitoring, deliver at 37 weeks
Obstetric cholestasis is benign — reassure and moisturize
D120.rationale: Intrahepatic Cholestasis of Pregnancy: Elevated serum bile acids, intense pruritus (especially palms/soles), worse at night. RISK: sudden intrauterine fetal demise (mechanism not fully understood — possibly bile acid-induced fetal arrhythmia). Treatment: ursodiol (reduces bile acids, improves symptoms), twice-weekly NST, delivery at 37 weeks. **Board tip:** Bile acids >40 μmol/L = high risk of fetal demise. Laboratory: elevated bile acids, elevated AST/ALT, mildly elevated bilirubin. Distinguish from PUPP (rash within stretch marks, no liver involvement, no fetal risk).

D120.q: What is the recommended weight gain during pregnancy for a woman with a normal pre-pregnancy BMI (18.5-24.9)?
a: 25-35 lbs total, with approximately 1 lb/week in second and third trimesters
No weight gain guidelines — just eat healthy foods
D120.rationale: IOM recommended pregnancy weight gain: Underweight (BMI <18.5): 28-40 lbs; Normal (18.5-24.9): 25-35 lbs; Overweight (25-29.9): 15-25 lbs; Obese (≥30): 11-20 lbs. Inadequate gain: IUGR, preterm birth. Excessive gain: macrosomia, GDM, C-section, long-term maternal obesity. **Board tip:** Weight gain distribution: first trimester ~1-4 lbs total; second/third trimesters ~1 lb/week for normal BMI women. Components: fetus (~7-8 lbs), placenta/fluids/breast tissue/uterus expansion makes up the remainder.

D120.q: A 28-year-old G1P0 at 11 weeks asks about chorionic villus sampling (CVS). How does CVS differ from amniocentesis?
a: CVS and amniocentesis are interchangeable — no difference
CVS is performed at 10-13 weeks (earlier than amniocentesis at 15-20 weeks), samples placental tissue (not amniotic fluid), allows earlier diagnosis but cannot test for neural tube defects
D120.rationale: CVS (10-13 weeks): samples chorionic villi (placental tissue) — provides chromosomal diagnosis 5-6 weeks earlier than amniocentesis. Cannot diagnose open NTDs (no amniotic AFP). Procedure-related loss rate: ~0.5-1%. Amniocentesis (15-20 weeks): samples amniotic fluid, can diagnose NTDs via AFP, slightly lower procedure risk (~0.1-0.3%). **Board tip:** Both are DIAGNOSTIC (not screening) procedures — they provide definitive chromosomal diagnosis. Offered to all patients (not just AMA). Transplacental CVS → avoid Rh-negative mothers if possible (or give RhoGAM).

D120.q: Which nutrient supplementation is specifically recommended in the third trimester and while breastfeeding, particularly for vegetarians and those with limited dairy intake?
a: Vitamin D 600 IU/day and calcium 1000 mg/day — fetal bone mineralization peaks in third trimester; breastfeeding depletes maternal calcium
D120.rationale: Calcium and Vitamin D: critical for fetal bone development (third trimester most critical). Recommended intake: calcium 1000 mg/day, Vitamin D 600 IU/day (higher doses may be needed if deficient). Breastfeeding: maternal bone resorption of 3-5% occurs to supply breast milk calcium — recovers after weaning. **Board tip:** Iron supplementation: 27 mg/day prenatal (more if anemic). DHA/omega-3: 200mg/day from week 20 (brain and retinal development). Iodine: 220 mcg/day (important for thyroid/fetal brain — many prenatal vitamins are inadequate). Avoid vitamin A megadose (>10,000 IU): teratogenic.

D120.q: A pregnant patient at 28 weeks tests positive for asymptomatic bacteriuria (ASB) with >100,000 CFU/mL of E. coli. How should this be managed?
a: Treat immediately with appropriate antibiotics (nitrofurantoin, cephalexin, or amoxicillin-clavulanate) — ASB in pregnancy MUST be treated to prevent progression to pyelonephritis (which increases preterm labor risk)
Repeat culture in 4 weeks before treating
D120.rationale: Asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy: ALWAYS treat (unlike non-pregnant women). Untreated ASB in pregnancy progresses to pyelonephritis in 30-40% of cases, which is associated with preterm labor and low birth weight. Preferred antibiotics: nitrofurantoin (avoid at term/≥36 weeks), cephalexin, or amoxicillin-clavulanate. Test of cure culture 1-2 weeks after treatment. **Board tip:** Screen for ASB with urine culture at first prenatal visit. Monthly dipstick alone is insufficient — culture is required. Avoid fluoroquinolones in pregnancy. Avoid TMP-SMX in first trimester (folate antagonism) and near term.

D120.q: A 29-year-old at 20 weeks has an anatomy ultrasound. Which fetal structural abnormality cannot be detected on the 20-week anatomy scan?
a: Phenylketonuria (metabolic disorder — requires biochemical testing, not ultrasound)
D120.rationale: Anatomy ultrasound at 18-20 weeks evaluates: fetal anatomy (brain, spine, heart, abdominal organs, face, limbs), placental location, amniotic fluid volume, cervical length. It CANNOT diagnose metabolic/biochemical disorders (PKU, cystic fibrosis, inborn errors of metabolism) — these require genetic testing (amniocentesis, newborn screening). **Board tip:** The 20-week anatomy scan is the single most important ultrasound of pregnancy. It detects major structural anomalies. Fetal echocardiography (done at 18-24 weeks) is recommended for high-risk pregnancies (maternal diabetes, CHD family history, abnormal screening).

D120.q: What is the FIRST-LINE treatment for nausea and vomiting of pregnancy (morning sickness) in the first trimester?
a: Dietary modifications (small frequent meals, avoid triggers, ginger) + vitamin B6 (pyridoxine) ± doxylamine (Unisom) — combination is FDA-approved (Diclegis/Bonjesta)
D120.rationale: NVP management ladder: (1) Dietary modifications + vitamin B6 10-25mg TID; (2) Add doxylamine 12.5mg (Unisom SleepTabs half tablet) — the B6+doxylamine combination is FDA Pregnancy Category A (Diclegis/Bonjesta approved); (3) Add antihistamines, promethazine, metoclopramide; (4) Ondansetron (Category B — limited safety data). **Board tip:** Hyperemesis gravidarum (>5% weight loss, dehydration, electrolyte abnormalities) requires IV fluids and IV antiemetics. Rule out thyroid storm, UTI, molar pregnancy. Ondansetron: avoid if possible in first trimester (possible QTc and cleft concerns, limited data).

D120.q: What is the indication for low-dose aspirin (81 mg/day) initiated at 12-16 weeks of pregnancy?
a: All pregnant women to prevent miscarriage

Women at high risk for preeclampsia (prior preeclampsia, chronic HTN, diabetes, renal disease, autoimmune disease, multifetal gestation, first pregnancy, Black race, BMI >30, age >35) — reduces risk of preeclampsia by 10-24%
D120.rationale: USPSTF recommends low-dose aspirin (81 mg/day) initiated at 12-16 weeks (before 16 weeks for maximal benefit) for women with ≥1 high-risk factor or ≥2 moderate-risk factors for preeclampsia. It inhibits thromboxane A2 production and improves uteroplacental blood flow. **Board tip:** ASPRE trial and systematic reviews confirm 10-24% reduction in preterm preeclampsia with low-dose aspirin. Continue until delivery. Also used for antiphospholipid syndrome in pregnancy (with heparin). High-risk factors: prior preeclampsia, multifetal gestation, CKD, autoimmune, diabetes, HTN.

D120.q: A 22-year-old sexually active woman has a routine STI screen. Her gonorrhea/chlamydia NAAT returns positive for Chlamydia trachomatis. She is not pregnant. What is the first-line treatment?
a: Doxycycline 100mg BID x 7 days (preferred) OR azithromycin 1g single dose (alternative — higher resistance rates)
Azithromycin 1g single dose — equally preferred as doxycycline
D120.rationale: Chlamydia treatment (2021 CDC STI Treatment Guidelines): Doxycycline 100mg BID x 7 days is now PREFERRED over azithromycin single dose due to superior efficacy (especially for rectal chlamydia). Azithromycin 1g x 1 is alternative. Sexual partners should be treated. **Board tip:** Test of cure is NOT needed for uncomplicated chlamydia unless pregnant, symptoms persist, or reinfection suspected. Retest at 3 months (high reinfection rate). Expedited Partner Therapy (EPT) is legal in most states — provide Rx for partner without them being seen.

D120.q: A 25-year-old has cervical discharge, pelvic pain, and a positive gonorrhea NAAT. She has no drug allergies. What is the recommended treatment per 2021 CDC guidelines?
a: Ceftriaxone 500mg IM single dose (or 1g if weight ≥150 kg) PLUS doxycycline 100mg BID x 7 days (if chlamydia not excluded)
D120.rationale: Gonorrhea treatment (2021 CDC): Ceftriaxone 500mg IM single dose (increased from 250mg due to rising ceftriaxone MICs). If chlamydia co-infection not excluded, add doxycycline 100mg BID x 7 days. Ceftriaxone 1g if weight ≥150 kg. **Board tip:** Dual therapy for gonorrhea (cephalosporin + doxycycline) was standard to cover chlamydia — NOW, if NAAT confirms gonorrhea only and chlamydia excluded, ceftriaxone alone is recommended. Fluoroquinolone resistance to gonorrhea is widespread — fluoroquinolones are NO LONGER recommended for gonorrhea.

D120.q: USPSTF recommends chlamydia and gonorrhea screening for which population?
a: Sexually active women ≤24 years (annually) and older women with risk factors (new/multiple partners); also screen MSM and others with risk factors
Men are never screened for chlamydia
D120.rationale: USPSTF Grade B recommendation: Screen for chlamydia and gonorrhea in sexually active women ≤24 years AND in older women who are at increased risk. MSM: screen at all sites of exposure (urethra, rectum, pharynx) at least annually (more frequently if high risk). **Board tip:** Many STIs are asymptomatic — systematic screening is essential. Chlamydia is the most commonly reported notifiable STI in the U.S. PID (pelvic inflammatory disease) from untreated chlamydia causes infertility, ectopic pregnancy, and chronic pelvic pain.

D120.q: A patient has a painless indurated ulcer (chancre) on the labia that appeared 3 weeks ago, with non-tender inguinal lymphadenopathy. RPR returns as reactive. What is the diagnosis and treatment?
a: Primary syphilis (Treponema pallidum) — Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units IM single dose
D120.rationale: Primary syphilis: painless indurated chancre at infection site, non-tender lymphadenopathy. Treatment: Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units IM single dose. Confirm with RPR/VDRL (nontreponemal) + FTA-ABS or TP-PA (treponemal test). **Board tip:** Syphilis stages: Primary (chancre, painless), Secondary (rash on palms/soles, condyloma lata, mucous patches, flu-like), Latent (asymptomatic), Tertiary (gummas, cardiovascular, neurosyphilis). Penicillin is the ONLY acceptable treatment for all stages. Pregnant women with penicillin allergy: desensitize and treat with penicillin.

D120.q: A 28-year-old woman has multiple painful vesicular lesions on the vulva. She has fever and tender inguinal lymphadenopathy. HSV-2 PCR is positive. This is her FIRST outbreak. What is the management?
a: Oral acyclovir 400mg TID x 7-10 days OR valacyclovir 1g BID x 7-10 days for primary genital herpes — reduces severity and duration; suppressive therapy should be discussed
No treatment — HSV is a lifelong virus so treatment is futile
D120.rationale: Primary genital HSV: more severe first episode (bilateral lesions, systemic symptoms, longer duration). Treatment: oral antiviral (acyclovir or valacyclovir) x 7-10 days reduces duration and severity. After primary episode, discuss daily SUPPRESSIVE therapy to reduce recurrences (by 70-80%) AND transmission to partners (reduces transmission by 48%). **Board tip:** HSV disclosure: counsel patient to tell partners. Condoms reduce (not eliminate) transmission risk. Most HSV transmission occurs during asymptomatic viral shedding. Type 1 and 2 can cause genital herpes.

D120.q: Which HPV strains are responsible for 70% of cervical cancers, and which strains cause genital warts?
a: HPV 6 and 11 cause cervical cancer; HPV 16 and 18 cause warts
HPV 16 and 18 cause 70% of cervical cancers (high-risk oncogenic); HPV 6 and 11 cause genital warts (low-risk, not oncogenic)
All HPV strains cause cervical cancer equally
HPV 31 and 33 cause most cervical cancers
D120.rationale: HPV types: High-risk/oncogenic (types 16, 18, 31, 33, 45, 52, 58) → cervical cancer, oropharyngeal cancer, anal cancer. Types 16 + 18 = ~70% of cervical cancers. Low-risk (types 6 and 11) → genital warts (condyloma acuminata) — NOT oncogenic. **Board tip:** Gardasil 9 covers 9 strains (6, 11, 16, 18, 31, 33, 45, 52, 58) — covers ~90% of cervical cancer-causing HPV types. HPV vaccination prevents cancer — recommend to all age 9-26, shared decision-making 27-45. HPV infections are the most common STI in the U.S.

D120.q: A 19-year-old male MSM presents for routine STI screening. He is HIV-negative and reports occasional condomless receptive anal intercourse. What is the appropriate HIV prevention strategy to discuss?
a: Pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) — emtricitabine/tenofovir (Truvada or Descovy) reduces HIV acquisition risk by >99% when taken daily; indicated for high-risk HIV-negative individuals
Condoms alone are sufficient — PrEP not needed
D120.rationale: PrEP (Pre-Exposure Prophylaxis): emtricitabine/tenofovir alafenamide (Descovy) or emtricitabine/tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (Truvada) — reduces HIV acquisition risk by >90-99% when taken daily. Indicated for HIV-negative individuals with high risk (MSM with condomless sex, serodiscordant couples, people who inject drugs, etc.). **Board tip:** Before prescribing PrEP: confirm HIV-negative status, baseline renal function (eGFR), STI screen, Hep B status. Follow-up every 3 months: HIV test (detect acute infection), STI screen, BP, and renal function. Cabotegravir LA injection (every 2 months) is an alternative to daily oral PrEP.

D120.q: A 32-year-old woman with gonorrhea/chlamydia cervicitis presents with bilateral lower abdominal pain, cervical motion tenderness, and adnexal tenderness. What is the diagnosis and outpatient treatment?
a: Pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) — outpatient: ceftriaxone 500mg IM x1 PLUS doxycycline 100mg BID x 14 days PLUS metronidazole 500mg BID x 14 days
D120.rationale: PID: polymicrobial ascending infection (GC, chlamydia, anaerobes, GBS). Minimum criteria: cervical motion tenderness + uterine/adnexal tenderness. Outpatient: ceftriaxone IM + doxycycline + metronidazole x 14 days. Hospitalize if: unable to take oral meds, tubo-ovarian abscess, surgical emergency, failure to improve in 72 hours. **Board tip:** PID sequelae: infertility (12% after 1 episode, 23% after 2, 40% after 3), ectopic pregnancy risk 6-10x increased, chronic pelvic pain. 'Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome' = PID with perihepatitis (RUQ pain, violin string adhesions on laparoscopy).

D120.q: Syphilis screening is recommended by USPSTF for which populations?
a: All persons at increased risk (MSM, HIV+ individuals, sex workers, persons in high-prevalence areas, those with prior syphilis) AND all pregnant women
D120.rationale: USPSTF Grade B: Screen for syphilis in persons at increased risk, and screen all pregnant women at first prenatal visit (repeat at 28 weeks and delivery in high-prevalence areas or high-risk). U.S. syphilis rates have been rising dramatically, including congenital syphilis. **Board tip:** Syphilis serologic testing: SCREEN with nontreponemal (RPR, VDRL) → confirm with treponemal (FTA-ABS, TP-PA). OR reverse algorithm: screen with treponemal EIA → confirm with RPR. Treponemal tests remain positive for life even after treatment — RPR titer used to monitor treatment response.

D120.q: A 24-year-old woman has a fishy-smelling vaginal discharge after unprotected sex. pH is 5.2, whiff test positive, and clue cells on wet mount. Treatment is prescribed. What is ALSO indicated?
a: No partner treatment needed for BV
Screen for concurrent STIs (gonorrhea, chlamydia) since BV is associated with increased STI acquisition risk; test and treat partners only if symptomatic
Treat all sexual partners with metronidazole regardless
D120.rationale: BV increases susceptibility to STIs (HIV, gonorrhea, chlamydia, trichomonas) — women with BV should be screened for concurrent STIs. BV is NOT considered an STI per se (male partners are NOT routinely treated), but sexual activity does influence vaginal flora. **Board tip:** BV treatment: metronidazole 500mg BID x 7 days (oral) or metronidazole 0.75% gel x 5 days (vaginal) or clindamycin 2% cream x 7 days. Recurrence is common (50% at 6 months). Avoid alcohol during and 24-48 hours after metronidazole (disulfiram-like reaction).

D120.q: A 21-year-old has trichomonas vaginitis. Treatment is prescribed. What is important to emphasize regarding partner treatment?
a: Partners need not be treated since trichomonas is not an STI
Both partners MUST be treated simultaneously (sexual partners notified and treated) — trichomonas is an STI; reinfection rate is high without partner treatment
Only treat if partner has symptoms
Use topical clotrimazole for both partners
D120.rationale: Trichomonas vaginalis: STI caused by flagellated protozoa. BOTH partners must be treated simultaneously (metronidazole 2g single dose or 500mg BID x 7 days) to prevent reinfection. In HIV+ women, 500mg BID x 7 days is preferred. **Board tip:** Trichomonas is the most common curable non-viral STI in the U.S. Men are usually asymptomatic. Trichomonas in women: frothy yellow-green discharge, strawberry cervix (punctate hemorrhages), pH >4.5. Metronidazole resistance is increasing — tinidazole 2g single dose for treatment failures.

D120.q: Which of the following is the MOST common bacterial STI in the United States?
a: Chlamydia — ~1.6 million reported cases annually (the most common notifiable STI)
D120.rationale: Chlamydia trachomatis is the most commonly reported notifiable disease in the United States. Approximately 1.6 million cases are reported annually, but true incidence is estimated at 4 million (due to significant underreporting from asymptomatic cases). Most cases are in young women 15-24 years old. **Board tip:** Chlamydia is called the 'silent epidemic' — 70-75% of infections in women are asymptomatic. This is why universal screening of sexually active women ≤24 is essential. Untreated: PID, infertility, ectopic pregnancy, reactive arthritis (Reiter's syndrome in males).

D120.q: HIV testing is recommended by USPSTF for which age group as a universal screen?
a: Only persons who report IV drug use or MSM
All adolescents and adults aged 15-65 as a routine universal screen (Grade A recommendation); younger adolescents and older adults if at increased risk
Women only — men have lower HIV risk
D120.rationale: USPSTF Grade A: Screen for HIV in adolescents and adults aged 15-65, and in all pregnant women. Persons at high risk (MSM, PWID, sex workers) should be screened more frequently (at least annually). Early detection allows antiretroviral therapy (ART) that suppresses viral load to undetectable and prevents transmission (U=U: Undetectable = Untransmittable). **Board tip:** U=U principle: people with HIV on effective ART with sustained undetectable viral load have effectively zero risk of sexual transmission. This is a major public health message for reducing HIV stigma and encouraging testing.

D120.q: A 17-year-old presents with a 1 cm painless genital ulcer. You are considering the differential. Which ulcer characteristic distinguishes syphilis from herpes and chancroid?
a: Syphilis chancre = painless, indurated, clean base, non-tender lymphadenopathy. Herpes = painful, multiple, vesicular → ulcers, tender lymphadenopathy. Chancroid = painful, purulent, undermined edges, tender suppurative lymphadenopathy (buboes)
D120.rationale: Genital ulcer differential: Syphilis (painless, firm, single, indurated) vs. Herpes (painful, multiple, preceded by vesicles) vs. Chancroid (H. ducreyi — painful with tender suppurative 'bubo' lymph nodes, rare in U.S.) vs. LGV (initial painless papule → painful inguinal lymphadenopathy). **Board tip:** In clinical practice, test for all three (RPR, HSV PCR, culture) because co-infection occurs. HIV testing always indicated with STI diagnosis. Donovanosis (granuloma inguinale): beefy-red painless ulcer, Klebsiella granulomatis, rare in U.S. — Donovan bodies on biopsy.

D120.q: When treating secondary syphilis (diffuse rash including palms/soles, flu-like symptoms), what is the treatment and how does it differ from primary syphilis treatment?
a: Oral doxycycline for secondary — IV penicillin for primary
Same treatment as primary: Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units IM single dose for primary AND secondary syphilis (early syphilis)
Doxycycline for 14 days instead of penicillin
Secondary syphilis requires 3 doses of Benzathine penicillin G (same as latent syphilis >1 year)
D120.rationale: Both primary and secondary (early) syphilis: Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units IM single dose is the treatment. Late latent or latent of unknown duration: 3 doses of Benzathine penicillin G weekly x 3 weeks. Neurosyphilis: IV aqueous penicillin G x 10-14 days. **Board tip:** Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction: fever, chills, headache 2-8 hours after penicillin treatment of early syphilis — not penicillin allergy; caused by cytokine release from spirochete killing. Treat with NSAIDs/acetaminophen. Warn patients especially if pregnant.

D120.q: An 80-year-old man has hypertension, atrial fibrillation, osteoarthritis, GERD, depression, and insomnia. He is on amlodipine, warfarin, naproxen, omeprazole, mirtazapine, and diphenhydramine (Benadryl). Which medication should be immediately discontinued per BEERS Criteria?
a: Diphenhydramine (Benadryl) — antihistamines are strongly anticholinergic, cause confusion, sedation, falls, urinary retention in elderly; BEERS Class A — avoid in older adults
D120.rationale: Beers Criteria (AGS): Diphenhydramine/antihistamines are STRONGLY anticholinergic medications to AVOID in older adults — causes confusion, excessive sedation, falls, urinary retention, constipation. **Board tip:** Other BEERS medications to avoid in elderly: benzodiazepines (fall risk, cognitive impairment), non-BZD hypnotics (Z-drugs — zolpidem), tricyclic antidepressants, muscle relaxants (cyclobenzaprine), anticholinergic bladder drugs, NSAIDs (GI bleed risk, fluid retention), meperidine, antipsychotics (stroke risk). The 'START/STOPP' criteria is another useful tool.

D120.q: Which validated tool is recommended by USPSTF for screening cognitive impairment in older adults and consists of a 30-question, 10-minute test assessing orientation, memory, language, and attention?
a: Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) — 30 points total, widely used, scores: 24-30 normal, 18-23 mild, 12-17 moderate, <12 severe impairment
Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) — 30 points, more sensitive for mild cognitive impairment
D120.rationale: MMSE: 30-point test assessing: orientation (10 pts), registration/recall (6 pts), attention/calculation (5 pts), language (8 pts), visuospatial (1 pt). Score <24 = cognitive impairment. SENSITIVITY for dementia: ~70-90%. **Board tip:** MoCA is MORE SENSITIVE than MMSE for mild cognitive impairment (MCI) — better at detecting early dementia in high-functioning individuals (college-educated). Both are used in practice: MMSE for following progression, MoCA for initial MCI screening. USPSTF states evidence is insufficient to recommend for or against universal dementia screening (2020).

D120.q: A 78-year-old woman has fallen twice in the past 6 months. What is the comprehensive falls risk assessment approach?
a: X-ray only to evaluate for fractures

Comprehensive assessment: medication review (polypharmacy), orthostatic BP, vision testing, gait and balance assessment (Timed Up and Go test), cognitive screen, home environment assessment, bone density for fracture risk
Tell her to use a cane and fall prevention is complete
D120.rationale: Falls risk assessment: USPSTF recommends exercise interventions for community-dwelling adults ≥65 with fall risk. Comprehensive multifactorial intervention: TUG test (≥12 seconds = high risk), orthostatic hypotension, medication review (eliminate Beers medications), vision correction, vitamin D supplementation, home safety assessment, and referral to PT for balance/strength training. **Board tip:** Timed Up and Go (TUG) test: >12 seconds = high fall risk. Vitamin D 800 IU/day reduces falls in deficient older adults. Major fall risk medications: benzodiazepines, antipsychotics, antihypertensives (orthostasis), sleep aids, anticholinergics.

D120.q: An 82-year-old patient with multiple comorbidities is on 11 medications. She presents with new confusion, falls, and urinary incontinence. What clinical approach addresses this?
a: Add medications to treat each new symptom separately

Conduct a medication reconciliation (brown bag review) — drug-drug interactions, cumulative anticholinergic burden, and unnecessary medications are likely contributing to new symptoms (polypharmacy cascade)
Assume these are new diseases and order extensive workup only
Refer to specialist for each symptom separately
D120.rationale: Polypharmacy (≥5 medications): very common in older adults, increases risk of adverse drug reactions, drug-drug interactions, falls, cognitive impairment, hospitalization. 'Prescribing cascade': new medication prescribed to treat side effect of another — cascade of new prescriptions. **Board tip:** Approach: Conduct 'brown bag' medication review (patient brings all medications), identify and deprescribe inappropriate medications using BEERS or STOPP criteria, review OTC medications and supplements (often overlooked). In geriatrics, less is often more — deprescribing is a therapeutic intervention.

D120.q: A 75-year-old woman is diagnosed with Alzheimer's dementia (mild stage). What pharmacologic treatment is FDA-approved for this stage?
a: Memantine (Namenda) — approved for moderate-severe Alzheimer's only
Donepezil (Aricept) — cholinesterase inhibitor approved for all stages of Alzheimer's; modest symptomatic benefit
No FDA-approved medications exist for early Alzheimer's
Amyloid antibody therapy only for late-stage
D120.rationale: Alzheimer's disease treatment: Cholinesterase inhibitors (donepezil, rivastigmine, galantamine) for mild-moderate AD. Memantine for moderate-severe. Combination (donepezil + memantine) for moderate-severe. Lecanemab (Leqembi) and donanemab: new anti-amyloid monoclonal antibodies FDA-approved for early/mild AD — modest disease modification. **Board tip:** Cholinesterase inhibitors: mechanism = inhibit acetylcholinesterase → more acetylcholine available (compensates for neuron loss). Side effects: nausea/vomiting, diarrhea, bradycardia (use caution in cardiac disease). Benefit is modest but real — treatment should not be withheld.

D120.q: Which screening test does USPSTF recommend for abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) and in which population?
a: Annual CT scan for all adults over 60
One-time screening abdominal ultrasound for men aged 65-75 who have ever smoked (≥100 lifetime cigarettes) — Grade B recommendation
Annual abdominal ultrasound for all adults over 65
No screening recommended — AAA is symptomatic when it ruptures
D120.rationale: USPSTF Grade B: One-time abdominal ultrasound screening for AAA in men aged 65-75 who have EVER smoked (≥100 cigarettes lifetime). AAA is largely asymptomatic until rupture (which has >90% mortality). Screening ultrasound is safe, cost-effective, and reduces AAA-related mortality. **Board tip:** AAA surveillance intervals: <3 cm = no surveillance; 3-3.9 cm = rescreen in 3 years; 4-4.9 cm = every 12 months; ≥5 cm = surgical referral. Surgical repair threshold: ≥5.5 cm in men, ≥5 cm in women, or rapid growth >0.5 cm in 6 months.

D120.q: An 80-year-old man has blood pressure 158/88. He has no symptoms and is currently on no medications. What is the current evidence-based approach to his hypertension?
a: No treatment needed — blood pressure over 140 is normal at age 80

The SPRINT trial supports treating systolic BP to a goal of <130 mmHg even in adults ≥75 with good functional status; balance benefits against risks (falls, orthostatic hypotension). Individualize goals based on frailty.
Aggressive treatment to 120/70 is the goal in all elderly
D120.rationale: Hypertension in elderly: AHA/ACC guidelines recommend BP target <130/80 for most adults (including fit elderly ≥65). SPRINT trial showed intensive control (SBP <120) reduced cardiovascular events and mortality in adults ≥75 with high CV risk. **Board tip:** In FRAIL elderly: less aggressive targets may be appropriate (individualize). Orthostatic hypotension and falls risk must be balanced against CV benefit. Start low, go slow. Preferred agents in elderly: thiazide diuretics, CCBs, ACE inhibitors/ARBs. Avoid high-dose beta-blockers as first-line.

D120.q: A 77-year-old woman is brought in by her daughter due to confusion that developed over 24 hours. She had a UTI treated last week, is on multiple medications, and seems 'not herself.' Mini-Cog shows significant impairment. What is the most likely diagnosis?
a: Delirium — acute, fluctuating confusion with a likely precipitating cause (UTI, medications, dehydration) — NOT dementia. Treat the underlying cause.
Stroke — MRI brain stat for all acute confusion
D120.rationale: Delirium: Acute onset, fluctuating course, inattention + disorganized thinking or altered consciousness. Key distinguishing feature from dementia: ACUTE onset and FLUCTUATING course. Precipitants (DELIRIUM mnemonic): Drugs, Electrolyte abnormalities, Lack of drugs (withdrawal), Infection, Reduced sensory input, Intracranial, Urinary/fecal retention, Myocardial/metabolic. **Board tip:** CAM (Confusion Assessment Method) is the gold-standard tool to diagnose delirium: acute onset + fluctuating course + inattention + either disorganized thinking OR altered consciousness. Delirium has high mortality (25-33%) in hospitalized elderly.

D120.q: An 82-year-old man reports urinary urgency, frequency, and nocturia 3x/night. This is affecting his sleep and quality of life. He denies incontinence. What is the first-line management for overactive bladder (OAB)?
a: Bladder training, scheduled voiding, pelvic floor exercises (Kegel), and fluid management — behavioral interventions are FIRST-LINE; pharmacotherapy if these fail (prefer beta-3 agonist mirabegron over anticholinergics in elderly)
D120.rationale: OAB management: First-line = behavioral therapy (bladder training, voiding schedule, fluid management, pelvic floor exercises). If pharmacotherapy needed: prefer MIRABEGRON (beta-3 adrenergic agonist) over anticholinergics (oxybutynin, tolterodine) in elderly — anticholinergics increase dementia risk and are on BEERS list. **Board tip:** BEERS criteria strongly advises AGAINST anticholinergic bladder agents (oxybutynin, tolterodine, solifenacin, darifenacin, fesoterodine) in adults ≥65. Mirabegron is preferred: no anticholinergic effects, safe in elderly. Botulinum toxin injection or sacral nerve modulation for refractory OAB.

D120.q: A 72-year-old woman has recently lost her husband of 45 years and presents with sadness, poor appetite, difficulty sleeping, and occasional thoughts that 'life is not worth living.' She denies active suicidal ideation. How should this be approached?
a: Grief is normal — no intervention needed, come back in 6 months

Assess for major depressive disorder (complicated grief) using PHQ-9; grief can trigger MDD requiring treatment. Provide bereavement support, consider therapy, and treat MDD if criteria met. Elderly suicide risk is high — reassess regularly.
D120.rationale: Grief vs. MDD: Grief is normal but can trigger major depressive disorder (MDD). Distinguish: grief is focused on loss, waves of sadness, may improve. MDD: persistent depressed mood for ≥2 weeks, anhedonia, affecting function. Elderly men are the highest-risk group for suicide completion. PHQ-9 screening essential. **Board tip:** Elderly depression is frequently undetected. PHQ-9 is validated for elderly. Treatment: psychotherapy (CBT, grief therapy) + antidepressant (SSRIs preferred in elderly — sertraline, escitalopram). Avoid TCAs in elderly (cardiac side effects, anticholinergic effects).

D120.q: An 85-year-old woman with advanced dementia is admitted with aspiration pneumonia — her third hospitalization in 6 months. Her daughter, listed as healthcare proxy, insists on 'everything done.' What is the appropriate response?
a: Always do everything requested by family

Explore the patient's previously expressed wishes (advance directives), discuss goals of care with the daughter (distinguishing between life-sustaining treatments vs. comfort-focused care), and clarify what 'everything' means to the family
Immediately initiate hospice without discussing with family
D120.rationale: Goals of care conversations: Essential in geriatric primary care. Key elements: review advance directives/POLST, clarify patient's previously expressed values, educate family about disease trajectory (advanced dementia is a terminal illness), discuss burdens vs. benefits of interventions (hospitalization, tube feeding — evidence shows harm in advanced dementia). **Board tip:** Tube feeding in advanced dementia: Multiple RCTs show tube feeding does NOT improve survival, prevent aspiration, improve quality of life, or reduce pressure ulcers. Careful hand feeding is preferred. This is a critical, board-tested fact about advanced dementia management.

D120.q: A 70-year-old man with new diagnosis of type 2 diabetes has an A1C of 8.1%. What is the appropriate A1C target for this patient?
a: A1C <7.5-8% is an appropriate target for older adults with moderate life expectancy and multiple comorbidities — less stringent targets reduce hypoglycemia risk (which is especially dangerous in elderly)
<9% — only treat if A1C is above 9%
D120.rationale: Diabetes management in elderly: ADA recommends individualized A1C targets. Healthy elderly (good functional status, long life expectancy): <7-7.5%. Complex/intermediate (multiple chronic conditions, early cognitive impairment): <8%. Very complex/poor health: <8.5-9%. **Board tip:** In elderly, hypoglycemia is MORE dangerous than in younger adults — falls, cardiac events, cognitive deterioration. Avoid sulfonylureas in elderly (hypoglycemia risk). Preferred agents: metformin (if tolerated), SGLT2i (CV benefit), GLP-1 agonist, or basal insulin with careful titration.

D120.q: The FRAIL scale assesses frailty in older adults. Which five components does it measure?
a: Falls, Renal function, Age, Illness, Loss of weight
Fatigue, Resistance (ability to climb stairs), Ambulation (ability to walk a block), Illness (5+ comorbidities), Loss of weight (>5%)
Fasting glucose, Renal function, Anemia, Inflammation, Low albumin
Fear, Resistance to care, Activity limitation, Irritability, Loss of memory
D120.rationale: FRAIL scale: Fatigue, Resistance (stairs), Ambulation (blocks), Illness (≥5 chronic conditions), Loss of weight (>5%). Score: 0 = robust; 1-2 = pre-frail; 3-5 = frail. Frailty is associated with adverse health outcomes (hospitalization, falls, disability, mortality). **Board tip:** Fried Frailty Phenotype (more complex): weakness, slow walking speed, exhaustion, low physical activity, unintentional weight loss. Any 3+ = frail. 1-2 = pre-frail. Frailty assessment should influence treatment decisions and goals of care.

D120.q: An 80-year-old woman is newly prescribed a proton pump inhibitor (PPI) for GERD. What long-term monitoring concern should be addressed?
a: PPIs cause kidney failure after 1 month

Long-term PPI use (>1 year) is associated with: magnesium deficiency, vitamin B12 deficiency, Clostridioides difficile infection risk, bone fracture risk (calcium absorption), and hyponatremia — use lowest effective dose and reassess need annually
PPIs increase cardiac risk in elderly
D120.rationale: Long-term PPI concerns: hypomagnesemia (monitor Mg2+ in patients on diuretics or digoxin), vitamin B12 deficiency (reduced absorption), C. diff risk, osteoporosis/hip fracture (impaired calcium absorption). In elderly: use lowest effective dose, 'step-down' to H2 blocker or PRN use when possible. **Board tip:** PPIs are one of the most overprescribed medication classes. Many patients prescribed PPIs in hospital continue indefinitely without indication. Reassess annually: is there an active indication? Can the patient use H2 blocker instead? Appropriate long-term use: Barrett's esophagus, severe GERD, prophylaxis during NSAID use.

D120.q: Urinary incontinence (UI) affects 30-60% of older women. Which type presents as involuntary leakage with cough, sneeze, or physical activity?
a: Urge incontinence — strong urge precedes leakage
Stress incontinence — weakened pelvic floor muscles/urethral sphincter allow leakage with increased intra-abdominal pressure. Treatment: pelvic floor muscle exercises (Kegel), weight loss, pessary
Functional incontinence — inability to reach toilet in time
D120.rationale: Stress urinary incontinence: Most common type in younger and middle-aged women. Caused by pelvic floor laxity, urethral hypermobility from childbirth, obesity, aging. Leakage with cough, sneeze, exercise, laugh. Treatment: Kegel exercises (PFMT), weight loss, duloxetine (off-label), or surgical sling. **Board tip:** Incontinence types: Stress = leaks with physical activity; Urge = OAB, strong urge; Overflow = continuous dribbling, large post-void residual (benign prostatic hyperplasia in men); Functional = immobility, cognitive impairment prevents toileting. Mixed UI (stress + urge) is most common in older women.

D120.q: An older adult patient mentions she has been feeling isolated and lonely since her husband died and her children moved away. What is the health impact of social isolation in older adults?
a: Social isolation has no clinically significant health effects

Social isolation in older adults is associated with equivalent mortality risk to smoking 15 cigarettes/day, and is linked to increased risk of dementia (50% increase), depression, cardiovascular disease, and premature death — address at every visit
Social isolation only affects mental health, not physical health
Loneliness is a normal part of aging — no intervention needed
D120.rationale: Social isolation and loneliness: Recognized as a major public health concern (U.S. Surgeon General advisory 2023). Associated with: 50% increased dementia risk, 29% increased heart disease, 32% increased stroke risk, and mortality equivalent to smoking. Interventions: community programs, senior centers, telehealth for isolated patients, faith communities, volunteer programs. **Board tip:** Screen for social isolation at geriatric visits (UCLA Loneliness Scale or simple questions). Address at every visit. Refer to community resources. Social prescribing (connecting patients to community activities) is an emerging evidence-based approach.

D120.q: An 85-year-old man on warfarin (INR therapeutic at 2.3) for atrial fibrillation needs a hip replacement. His CHA2DS2-VASc score is 5. What is the appropriate perioperative management?
a: Stop warfarin 24 hours before surgery — no bridging needed

Hold warfarin 5 days before surgery; bridge with LMWH (enoxaparin) if high thromboembolic risk (CHA2DS2-VASc ≥5). Discuss risk/benefit of perioperative bridging (increased bleeding risk vs. stroke prevention) with surgical team.
D120.rationale: Perioperative anticoagulation: Hold warfarin 5 days before major surgery. CHA2DS2-VASc ≥5 (high thromboembolic risk) may warrant LMWH bridging — but recent studies (BRIDGE trial) showed bridging in AFIB did NOT reduce thromboembolism but INCREASED bleeding. Individualize decision with surgical team. **Board tip:** CHA2DS2-VASc score: CHF (1), Hypertension (1), Age ≥75 (2), Diabetes (1), Stroke/TIA (2), Vascular disease (1), Age 65-74 (1), Sex Category female (1). Score ≥2 in men, ≥3 in women = anticoagulation recommended.

D120.q: A 68-year-old woman asks about vaccines recommended for older adults. Which vaccines are recommended for all adults ≥65?
a: Annual influenza (inactivated), COVID-19 (updated annually), high-dose or adjuvanted influenza vaccine preferred ≥65, pneumococcal (PCV20 or PCV15+PPSV23 series), Tdap (if not previously vaccinated), zoster (Shingrix — 2-dose recombinant at age 50+)
No additional vaccines — childhood vaccines are sufficient
D120.rationale: Vaccines for adults ≥65: Annual flu (high-dose Fluzone or adjuvanted Fluad preferred ≥65 — 4x antibody response), COVID-19 (updated annually), Pneumococcal (PCV20 preferred — one dose, or PCV15 followed by PPSV23), Shingrix (recombinant zoster vaccine 2 doses 2-6 months apart, starting at age 50 — 97% efficacy ≥50 years), and Tdap if not previously given as adult. **Board tip:** Shingrix (RZV) is >97% effective vs. 51% for Zostavax (no longer available in U.S.). Shingrix replaces Zostavax. Even if had natural shingles or received Zostavax — still get Shingrix. Pneumococcal: PCV20 (Prevnar 20) is now the preferred single-dose option.

D120.q: What is the MOST important single intervention to reduce the overall burden of disease in older adults, according to geriatric population health research?
a: Prescribing more medications to control individual diseases

Advance care planning (ACP) — discussing and documenting patient goals, values, and preferences for future medical care (POLST/MOLST forms, healthcare proxy designation) — reduces unwanted aggressive interventions, reduces hospitalization, and improves quality of life and death
D120.rationale: Advance care planning (ACP): Discussing and documenting goals of care, naming a healthcare proxy, and completing POLST (Portable Medical Orders for Life-Sustaining Treatment) significantly improves end-of-life care quality, reduces unwanted aggressive interventions, and is associated with better quality of death. **Board tip:** POLST/MOLST is a medical order (signed by provider) — valid across healthcare settings. Different from advance directive (legal document). Every provider caring for adults ≥65 or with serious illness should initiate ACP conversations. Ask at every annual visit: 'Have you thought about who would make medical decisions for you if you couldn't?'

D120.q: A 74-year-old man has a serum creatinine of 1.4 mg/dL. His estimated GFR (CKD-EPI) is 42 mL/min. How should this affect his medication management?
a: This is normal for his age — no medication adjustment needed

eGFR 30-44 = CKD Stage 3b — dose-adjust renally cleared medications (metformin hold if eGFR <30, antibiotics adjust doses, NSAIDs avoid, SGLT2i reduce efficacy <45); monitor renal function every 3-6 months
No medication adjustments needed until dialysis is required
D120.rationale: CKD staging and medication management: eGFR 42 = CKD Stage 3b. Key medication adjustments: metformin (hold if eGFR <30, use caution 30-45), NSAIDs (avoid — worsen CKD), SGLT2i (efficacy reduced below eGFR 45), direct oral anticoagulants (dose adjust by drug and eGFR), aminoglycosides (avoid), antibiotics (dose adjust many). **Board tip:** Many elderly patients have 'normal' serum creatinine with reduced GFR due to decreased muscle mass (less creatinine production). ALWAYS calculate eGFR using CKD-EPI formula — do NOT rely on creatinine alone in elderly. This is why Cockcroft-Gault formula is also used for medication dosing.

D120.q: A 55-year-old man has a PSA of 5.2 ng/mL. He is asymptomatic. He is interested in prostate cancer screening. What is the current USPSTF recommendation on PSA screening?
a: PSA screening is absolutely contraindicated — causes more harm than good

For men aged 55-69: shared decision-making — discuss benefits (early detection) and harms (false positives, biopsy complications, overtreatment) of PSA screening. For men ≥70: recommend AGAINST routine PSA screening (Grade D).
PSA screening is mandatory annually for all men ≥40
PSA ≤4.0 ng/mL is always normal — no further action needed
D120.rationale: USPSTF (2018): PSA screening for men 55-69: Grade C — shared decision-making. Men ≥70: Grade D — recommend against. PSA has significant limitations: many false positives leading to unnecessary biopsies (complications: bleeding, infection, erectile dysfunction, incontinence), and overdiagnosis of low-risk cancers. **Board tip:** PSA >4 ng/mL often prompts biopsy but is NOT diagnostic alone. PSA velocity (rapid rise over time) and free PSA % are additional considerations. Refer to urology for PSA 4-10 ng/mL or PSA velocity >0.75 ng/mL/year for consideration of biopsy.

D120.q: A 52-year-old man complains of decreased libido, erectile dysfunction, fatigue, and loss of muscle mass. Total testosterone is 220 ng/dL (normal >300). What is the diagnosis and treatment?
a: Normal aging — testosterone varies; no treatment warranted

Hypogonadism — confirm with two morning testosterone levels (<300 ng/dL) + LH/FSH; treat with testosterone replacement therapy (TRT) — topical gel, patch, or IM injection; monitor hemoglobin, PSA, LH/FSH
Start PDE-5 inhibitor for ED only
D120.rationale: Male hypogonadism diagnosis: Two morning total testosterone levels <300 ng/dL (labs should be 8-10am as testosterone peaks in the morning) + symptoms. Causes: primary (hypergonadotropic — elevated LH/FSH, testicular failure) vs. secondary (hypogonadotropic — low/normal LH/FSH, hypothalamic-pituitary cause). TRT forms: topical gel (daily), IM testosterone cypionate or enanthate (every 2 weeks), or subcutaneous pellets. **Board tip:** TRT monitoring: testosterone level (goal: mid-normal range), hematocrit (polycythemia risk), PSA, DRE. Contraindications: prostate cancer, breast cancer, polycythemia, untreated sleep apnea. TRT causes azoospermia — discuss fertility if patient desires children.

D120.q: A 64-year-old man has BPH with lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS): urinary frequency, weak stream, hesitancy, and nocturia 3x/night. IPSS score is 18 (moderate). He has no obstructive uropathy. What is the initial pharmacologic treatment?
a: Finasteride alone (5-alpha reductase inhibitor) for all BPH
Alpha-1 blocker (tamsulosin, alfuzosin, silodosin) for quick symptom relief — work within days; combine with 5-ARI (finasteride) for large prostate (>40g) or high PSA for additive benefit
Antibiotics — BPH is caused by infection
Immediate transurethral resection of the prostate (TURP)
D120.rationale: BPH pharmacotherapy: Alpha-1 blockers (tamsulosin, alfuzosin, silodosin) relax smooth muscle in prostate/bladder neck — work within days, don't reduce prostate size. 5-ARI (finasteride, dutasteride) reduce prostate size 20-30% over 6 months — better for large prostates, reduce progression. Combination (alpha-blocker + 5-ARI) for moderate-severe symptoms with large prostate. **Board tip:** Tamsulosin side effects: retrograde ejaculation (urine-ejaculate mixing), orthostatic hypotension. 5-ARI side effects: sexual dysfunction (decreased libido, ED), gynecomastia; also REDUCE PSA by 50% (adjust interpretation). TURP is gold-standard surgical treatment for refractory BPH.

D120.q: A 45-year-old man requests help for erectile dysfunction (ED). He smokes, has hypertension and hyperlipidemia on amlodipine and atorvastatin. What is the first step in evaluation?
a: Evaluate for cardiovascular risk — ED is often an early marker of atherosclerosis/endothelial dysfunction. Check fasting glucose, lipids, testosterone, PSA. Lifestyle modification (smoking cessation, exercise) before or alongside PDE-5 inhibitor therapy.
Testosterone testing is the first step for all ED patients
D120.rationale: ED evaluation: IMPORTANT — ED is a cardiovascular risk equivalent. Men with new ED have 3x higher risk of future cardiac event. Evaluate: cardiovascular risk factors (HTN, DM, smoking, dyslipidemia), testosterone (low T causes ED), psychosocial factors, medication side effects (beta-blockers, antidepressants, antihypertensives cause ED). **Board tip:** PDE-5 inhibitors (sildenafil/Viagra, tadalafil/Cialis, vardenafil): first-line for ED. Absolute contraindication: nitrates (causes severe hypotension). Tadalafil 5mg daily is also FDA-approved for BPH (dual benefit for men with both conditions).

D120.q: Testicular cancer is the most common solid tumor in men aged 15-35. Which examination is recommended for early detection?
a: Annual PSA testing in young men
Monthly testicular self-examination (TSE) is recommended for all young men — soft, painless swelling of a testicle, new hardness, or heaviness warrants immediate evaluation with testicular ultrasound
USPSTF recommends against routine TSE — testicular cancer screening has net harm
D120.rationale: Testicular cancer: Rare overall but leading cancer in males 15-35. Classic presentation: painless testicular swelling or mass. Risk factors: cryptorchidism (10x increased risk), Klinefelter syndrome, family history. Evaluation: testicular ultrasound (first-line imaging), tumor markers (AFP, beta-hCG, LDH). Treatment: orchiectomy (inguinal approach). **Board tip:** USPSTF states insufficient evidence for routine TSE screening in asymptomatic adolescents/adults. However, education about TSE and prompt evaluation of testicular symptoms is widely recommended. Any testicular mass = ultrasound first (never biopsy through scrotal approach — risk of lymphatic spread to inguinal nodes).

D120.q: A 62-year-old man with a 45-pack-year smoking history currently smokes 1 ppd. He is worried about lung cancer. What screening does USPSTF recommend?
a: Chest X-ray annually — effective and low-cost
Annual low-dose CT (LDCT) chest for adults aged 50-80 who have a 20-pack-year history and currently smoke or quit within the past 15 years (USPSTF 2021, Grade B)
No lung cancer screening is effective
D120.rationale: USPSTF (2021) lung cancer screening: Annual LDCT for adults 50-80 years with ≥20 pack-year history who currently smoke OR quit within past 15 years. NLST and NELSON trials: LDCT reduces lung cancer mortality by 20-24%. Discontinue screening if patient has not smoked for >15 years or develops health condition limiting life expectancy. **Board tip:** Updated 2021 criteria expanded from 2013 (age 55-80, 30 pack-years) to age 50-80 and 20 pack-years. This significantly increases screening eligibility. Smoking cessation counseling must accompany screening discussions.

D120.q: A 58-year-old man with hyperlipidemia asks about his cardiovascular risk. He has no history of CVD events. Total cholesterol 220, LDL 145, HDL 38, BP 134/82, and non-smoker. According to ASCVD risk calculator, his 10-year risk is 9%. What is the management?
a: No statin needed — risk is below 10%

Borderline risk (7.5-10%): shared decision-making; consider risk-enhancing factors. ACC/AHA threshold for statin therapy in primary prevention: ≥10% 10-year ASCVD risk (moderate-high intensity statin). At 9%, discuss lifestyle modification and consider statin if risk-enhancing factors present.
D120.rationale: ACC/AHA 2019 guidelines: Statin therapy in primary prevention for adults with LDL ≥70 mg/dL: High-risk (≥20%): high-intensity statin. Intermediate risk (7.5-19.9%): moderate-intensity statin recommended. Borderline (5-7.4%): consider statin with risk-enhancing factors. Low (<5%): lifestyle only. **Board tip:** Risk-enhancing factors that favor statin: family history premature ASCVD, LDL ≥160, metabolic syndrome, CKD, elevated hsCRP, elevated Lp(a), ABI <0.9. If uncertain: coronary artery calcium (CAC) scoring can help guide decision. Aspirin for primary prevention: USPSTF 2022 recommends AGAINST initiating aspirin for primary CVD prevention in adults ≥60 years.

D120.q: A 50-year-old man is diagnosed with obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) after polysomnography shows AHI of 28 (moderate-severe). What is the primary treatment?
a: Weight loss alone is curative — no device needed

Continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) therapy — gold standard treatment for moderate-severe OSA. Reduces AHI, improves daytime sleepiness, reduces cardiovascular risk (hypertension, atrial fibrillation, stroke).
D120.rationale: OSA management: CPAP is the gold standard for moderate-severe OSA (AHI ≥15). Benefits: resolves hypoxemia, reduces daytime sleepiness, reduces cardiovascular risk, improves insulin sensitivity. Alternatives for mild OSA or CPAP intolerance: mandibular advancement device, positional therapy (positional OSA), weight loss (if obese). **Board tip:** CPAP compliance (≥4 hours/night ≥70% of nights) is the key challenge. Adherence assessment at follow-up visits. OSA is strongly associated with: obesity, hypertension (resistant HTN), atrial fibrillation, type 2 diabetes, nocturnal angina. Screen with STOP-BANG questionnaire.

D120.q: A 48-year-old man is found to have chlamydia during an STI screen. His last sexual contact was a female partner 2 weeks ago. Per public health reporting requirements, what must occur?
a: Chlamydia is a mandatorily reportable STI — report to local/state health department. Provide partner notification services (or give patient expedited partner therapy — EPT — where legal) to treat all recent partners.
Only report if the patient has symptoms
Report only to the patient's primary care physician
D120.rationale: STI reporting: Chlamydia, gonorrhea, syphilis, HIV, and other STIs are MANDATORILY reportable to local/state health departments. Partner notification (contact tracing) is essential to prevent ongoing transmission. EPT (Expedited Partner Therapy): provider gives prescription/medication for patient to deliver to partner — legal in most states, reduces reinfection. **Board tip:** Healthcare providers are legally required to report specific communicable diseases. Failure to report is both a legal and public health failure. Patient confidentiality is maintained through anonymous reporting protocols. EPT is particularly important for gonorrhea and chlamydia — studies show it reduces reinfection rates.

D120.q: Which lifestyle modification has the MOST impact on improving erectile dysfunction in men who are overweight and physically inactive?
a: Regular aerobic exercise and weight loss — shown in multiple RCTs to improve erectile function significantly, comparable to pharmacotherapy in men with metabolic syndrome and obesity
D120.rationale: Exercise for ED: Aerobic exercise 40 minutes, 4x/week significantly improves erectile function in overweight men, those with CVD, hypertension, and metabolic syndrome. Weight loss of 10% body weight improves testosterone levels and ED. Exercise reduces endothelial dysfunction — the underlying vascular mechanism of ED in most men. **Board tip:** Address cardiovascular risk factors FIRST in men with ED — hypertension, dyslipidemia, smoking, diabetes, and physical inactivity are all treatable contributors. ED is a 'canary in the coal mine' for cardiovascular disease (penile vessels are smaller than coronary arteries — symptoms appear first in penis, then heart).

D120.q: A 45-year-old male athlete is using anabolic androgenic steroids (AAS) purchased online for muscle building. What are the serious medical consequences he should be counseled about?
a: AAS are safe when used under physician supervision only — no risks

AAS abuse causes: testicular atrophy and azoospermia (temporary or permanent infertility), hypogonadism after cessation, left ventricular hypertrophy (cardiomyopathy), elevated hematocrit (thrombosis risk), dyslipidemia, liver toxicity (oral AAS), acne, and psychiatric effects (roid rage, depression)
Only weight gain is a concern
Anabolic steroids are too weak to cause harm
D120.rationale: AAS abuse consequences: Reproductive (testicular atrophy, azoospermia, reduced LH/FSH), Cardiovascular (LVH, dilated cardiomyopathy, sudden death, dyslipidemia — decreased HDL, elevated LDL), Hematologic (erythrocytosis), Hepatic (oral AAS cause peliosis hepatis, hepatocellular carcinoma), Dermatologic (severe acne, alopecia), Psychiatric (aggression, mood swings, depression with cessation). **Board tip:** Performance-enhancing drug use is common but underreported. Ask non-judgmentally in sports physicals. AAS are Schedule III controlled substances. Post-AAS hypogonadism: suppressed HPG axis needs months to years to recover.

D120.q: A 38-year-old man and his partner of 3 years are having difficulty conceiving after 12 months of unprotected intercourse. What is the evaluation for male factor infertility?
a: Semen analysis is the only test ever needed

Semen analysis is the first-line test: ≥15 million sperm/mL, ≥40% motility, ≥4% normal morphology (WHO 2010). If abnormal: repeat in 4-6 weeks, hormonal panel (FSH, LH, testosterone, prolactin), scrotal ultrasound, referral to reproductive urology.
D120.rationale: Male infertility evaluation: Semen analysis is the cornerstone (WHO 2010 reference values: concentration ≥16M/mL, motility ≥42%, morphology ≥4% normal). Male factor contributes to ~50% of infertility cases (alone or combined). If abnormal: repeat in 4-6 weeks (significant day-to-day variability), then hormonal evaluation (azoospermia + high FSH = primary testicular failure; azoospermia + low FSH = hypogonadotropic hypogonadism — treatable). **Board tip:** Male infertility causes: varicocele (most common correctable cause), cryptorchidism, Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY), hormonal (low T, elevated prolactin), genetic (Y chromosome microdeletions), obstructive (vasectomy, cystic fibrosis-related absence of vas deferens).

D120.q: Which of the following is the most common cancer in American men?
a: Prostate cancer — most common cancer in American men (excluding skin cancer); second leading cause of cancer death in men (after lung cancer)
D120.rationale: Prostate cancer: Most common cancer in American men (estimated 300,000 new cases/year) but NOT the leading cause of cancer death (lung cancer kills more). Most prostate cancers are slow-growing and indolent. Gleason score/ISUP grade determines aggressiveness. **Board tip:** Prostate cancer racial disparity: Black men have 2x higher incidence and 2x higher mortality than white men — likely start PSA screening conversations at age 40-45 for Black men. Family history of prostate, breast, or ovarian cancer (BRCA1/2 mutations) also increases risk and warrants earlier discussion.

D120.q: A 35-year-old man presents with painful scrotal swelling, dysuria, and urethral discharge. He is sexually active with multiple partners. Exam shows epididymis tenderness. What is the most likely cause and treatment?
a: Epididymitis/orchitis — likely sexually transmitted (Chlamydia trachomatis, Neisseria gonorrhoeae in sexually active men <35). Treat: ceftriaxone 500mg IM x1 + doxycycline 100mg BID x 10 days. Must distinguish from torsion.
D120.rationale: Epididymitis in sexually active men <35: STI-related (GC/chlamydia most common). Treatment: ceftriaxone + doxycycline. In older men (>35): E. coli/gram-negatives (urinary tract organisms) — treat with fluoroquinolone or TMP-SMX. **Board tip:** Distinguish from testicular torsion (surgical emergency): torsion = sudden severe pain, absent cremasteric reflex, abnormal testicular lie; Prehn's sign (pain relief with elevation) is POSITIVE in epididymitis, NEGATIVE in torsion. Any suspicion for torsion = immediate urologic consultation. Torsion window: 6 hours for testicular salvage.

D120.q: A 42-year-old man on testosterone replacement therapy (TRT) for 2 years presents for follow-up. His hematocrit is 55%. What is the appropriate response?
a: This is expected on TRT — continue unchanged

Hematocrit ≥54% (52% if high cardiovascular risk): withhold or reduce TRT dose until hematocrit normalizes. TRT-induced erythrocytosis increases risk of thrombosis (DVT, PE, stroke). Consider phlebotomy.
Switch to a different testosterone formulation immediately
D120.rationale: TRT monitoring: Check hematocrit at 3-6 months, then annually. Polycythemia (Hct ≥54%) is the most common serious adverse effect of TRT — increases blood viscosity and thromboembolism risk. Management: hold TRT until Hct normalizes, reduce dose, change formulation (IM injections cause higher peaks than topical), or therapeutic phlebotomy. **Board tip:** TRT monitoring checklist: testosterone level (mid-normal range goal), hematocrit, PSA (rise >1.4 ng/mL/year = urologic evaluation), liver function (oral androgens only), lipids, and mood assessment. TRT does NOT increase prostate cancer risk in men without existing cancer.

D120.q: A 30-year-old woman asks about Pap smear screening. What is the current USPSTF recommendation for cervical cancer screening?
a: Annual Pap smear starting at age 18
Cytology alone (Pap) every 3 years for ages 21-29; HPV/cytology co-test every 5 years (or Pap alone every 3 years) for ages 30-65. Discontinue at age 65 if adequate prior negative screening.
Pap smear every 5 years starting at age 30 only
Annual Pap smear for all sexually active women
D120.rationale: USPSTF cervical cancer screening (2018): Ages 21-29: cytology alone every 3 years. Ages 30-65: cytology every 3 years OR hrHPV testing alone every 5 years OR co-testing (Pap + hrHPV) every 5 years — any of the three is acceptable. Discontinue at 65 with adequate prior screening (3 consecutive negative cytology OR 2 consecutive negative co-tests within last 10 years, most recent within 5 years). **Board tip:** Screen regardless of sexual activity history (HPV can persist for years). Do NOT screen women <21. Do NOT screen women who have had total hysterectomy for benign disease with no history of CIN2+.

D120.q: An HPV/cytology co-test returns: Pap = ASCUS (atypical squamous cells of undetermined significance), HPV = positive for high-risk HPV. What is the appropriate management?
a: Colposcopy — ASCUS with positive high-risk HPV is managed the same as LSIL (colposcopy indicated)
D120.rationale: ASCCP 2019 guidelines: ASCUS + positive hrHPV = colposcopy preferred (equivalent to LSIL). ASCUS + negative HPV = routine screening in 3 years (HPV-negative ASCUS has very low cancer risk). **Board tip:** Risk-based management: ASCUS alone (no reflex HPV) → reflex HPV testing. HPV-positive ASCUS = same risk as LSIL → colposcopy. HPV16/18 positive (regardless of cytology) → colposcopy. This ASCCP 2019 risk-based management replaced the older 'results-based' tables — know the basic pathways.

D120.q: What is the USPSTF recommendation for breast cancer screening with mammography in average-risk women?
a: Annual mammogram starting at age 40 for all women
Biennial mammogram for ages 40-74 (USPSTF 2024 updated to start at age 40, down from 50) — individualize based on patient values and risk
MRI instead of mammogram for all women
D120.rationale: USPSTF 2024 update: Biennial mammography recommended for women aged 40-74 (updated from previous recommendation to start at age 50). Ages 75+: insufficient evidence. Dense breast tissue: may benefit from supplemental screening (ultrasound or MRI) — patient notification of breast density is required in most states. **Board tip:** ACS recommends annual mammogram starting at 40 (or 45 based on patient choice). USPSTF uses biennial. Key distinction for boards: USPSTF Grade B (ages 40-74, biennial) vs ACS (annual at 40). High-risk women (BRCA1/2, family history): Annual MRI + mammogram starting at 30.

D120.q: USPSTF recommendations for colorectal cancer (CRC) screening — at what age should screening begin for average-risk adults?
a: Age 45 for all average-risk adults (USPSTF 2021, lowered from 50) — multiple screening modalities available: colonoscopy every 10 years (gold standard), FIT annually, CT colonography every 5 years, stool DNA (Cologuard) every 1-3 years
Age 40 — screen early to find all polyps
D120.rationale: USPSTF 2021: Start CRC screening at age 45 (Grade B) for average-risk adults, continue through age 75. Ages 76-85: individualize based on health status. Ages >85: recommend against screening. Colonoscopy every 10 years is the gold standard (therapeutic and diagnostic). **Board tip:** High-risk screening (earlier start): personal/family history of CRC or adenomas (start at 40 or 10 years before youngest affected relative), Lynch syndrome (start at 20-25), FAP (start at 10-12 years). IBD (UC, Crohn's): start 8-10 years after diagnosis, every 1-2 years.

D120.q: BRCA1/2 genetic testing: Which patients should be offered BRCA counseling and testing per USPSTF?
a: Women with personal or family history suggesting hereditary breast/ovarian cancer syndrome (HBOC): first-degree relative with BRCA mutation, breast cancer diagnosed ≤50, bilateral breast cancer, male breast cancer, ovarian cancer, Ashkenazi Jewish heritage with breast/ovarian cancer history
Only women who have had breast cancer
No genetic testing — it causes anxiety
D120.rationale: USPSTF (2019) recommends: Refer women with family history suggesting hereditary breast/ovarian cancer for genetic counseling, and offer BRCA1/2 testing if appropriate. Risk assessment tools (Ontario Family History Assessment Tool, Family History Screen 7) help identify who needs referral. **Board tip:** BRCA1 mutation: 55-65% lifetime breast cancer risk, 39-46% ovarian cancer risk. BRCA2: 45-55% breast, 10-27% ovarian. Options for BRCA+ women: enhanced surveillance (annual MRI + mammogram), chemoprevention (tamoxifen, raloxifene), or risk-reducing surgery (mastectomy, salpingo-oophorectomy).

D120.q: A 52-year-old woman asks about ovarian cancer screening. What is the USPSTF recommendation?
a: Annual CA-125 and pelvic ultrasound for all women ≥40
USPSTF recommends AGAINST routine ovarian cancer screening in average-risk women (Grade D) — benefits do not outweigh harms (false positives leading to unnecessary surgery)
Annual transvaginal ultrasound for all postmenopausal women
Ovarian cancer screening is highly effective and should be universal
D120.rationale: USPSTF Grade D: Do NOT routinely screen average-risk women for ovarian cancer. Existing screening tools (CA-125, TVUS) have not been shown to reduce ovarian cancer mortality and cause significant harm (false positives → unnecessary oophorectomy → surgical complications, premature menopause). **Board tip:** CA-125: NOT a good screening test. It is better used for monitoring known ovarian cancer treatment response. Elevated in many benign conditions (endometriosis, fibroids, peritonitis, pregnancy). BRCA1/2 carriers may benefit from risk-reducing bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy after childbearing (not routine screening).

D120.q: A 35-year-old woman has never had an abnormal Pap smear and had a negative co-test at age 33. She asks if she can skip her next Pap smear. What is the appropriate response?
a: She can stop screening permanently if she has had two negative tests
With two consecutive negative co-tests, her next co-test is due at age 38 (5-year interval) — she does not need to be screened before then
She should have annual Pap smears regardless of prior results
She needs an HPV vaccine booster before her next Pap
D120.rationale: Co-testing (Pap + HPV) every 5 years for women 30-65 is an USPSTF Grade A recommendation. With a negative co-test at 33, the next screening is due at 38. Rescreening earlier provides no additional benefit and leads to unnecessary follow-up tests. **Board tip:** Extended intervals with co-testing are safe because: negative hrHPV dramatically lowers 5-year CIN3+ risk (<0.3%). Women who have not had HPV vaccination still benefit from vaccination up to age 26 (reducing future HPV exposure) but vaccination status does NOT change current screening intervals.

D120.q: Which modality is recommended for colorectal cancer screening for patients who DECLINE colonoscopy?
a: Fecal immunochemical test (FIT) annually is an acceptable first-line screening option — positive FIT requires follow-up diagnostic colonoscopy
Digital rectal exam annually is sufficient
D120.rationale: CRC screening alternatives to colonoscopy: FIT (fecal immunochemical test) annually — highly acceptable (non-invasive, home test), sensitive for CRC (74-79%), less sensitive for advanced adenomas. Positive FIT → diagnostic colonoscopy. Cologuard (stool DNA FIT) every 1-3 years — more sensitive but higher false positive rate. CT colonography every 5 years — non-invasive but radiation, bowel prep required. **Board tip:** Patient adherence matters most — the best test is the one the patient will actually do. Engage in shared decision-making about screening method. FIT is preferred for population-level adherence campaigns due to low burden.

D120.q: A 29-year-old sexually active woman with no prior Pap smears asks if she should have a Pap test today. What is the correct response?
a: Yes — sexually active women should be screened annually

No Pap smear until age 21 regardless of sexual activity onset (USPSTF Grade D for women <21) — HPV infection in young women typically clears spontaneously and treating young women causes more harm than benefit
D120.rationale: Wait — this is a 29-year-old. She should have a Pap smear. Ages 21-29: cytology (Pap) alone every 3 years. She should be screened today. If her last screening was within 3 years and normal, she can defer. But if never screened, she should be screened now. **Board tip:** The critical board point is: Do NOT screen women UNDER 21, regardless of sexual activity. Starting at 21, cytology every 3 years. At 30-65: option to switch to co-testing every 5 years or continue cytology every 3 years. Women immunocompromised (HIV+): start at sexual debut, screen more frequently.

D120.q: A 60-year-old woman has no family history of cancer, has never smoked, and is a healthy BMI. Which cancer screenings are indicated at this visit?
a: No cancer screening needed at age 60

Mammogram (biennial), Pap/HPV co-test (if not screened in 5 years), colorectal cancer screening (colonoscopy or FIT), and DEXA scan. Also: skin cancer awareness counseling, lung CT if 20 pack-year smoking history.
Annual CT of chest, abdomen, pelvis
D120.rationale: Standard cancer screenings at 60: Mammogram (biennial, USPSTF; or annual, ACS), cervical (co-test every 5 years or cytology every 3 years through age 65), CRC (continue through age 75), skin cancer awareness. No routine ovarian, thyroid, or pancreatic cancer screening. Lung CT: only if 20+ pack-year history. DEXA: all women ≥65 (or earlier if fracture risk). **Board tip:** USPSTF screening summary card: know Grade A and B recommendations. Grade A = recommend (breast cancer genetic risk referral, colorectal, cervical, HIV, lung CT in smokers). Grade D = recommend against (ovarian, prostate PSA ≥70, testicular).

D120.q: A postmenopausal woman has abnormal uterine bleeding. What is the initial evaluation?
a: Reassure — bleeding is common in menopause

Any postmenopausal bleeding is ABNORMAL until proven otherwise — evaluate with transvaginal ultrasound (endometrial stripe <4mm = low risk) AND endometrial biopsy (or office hysteroscopy with biopsy) to rule out endometrial hyperplasia/cancer
Prescribe estrogen — it is atrophic vaginitis
D120.rationale: Postmenopausal bleeding (PMB): most common cause is endometrial atrophy (benign), but endometrial cancer must be ruled out. Endometrial cancer is the most common gynecologic cancer in the U.S. Evaluation: TVS (endometrial thickness) AND tissue sampling (endometrial biopsy or hysteroscopy). **Board tip:** Endometrial cancer risk factors: obesity (excess estrogen from adipose), unopposed estrogen HT, polycystic ovary syndrome, diabetes, hypertension, nulliparity, tamoxifen use, Lynch syndrome. All postmenopausal bleeding → evaluate. Never attribute to atrophy without workup.

D120.q: Skin cancer is the most common cancer in the U.S. What USPSTF recommendation exists for skin cancer screening?
a: Annual full-body skin examination for all adults

USPSTF has insufficient evidence for routine skin cancer screening in average-risk adults (I statement) — however, counsel all patients about sun protection, self-examination, and evaluate suspicious lesions promptly
Routine screening is strongly recommended for all adults ≥40
D120.rationale: USPSTF: Insufficient evidence (I statement) to recommend for or against routine skin cancer screening in asymptomatic adults. However, PRIMARY PREVENTION counseling (sunscreen, protective clothing, avoiding tanning beds) in children, adolescents, and young adults (6 months to 24 years, and adults 24-64 with fair skin) is recommended. **Board tip:** Refer promptly for: changing mole (ABCDE: Asymmetry, Border irregularity, Color variation, Diameter >6mm, Evolution). Melanoma: surgical excision with appropriate margins. Basal cell and squamous cell carcinoma: very common, rarely metastatic, highly treatable with early detection.

D120.q: A 58-year-old woman with a BMI of 32 (obese) is concerned about her endometrial cancer risk. Obesity increases endometrial cancer risk through which mechanism?
a: Peripheral aromatization of androgens to estrogen in adipose tissue causes unopposed estrogen stimulation of the endometrium, increasing hyperplasia and cancer risk
D120.rationale: Endometrial cancer: Obesity is the #1 modifiable risk factor. Adipose tissue converts androgens to estrone (via aromatase enzyme) — this creates an 'estrogenic environment' causing endometrial stimulation without progesterone opposition (similar to unopposed estrogen HT). 10-unit increase in BMI increases EC risk by 30-40%. **Board tip:** Obese postmenopausal women are at significantly elevated risk for endometrial cancer. Weight loss reduces risk. No routine screening exists, but low threshold for biopsy in obese women with ANY abnormal bleeding. Progestin-only therapy (IUD or oral) can reduce risk in women at high risk who cannot have surgery.

D120.q: A Lynch syndrome (hereditary non-polyposis colorectal cancer — HNPCC) diagnosis is identified in a 32-year-old woman. What screening recommendations apply?
a: Same as average-risk guidelines — start at 45

Colonoscopy every 1-2 years starting at age 20-25 (or 5 years earlier than youngest affected relative), AND annual endometrial biopsy/sampling starting at 30-35 years, AND consider aspirin chemoprevention
No screening — Lynch syndrome only affects men
D120.rationale: Lynch syndrome (MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PMS2, EPCAM mutations): Colonoscopy every 1-2 years starting at 20-25 years. Endometrial/ovarian: annual endometrial sampling from 30-35; consider risk-reducing hysterectomy + bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy after childbearing. Gastric: upper endoscopy in high-risk ethnic groups. Urinary tract: annual urinalysis. **Board tip:** Lynch syndrome is the most common hereditary CRC syndrome (1/280 people carry Lynch gene variants). Aspirin 600mg/day for 2 years reduces Lynch syndrome CRC risk (CAPP2 trial). Refer all Lynch families for genetic counseling and cascade testing.

D120.q: A 48-year-old woman has a first-degree relative (sister) diagnosed with breast cancer at age 42. She is Ashkenazi Jewish. What screening modifications are appropriate?
a: No modification — USPSTF average-risk recommendations apply

Annual mammogram starting at age 40 (or 10 years before sister's diagnosis = age 32, whichever is earlier), consider MRI supplemental screening, and refer for BRCA genetic counseling and testing given Ashkenazi Jewish heritage + family history
